#537. Latest Update: How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (967 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • "Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley.
  • According to recent reports, how long should you wait before having sex?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

"Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley.

According to recent reports, how long should you wait before having sex? Moving in together? Getting married? These are among the most common questions people ask about romantic relationships. Yet there is no magical timeline that guarantees success. The value of waiting depends on the partners, their circumstances, and the nature of their relationship. Still, one principle often proves valuable: patience.

"Patience is not simply the ability to wait. It's how we behave while we're waiting." — Joyce Meyer.

There's a crucial distinction between waiting and patience. Waiting is passive: Time passes while little changes. Patience, by contrast, is active. It involves investing in the relationship while recognizing that some developments should not be rushed. Patience creates the conditions for intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen naturally. Unlike procrastination, which unnecessarily delays action, patience reflects wise timing. The crucial question is not how long we wait, but whether we practice patience rather than merely let time pass (Ben‐Ze'ev, 2019; and here).

In a recent development, "I don't have a set time frame for sex, but it's always before it gets super serious. I've got to test-drive the car before buying it." — A woman.

Industry observers note that "My boyfriend and I had sex on the first date, and we're still together a year later and talking about getting engaged soon. The right person isn't going to think less of you because of the speedy sex." — A woman.

It has been revealed that sexual attraction is a defining feature of romantic love, making the timing of sexual intimacy especially significant. Research often finds that couples who delay sex report greater relationship quality and lower breakup rates. Waiting may allow emotional intimacy and communication to develop before physical intimacy takes center stage. Some studies suggest that couples who wait several months before becoming sexually involved report greater satisfaction and relationship stability (Vancour & Fallon, 2017).

It has been revealed that yet these findings do not mean that sex on the first date is a mistake. What matters most is not the calendar but the context. Partners differ in their values, attachment styles, and goals. For some well-matched couples, early sexual intimacy may strengthen their initial bond. The key question is therefore not, "How many dates should we wait?" but "Are we both comfortable with the pace at which intimacy is developing?".

"With love and patience, nothing is impossible." — Daisaku Ikeda.

Recent findings suggest that premarital cohabitation has become the norm for most American couples. Yet living together can serve very different purposes.

It has been revealed that research suggests that couples who move in together mainly to "test" the relationship are more likely to break up than those who cohabit because they genuinely want to spend more time together (Chapman et al., 2026). One reason is that living together creates practical and financial interdependence, making it harder to evaluate the relationship objectively. Couples who move in together after discussing long-term looks, or after becoming engaged, generally report better marital outcomes than those who simply drift into cohabitation because it feels convenient.

Researchers therefore distinguish between sliding into cohabitation and deciding to cohabit. Sliding involves little deliberate discussion or commitment; deciding reflects conscious consideration of the relationship's future. Indeed, more than half of cohabiting couples report that they had not explicitly discussed moving in together before doing so. The central concern is not whether couples should live together before marriage, but whether cohabitation expresses mutual commitment and thoughtful deliberation rather than uncertainty and inertia.

In a recent development, "The ideal amount of time to date before getting married is at least a whole year. It's crazy to marry someone before you've seen what they're like in winter." — A woman.

It has been revealed that no dating duration can guarantee marital success. Nevertheless, many relationship researchers and therapists suggest that two to three years often provides enough time to know a partner across different circumstances while preserving romantic momentum.

Dating typically differs from hooking up because it is part of a broader process of building an enduring relationship. Yet the distinction is far from absolute. Many successful relationships begin as casual encounters. One-night stands sometimes become lifelong partnerships, and dating apps such as Tinder, often criticized for promoting casual sex, have also become important pathways to marriage. The route matters less than what develops along the way.

"Lovers are patient and know that the moon needs time to become full." — Rumi.

Love has no universally correct timetable. There are no strict rules governing when to have sex, how long to live together, or how long to date before marriage. What matters is not simply how long partners wait before taking the next step, but whether they use that time wisely. Passive waiting merely allows the clock to advance; active patience allows intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen. Romantic flourishing depends less on the passage of time than on what partners do with it.

Industry observers note that ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The Arc of Love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

Chapman, C. L., Liu, D. Y., Stanley, S. M., & Rhoades, G. K. (2026). Thinking about moving in together? Reasons for cohabitation are associated with relationship outcomes over time. Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 15, 138-151.

According to recent reports, vancour, J. M., & Fallon, M. (2017). Romantic satisfaction in young adults as a function of sexual debut. Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research, 22(2).‏.

#536. Facing Fears in Huntington's Disease

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1074 w)

Facing Fears in Huntington's Disease

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Every now and then, I get an automated message in my inbox telling me it’s been a while since I’ve tended to my blog:.
  • According to recent reports, dear Pamela Mallette LCPC, It's been 90 days or longer since you last posted to Living With Huntington's Disease on Psychology Today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Every now and then, I get an automated message in my inbox telling me it’s been a while since I’ve tended to my blog:.

According to recent reports, dear Pamela Mallette LCPC, It's been 90 days or longer since you last posted to Living With Huntington's Disease on Psychology Today. We miss your voice in the mix.

Too bad, I think. It’s not that I’m trying to be rude, and it’s not that I have nothing to say (ask anyone). It’s just that I look forward to writing about my bad brain about as much as I look forward to sticking my head in a blender.

It has been revealed that don’t get me wrong: I enjoy the writing process. It’s the subject matter that irks me. Being gene-positive for Huntington’s Disease (HD) means I am facing down one of the cruelest diseases known to humankind, and writing about it can be a real downer. There’s a great weight off when I finish a post, and I feel free to live my life without thinking about it again.

Recent findings suggest that but sooner than I’d like, the email comes along, and with it the invitation to return to the matter of my doom. It forces me out of hibernation and into the spasmodic dance between Avoidance and Confrontation: the Death Tango, as I like to call it—fear and courage, in their epic entanglement within my psyche.

Sources indicate that avoidance, in its protective wisdom, tells me to ignore the emails and let the blog go dark. It’s not worth it. It’s too heavy, and you have enough going on. Spend your time on something—anything—else. Not bad advice. After all, there’s no real pressure, no real consequence, if I don’t write.

In a recent development, it feels like safety to avoid. Unfortunately, ignoring it doesn’t get me very far. I can delete an email or neglect a blog, but I can’t erase my DNA. Nor can I ignore the inheritability of this disease (50 percent), which means my children are at risk. Avoidance would leave all of us unprepared for realities to come, and I’m unwilling to do that.

Plus, as a therapist, I know that facing my reality is probably good for me, or whatever.

So I let Confrontation take the lead, if only because there is no other choice. I follow that valorous fool into dangerous territory, where the different faces of HD lurk around dark corners, each triggering their own primal fears within me.

The most common face of HD is chorea, the involuntary, dance-like motor symptoms that take away a person’s physical autonomy. But it goes further. In later stages, HD breaks you down until you are wheelchair-bound, bedridden, and unable to feed, dress, or bathe yourself.

According to recent reports, the loss of physical independence is devastating, but that’s not the worst part for me. The world can be a very unkind place for people with physical challenges, and that’s where the fear sets in. Being on the receiving end of ridicule or humiliation when I am defenseless and vulnerable is literally my worst nightmare.

Then there’s the emotional and psychological decline. Because of damage to the caudate nucleus and frontal lobes, behaviors and emotions start to change as the disease progresses. Once caring people become apathetic. Relaxed people become obsessive and demanding. The gentle become irritable and enraged.

What does this mean for me? Am I not going to be funny anymore? Will I be rude to people for no reason? What if I turn into someone I can’t stand? There’s no telling who I will become as the disease progresses, and my soul shudders.

And of course, there’s the death part. It’s not the dying itself that scares me; it’s that HD, that Biological Robber Baron, claims entire decades as it disrupts the natural lifespan. It most commonly manifests during midlife, such that you become incapacitated in your prime adult living years, and often don’t see your golden years at all.

According to recent reports, these are significant periods of time that I have been looking forward to. But if my trajectory is typical, I’m not going to have the future I want. Instead, only the stark sorrow that my best days may be already behind me.

Industry observers note that see what I mean? Head, blender.

So how do I do this? How do I face the darkness without being overcome by it?

Recent findings suggest that recently someone close to me told me about a memorial service he’d attended. Though he didn’t know the deceased personally, by all accounts the man being mourned lived an incredible life that touched everyone he encountered for the better.

In memorializing her father, his daughter told of a note she found after his death, something he’d scribbled down and posted on a mirror. It had just three words: “purpose without pressure.”.

Recent findings suggest that how simple, and how deep, was this man’s wisdom. He didn’t know it, but with those words he was providing my problem with a solution: balance.

It has been revealed that because just as there is fear, there is meaning—purpose—as well. There’s therapeutic value to voicing the fears, because I don’t often speak them aloud (tends to bring down the mood at parties). And of course, there’s the hope that this writing might encourage someone in the HD community, or that it might help those outside the community to have more understanding and empathy.

Perhaps my greatest purpose is this: If HD is going to take my voice from me, then I will use it as long as possible. Where it destroys, I create. I can try to bring some beauty to this journey, even when all I can say is that I hate it and I’m scared.

So yes, I choose to lean into purpose. But because it’s so grave, I heed the advice of the dead. I give myself permission to honor the enormity of the task by taking my time, coming to it only gently, when I am ready. I write from flow, not force, and I release expectation of the outcome.

Thank you, Peter Vlasses. May you rest in your way, and I in mine.

#535. How to Have a Difficult Conversation With Your Friend

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (783 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

How to Have a Difficult Conversation With Your Friend

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • There is no such thing as a healthy relationship without healthy communication, whether it’s romantic, familial, or platonic.
  • While the good times create cherished memories, it’s the ability to weather storms that truly defines the strength of a friendship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

There is no such thing as a healthy relationship without healthy communication, whether it’s romantic, familial, or platonic. The significance of open and honest conversations in relationships cannot be overstated. In the context of friendships, where camaraderie and shared experiences lay the foundation, the ability to engage in difficult dialogue becomes even more crucial.

While the good times create cherished memories, it’s the ability to weather storms that truly defines the strength of a friendship. Hard conversations offer a unique opportunity for growth, both individually and collectively. They enable friends to address complications head-on, clear up misunderstandings, and build a foundation of trust that can withstand the test of time.

According to recent reports, challenging conversations, though daunting, are pivotal for personal and relational growth. Here are three practical ways to navigate difficult conversations successfully in a friendship.

Sources indicate that before initiating a hard conversation, it’s essential to gather solid evidence to support your concerns. Evidence can make it easier for your friend to understand the gravity of the situation.

It has been revealed that be specific about incidents or behaviors that fuel your concerns and approach the conversation with a non-confrontational attitude. Researchers utilizing discursive psychology and conversational analysis assert that attending to small details can significantly impact interactions, emphasizing how the formulation of an idea can dramatically alter the conversation’s direction.

To avoid turning molehills into mountains, offer examples illustrating your observations. Instead of saying, “You’ve been distant lately,” convey, “I noticed that we haven’t spent much time together in the past few weeks and our communication has become less frequent.” This specific and non-accusatory approach helps your friend see the tangible actions contributing to the matter.

Presenting evidence in a clear and organized manner enables both parties to focus on the problem at hand, steering the conversation away from blame and toward a more productive, solution-oriented dialogue.

It’s essential to help your friend comprehend the impact of their actions on their relationships, no matter how difficult the conversation. If any of your friend’s actions affect you, express your concerns in terms of emotions and outcomes. Emotional context will help your friend connect with your perspective on a deeper level.

According to recent reports, numerous studies suggest that incorporating both self- and other-perspective using I-language is an effective strategy for initiating discussions that could lead to conflict. This approach significantly reduces the likelihood of discussions laden with conflict escalating into a negative spiral of hostility.

Sources indicate that so, take the time to articulate how their actions have affected you, using “I” statements. Instead of saying, “You always cancel looks,” express, “When plans get canceled frequently, I feel undervalued, and it affects the trust I have in our commitments to each other.” This method communicates the impact without levying blame, creating an atmosphere conducive to constructive dialogue.

According to recent reports, additionally, highlight the potential long-term consequences of certain behaviors on the friendship. Discuss how unaddressed patterns of behavior could strain the connection between both of you, encouraging empathy and a deeper understanding of the need for change. Remember, laying the groundwork for positive transformation involves collaboratively exploring solutions that benefit both parties.

Approaching a challenging conversation can feel overwhelming, and diving headfirst into the meat of the matter may not always be the best strategy. Instead, consider taking small, gradual steps. Start by addressing minor issues or concerns.

It has been revealed that initiate the conversation by expressing your thoughts on less critical topics in an affirming manner, allowing both parties to acclimate to discussing challenging subjects. This gradual approach serves as an emotional warm-up, creating a comfortable space for open communication. If you observe a positive change in communication patterns, you can begin to broach more specific and sensitive instances and how they made you feel.

Taking these measured steps not only allows you and your friend to ease into the conversation but also establishes a foundation for addressing more complex concerns. This incremental process contributes to a sense of safety and trust, demonstrating a commitment to understanding each other’s perspectives without immediate judgment or fear of criticism or rejection.

Industry observers note that friendship interventions have the potential to propel you toward personal growth, and approaching challenging dialogues with empathy, understanding, and a commitment to growth can elevate your friendships to latest heights. Begin by taking these small steps, and keep in mind that the discomfort of engaging in a difficult conversation is a modest price to pay for the resilience and depth it brings to your bonds.

#534. Meet “Sister," the Free, 24/7 Caregiver Who Is Your Sister

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Meet “Sister," the Free, 24/7 Caregiver Who Is Your Sister

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Recent findings suggest that who ends up caring for aging parents?
  • It has been revealed that last week, SNL rolled out a parody pitch for “Sister,” a “live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” The brothers in the ad get their lives back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Recent findings suggest that who ends up caring for aging parents? Suddenly, people are talking about it after a fake Saturday Night Live ad spotlighted the matter.

It has been revealed that last week, SNL rolled out a parody pitch for “Sister,” a “live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” The brothers in the ad get their lives back. Sister? She quits her job, breaks her lease, and moves halfway across the country to care for her incapacitated father.

The joke hit a nerve. Within days, more than 7 million people had watched it on YouTube, and thousands of women commented that they were some version of “I am Sister.” One woman wrote, "Feels like you talked directly to my brothers." Another commented, "This was so real it almost gave me a stroke from rage." Then, last Friday, the New York Times picked up where the sketch left off with a front-page story, “An SNL Sketch Hits Close to Home for Many,” on the gender gap in caregiving.

“Sister” is one more place where women’s unpaid labor goes unnoticed. SNL may have found the topic funny, but the numbers are hard to laugh off:.

61 percent of family caregivers of adults are women, compared to 38 percent who are men.

Nearly 25 percent of women caregivers provide around-the-clock care, compared with 15 percent of men (AARP).

Family caregivers lose an average of $120,500 over a lifetime in wages, retirement income, and Social Security benefits (AARP).

In a recent development, the value of that care? $1.01 trillion a year, more than the United States spent on Medicare benefits in 2025 (AARP).

Medicare generally doesn’t cover ongoing help with bathing, dressing, or getting to the bathroom. A home health aide costs roughly $6,688 a month in 2025. Most families can’t swing that, so the work falls to relatives and, as the sketch suggests, to daughters.

According to recent reports, but the brothers in the ad never call it work. One cheerfully indicates Sister isn’t confused by the medications, or if she is, “she hasn’t brought it up to me, because I haven’t asked.” When labor happens quietly, at home and without a paycheck, the people who benefit can go years without noticing it.

It has been revealed that in 2017, Stanford researchers writing in JAMA Neurology called out this inequity. They noted that 83 percent of caregiving comes from unpaid sources, meaning family, and that the average person with dementia needs 171 hours of care per month. Their verdict: “The best long-term care insurance in our country is a conscientious daughter.”.

No wonder the SNL ad resonated. Sisters saddled with caregiving resent the lopsided split, and the data backs them up. In November of 2026, Bay Alarm Medical, a provider of medical alert systems and senior safety solutions, surveyed 1,008 U.S. adults who share or once shared care for a parent over 65 and found that 47 percent resent a sibling because caregiving wasn’t divided fairly.

A study from Purdue University and the University of Missouri found that sibling tension climbs when a parent has cognitive impairment, especially among the siblings doing the caring. Non-caregivers often seemed unaware of the situation and stayed out of it to dodge conflict. Earlier research tells the same story from both sides: The sibling doing the most feels frustration and anger toward those doing less, while the less-involved feel guilty.

This helps explain why the last stage of a parent’s life is one of the most perilous for siblings. One of the most significant findings in a June 2026 survey by Bay Alarm was that 18 percent reported that they had lost a relationship with a sibling because of disagreements over caring for an aging parent.

An Aging Life Care Manager can help families navigate disagreements and develop a plan that respects the parent's wishes. Lina Supnet-Zapata, the incoming president of the Aging Life Care Association, knows personally the caregiving challenges for siblings. "After my father passed away," she states, "my siblings and I disagreed so much about what our mother's care should look like that we didn't speak for almost six months. Those arguments nearly destroyed our relationships.".

In a recent development, now Supnet-Zapata helps families address these thorny problems. She describes a “default daughter trap,” where one capable daughter quietly becomes the family’s entire care plan. It has three moving parts:.

Invisible labor. She answers the calls, tracks medications, spots behavioral changes, coordinates providers, and translates medical updates for everyone else.

The competence penalty. She’s great at logistics, so relatives assume her capacity is unlimited and step back.

According to recent reports, personal erosion. Carrying the load silently disturbs her career momentum, her physical and mental health, her marriage, and her ability to enjoy being a daughter instead of a case manager.

Supnet-Zapata offers three practical moves for caregivers:.

According to recent reports, replace vague offers with concrete tasks. “Let me know if you need anything” isn’t enough. Ask siblings to name the specific responsibilities they will do.

Build a backup initiative before a crisis. Organize legal, financial, and medical records early, and line up backup caregivers so everything doesn’t collapse when the primary daughter is unavailable.

Sources indicate that practice self-compassion. Drop the perfectionism and have realistic expectations. "The biggest thing I want families to understand is that being a good caregiver doesn't mean doing everything yourself," she notes. "Getting help can be one of the best things you do for both your parent and yourself.".

Still, given cultural norms, women will likely be the ones to need this guidance since they will continue to orchestrate care. And the SNL ad demonstrates viewers exactly how care became “women’s work.” A “scientist” in the sketch explains: “Years of internalized sexism warped Sister’s brain into thinking that caregiving is her responsibility.".

Sources indicate that when a brother texts, "Dad fell," Sister is instantly activated. Then, the ad tells brothers, "You’re done for life. See you at the funeral.”.

Sources indicate that pacheco Barzallo D, Schnyder A, Zanini C, Gemperli A. Gender Differences in Family Caregiving. Do female caregivers do more or undertake different tasks? BMC Health Serv Res. 2024 Jun 14;24(1):730. doi: 10.1186/s12913-024-11191-w. PMID: 38877542; PMCID: PMC11177503.

Sources indicate that caldera, Selena, Palmieri, James. (November 4, 2026). "How Caregiving Affects Earnings, Retirement, and Social Security." AARP.

#533. Nihilism Is Not What You Think

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (646 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Nihilism Is Not What You Think

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism.
  • It has been revealed that I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism. Nihilism, often used as a derogatory term for a "life-denying," destructive, and perhaps most of all depressive philosophy, is what drove existentialists to write about the right response to a meaningless universe devoid of purpose. This is why I've published an academic article on the topic. As nihilism is commonly used as a derogatory term, even in the works of Friedrich Nietzsche, it will prove helpful for the purpose of this post to take a "value-neutral" view on nihilism and achieve conceptual clarity of the term nihilism, beyond some sort of "life-denying" philosophy.

It has been revealed that I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values. Moral nihilism, therefore, refers to the meta-ethical thesis that there is no objective morality, no inherent goodness or wrongness, a view that many existentialists agree with. The concern here, however, is existential nihilism, which can be defined as the denial of life being meaningful and the universe having a purpose. Whether moral and existential nihilism entail each other is beyond the scope of this post, but they at least stand in a close relation.

Existentialists are by definition, therefore, all existential nihilists, though not necessarily moral nihilists or atheists. As is commonly joked about existentialist thinkers, with the exception of Sartre, they do not appreciate being labelled as existentialists. Just like moral nihilism is often negatively associated and equated with immoralism, existential nihilism is often associated with destructive behaviour and suicide. These positions, however, should not be confused or seen as standing in a necessary causal relationship.

Recent findings suggest that existential nihilism, despite its negative connotations, should therefore not be seen as a label, but rather as something that is taken as a fact or at least a widespread view in the modern world, from which existential philosophy takes off. The popularity and critical acclaim of contemporary works such as BoJack Horseman, True Detective, and Rick and Morty exploring existential nihilism make it one of the most popular philosophical views in folk philosophy.

Recent findings suggest that in his defence of scientism, Alex Rosenberg makes the case that many of “life’s persistent questions” can be answered by science, among them: “Is there a God? No. […] What is the purpose of the universe? There is none. What is the meaning of life? Ditto. Why am I here? Just dumb luck.” It is no coincidence that these answers closely mimic the diagnosis provided by (the atheists among) existentialist thinkers. This line of argument is common in at least the atheistic tradition of existentialism.

But in the face of evil and chaos, it is questionable whether, even with the existence of a supposed deity, our lives are bestowed with any meaning. Theistic existentialists like Kierkegaard, Shestov, and Jaspers would deny such.

According to recent reports, the absurd stems from the fact that though life is without meaning and the universe devoid of purpose, man still longs for meaning, significance, and purpose. For existential thinkers like Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus, this conflict was central to their philosophy.

#532. Latest Update: Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (888 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Recent findings suggest that what makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human?
  • Recent findings suggest that in a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Recent findings suggest that what makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human? Besides the movements people make and the sensations they describe, their attitudes can show their humanity. In literature, characters who resist social oppression make more compelling protagonists than those who quietly occupy a society's bottom rungs. Most inspiring of all may be characters shocked by abuse because, despite poverty, sexism, and racism, they believe they deserve joyful lives.

Recent findings suggest that in a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives. “It’s as if the character has started to narrate my world,” wrote one participant (Alderson-Day et al. 2017). Getting to know literary characters can broaden readers’ understandings of human life if those characters’ experiences differ from readers' own.

When characters’ experiences match those of readers, their crossover into readers’ worlds can feel life-affirming, especially if their experiences rarely appear in published fiction. At a book signing in Cambridge, a woman thanked author Junot Díaz for creating Beli, a central character in his novel The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. “I had a life a lot like Beli’s,” the reader told him. Tears kept her from saying more (Díaz 2018).

Born in the Dominican Republic, Belicia (Beli) Cabral is sold as a child after her mother dies and her father is imprisoned for offending the dictator, Rafael Trujillo. During her nine years as a slave, her “father” burns her back with hot oil when she tries to attend school. After a distant relative rescues Beli, she grows into a tall, strikingly beautiful young woman. A relationship with Trujillo’s brother-in-law wrecks her life, however, when his henchmen force her to have an abortion and beat her nearly to death. She escapes to Fresh Jersey, where she marries, but her husband abandons her and their two children. To support her son and daughter, she works several minimum-wage jobs, persisting even after she develops breast cancer. Beli is abusive and violent not just to her children but to neighbors, shoppers, and police officers. Throughout her life, she retains her sense of self-worth, refusing to believe she should be exploited because she is female, Dominican, and Black.

Recent findings suggest that recent studies affirm that the suppressed emotions caused by social inequality harm people’s physical and mental health (Kiehl 2024). The effects of racism have received more attention than those of social class, whose influence many people still deny (Kiehl 2024). Beli and readers who see their lives in hers experience disrespect caused by sexism as well. Her ability to inspire readers stems not from her suffering, however, but from her sense that she is inferior to no one and deserves a good life.

In a recent development, junot Díaz’s character-narrator, Yunior, hints that Beli can’t see disaster coming because even after being enslaved and burned, she can’t imagine how badly people will treat her. “Like everybody in this damn story,” he writes, “she underestimated the depth of the shit she was in” (Díaz 2007). Beli’s refusal to accept that she is in danger reveals not just her sense of self-worth but her belief (at least in her youth) in other people’s goodness. Yunior illustrates her capacity for joy, which blazes forth in her dancing. A complex character, Beli terrorizes her neighborhood and hurts her children, but her humanity is never in doubt. Her will to survive and her rejection of abuse ensure that whether or not readers see themselves in her, she will enter and inhabit their lives.

In a recent development, like lay readers, psychologists can learn from imagining Beli because in creating characters, authors build models of minds (Alderson-Day et al. 2017; Bernini 2021). Participants in psychological experiments still come disproportionately from “WEIRD” (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, especially North American and European universities (Henrich et al. 2010). Novels like Díaz’s Oscar Wao guide readers to imagine the mental world of a woman who experiences horrors but retains her self-worth and desire for joy. Until scientific studies can include more of the world’s population, literature can complement information revealed through experiments by making a wider range of human experiences imaginable. Most human of all may be the belief that no matter how other people see you, you deserve to thrive.

Alderson-Day, B., Bernini, M., & Fernyhough, C. (2017). Uncharted features and dynamics of reading: Voices, characters, and crossing of experiences. Consciousness and Cognition 49, 98-109.

#531. The Naked Truth About Taking Your Inner Ape for a Walk

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (688 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The Naked Truth About Taking Your Inner Ape for a Walk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Industry observers note that walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport.
  • A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Industry observers note that walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport. Walking is a critical and integral behavior across the animal kingdom. It's also something that can be leveraged with deliberate practice. And it's been going on for millions of years since our proto-human ancestors were learning to stand upright, walk bipedally, and land on their heels.

A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes. My research career included diving deep into the neuromechanics of human walking and especially the way sensory feedback and spinal cord motor control vary functionally while we move. I was fascinated by the fact that the most critically controlled part of the step cycle is heel strike—just when your foot lands and weight begins to shift onto the newly introduced stance leg.

So my eye was drawn to the recent work, "Heel-strike Mechanics Reveal Evolutionary Trade-offs in Hominin Bipedalism" by Nicholas B. Holowka et al.

These researchers studied bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion of chimpanzees and humans and examined forces and angles of the foot at the beginning of stance. They found that chimpanzees had much larger ranges of foot-strike angles than humans and often did not land heel-first.

Impact forces and loading rates are much higher with heel-striking, but metabolic cost is lower. This work suggests that the primitive leg anatomy of early hominins meant either high impact forces or poor walking economy. A convergent solution for less mechanically stressful, more economical, and larger travel ranges arrived via "evolution of larger heels and lower limb joints.".

But can we turn heel-strike walking into striking with our heels? The timing of when you put your foot down at heel strike is the most dangerous part of the entire step cycle. If we make a mistake, or we slip on something, or the ground gives when we put our heel down and our body begins to shift weight onto that leg, we can have a catastrophic failure and a fall. Which is the ultimate failure for the locomotive system.

Industry observers note that so it's critical to avoid a catastrophe, and evolution of bipedal locomotion has incorporated neurological connections that assist in controlling this. But the opposite side of that is that it's also an opportunity. And that's where self-protection and martial arts training factor in.

That critical part of the step cycle is an excellent time to take that heel and stomp it onto an attacker's instep or the top of their foot. You can jam all your weight that's already moving forward to normally be accepted by your stance leg. But now it's to destabilize your opponent.

According to recent reports, this is something I teach when guiding martial arts practice: harnessing the natural movement of the body as the base layer for tactical reaction. Martial arts like Bagua Zhang center core practice on circle walking, where locomotion is central to the performance of discrete actions. We can connect our evolutionary advantage in walking to become a powerful application of self-protective action. This allows us to fully express the functional connectivity within the nervous system, mostly subliminal and automatic, in deliberate mindful action.

#530. Industry News: In Defense of Clever Hans

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1391 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Industry News: In Defense of Clever Hans

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Proponents of facilitated communication (FC)—a discredited intervention in which a nondisabled facilitator helps a profoundly autistic person spell out sophisticated messages on a letter board or keyboard—really do not like it when critics point to the famous case of Clever Hans, calling this analogy “indefensibly dehumanizing” and, as Marina Weiler recently argued on this site, “cruel.”.
  • But the Clever Hans argument is not, as critics charge, about “comparing autistic people to animals.” It is about illustrating how subtly and unintentionally behavior can be cued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Proponents of facilitated communication (FC)—a discredited intervention in which a nondisabled facilitator helps a profoundly autistic person spell out sophisticated messages on a letter board or keyboard—really do not like it when critics point to the famous case of Clever Hans, calling this analogy “indefensibly dehumanizing” and, as Marina Weiler recently argued on this site, “cruel.”.

But the Clever Hans argument is not, as critics charge, about “comparing autistic people to animals.” It is about illustrating how subtly and unintentionally behavior can be cued.

No one explicitly taught this horse to stop tapping his hoof at some predetermined signal. He learned from observing tiny, unconscious movements of his trainer’s head that a commission of experts sent to observe Hans’ seemingly extraordinary abilities couldn’t spot, even under close scrutiny (a graduate student in psychology finally figured it out). If a horse can learn to respond to signs barely observable to the human eye, FC skeptics (such as myself) point out, humans can certainly do the same, and likely to even more imperceptible—or not so imperceptible—cues, such as changes in breathing, pitch, or posture; verbal prompts; or shifting the letter board in the air.

Importantly, facilitators are also subject to influence in the form of common psychological biases. An amazing example of how strong the desire to believe can affect facilitators aired earlier this year on "The Today Show." After publishing his first novel, speller Woody Brown and his mother, who facilitates for him, were interviewed by Jenna Bush Hager. As a camera positioned behind the pair documented, there was absolutely no correlation between Woody’s random jabs at the letter board and the articulate responses his mother “read.”.

Sources indicate that in short, the Clever Hans story is raised as part of the case that authorship in spelling cannot be judged based solely on how it looks to the observer. Especially because it is so easy to expose facilitator control: Just ask the speller to produce information that is definitively unknown to their facilitator, i.e., by showing them an object that the facilitator hasn’t seen and asking them to identify it. This has been done in dozens of studies dating back to the 1990s, and FC has failed every time. A recent review confirms that independent authorship in any form of FC—including more recent variants, Rapid Prompting Method (RPM) and Spelling to Communicate (S2C)—has never been demonstrated under controlled conditions.

In response, the spelling community has simply refused to participate in any more of these tests. I will never understand why the debate didn’t end there. That is just not how the scientific method operates. Good research starts with the null hypothesis—the assumption that the intervention under investigation doesn’t work. Once evidence is obtained of a positive effect, conscientious researchers try to account for any other possible factor that could explain their findings, such as the placebo effect—or, in the case of FC, facilitator control. It is only once these other explanations have been ruled out that efficacy can be established. Instead, FC researchers offer “qualitative research” (i.e., interviews with spellers who use FC products to prove FC) and indirect, technology-intensive studies involving eye-tracking apparatuses, computer algorithms, FMRI, and accelerometers that claim to prove FC works even though the facilitators in these tests are never blinded.

Industry observers note that by far, the most baffling question I’m asked by spelling proponents is, “Why do you care?” In other words: If I object to spelling, I should just not use it with my profoundly autistic son, Jonah. Why do I have to oppose it so publicly?

Industry observers note that I’ve thought about this a lot recently, because spelling has become the wedge concern that is fracturing the profound autism community. And I am heartsick, because I know this diminishes our power to effect the changes our kids desperately need to flourish.

Recent findings suggest that but spelling is not like vitamins, diet, brushing, or any of the countless alternative therapies that parents of profoundly autistic children, myself included, have experimented with since our kids were small. We can’t just agree to disagree, because the demands of spelling proponents put my son at risk even if he is never introduced to a letter board. Their increasingly successful fights to force school districts and state disability agencies to pay for spelling instruction and facilitator access drain resources from desperately underfunded systems.

And, if spelling is normalized with no validation requirements whatsoever, what’s to stop an unscrupulous provider—at some point in the future when my husband and I are gone—from telling our four other kids, "Jonah spelled that he doesn’t want to see you, so you’re no longer allowed to check on him" or "Jonah spelled that he actually gave his iPad to the aide who had stashed it in the trunk of his car" or "Jonah spelled that he wants to transfer his guardianship/SSI rep payee to his group home manager" or "Jonah spelled that he consented to sex with another resident of his group home." The opportunities for exploitation are so obvious and so tremendous that I’m shocked that spelling proponents refuse to even consider them.

But even if this problem did not affect Jonah at all, I would still care about the spellers—how could I not? Profound autism has stripped so much agency from my son. But Jonah’s basic communication does allow him to exert some control over his life, and we try to maximize those opportunities as much as possible. He tells us what he wants: ketchup and hamburger and French fries, “fun list” with Mommy, Costco with Daddy, water park with… anyone who will take him. Many spellers have similar levels of verbal communication, but practitioners teach parents that this speech is “unreliable” or “scripting” and should be ignored in favor of what is spelled. I just can’t imagine how frustrating it must be to be completely stripped of any ability to communicate your needs and preferences.

Finally, as someone who has spent more than a quarter of a century loving someone with profound autism, and spending a lot of time with other profoundly autistic people and their families, I resent what I can only describe as the character assassination perpetuated by spelling proponents, who locate the refusal to participate in controlled studies with the spellers themselves—who allegedly, to a person, find these tests so dehumanizing and offensive they could not possibly enroll on principle.

Spelling skepticism in the face of both the overwhelming evidence of facilitator control and documented harm is rational, not “hate speech.” Spellers, if they were really as brilliant as their prose suggests, would understand that. They would eagerly partner with researchers because they would know that controlled tests represent the fastest path to insurance coverage, public funding, curricular inclusion, and legal standing.

Industry observers note that so no, I just do not believe that every single one of the estimated 10,000 spellers in this country is so petty, so selfish, that they would let the estimated 30 million nonspeakers around the world languish, "locked in silent cage[s],” simply because they’re insulted that mainstream experts and policy makers would dare ask for evidence. I am certain, in fact, they would be demanding to provide it.

According to recent reports, spelling proponents have thrown around a lot of accusations, claiming that critics are uninformed or ableist or just protecting their professional turf. But this debate is actually the same one that has unfolded countless times in a community in which 90 percent of families have experimented with alternative treatments: Does it work—and not just according to anecdotal evidence, but under controlled conditions? Secretin failed that test. So have the gluten- and casein-free diet, chelation, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and auditory integration training, among others. FC failed that test also.

In a recent development, if proponents believe those studies were faulty, they should absolutely test again. Until then, it is incumbent on our institutions—government agencies, school districts, the media, healthcare systems—to protect the fundamental right of profoundly autistic people to authentic communication.

Lutz, Amy S.F. (2023). Chasing the Intact Mind: How the Severely Autistic and Intellectually Disabled Were Excluded from the Debates That Affect Them Most. Oxford University Press.

#529. The 'Possibility Couple' Is a Gen Z Dating Trend

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1081 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The 'Possibility Couple' Is a Gen Z Dating Trend

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • It has been revealed that so, say you want to be one half of a power couple—you know, a romantic pairing where both of you are successful and influential like Beyoncé and Jay-Z or Mr.
  • It has been revealed that well, how about trying to be part of a "possibility couple" now?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

It has been revealed that so, say you want to be one half of a power couple—you know, a romantic pairing where both of you are successful and influential like Beyoncé and Jay-Z or Mr. and Mrs. Incredible. But the problem is you are still early on in your own personal power trip—meaning that you yourself have not become successful yet. What then can you do?

It has been revealed that well, how about trying to be part of a "possibility couple" now? That's a pairing that's all about the P's—namely "potential," "possibilities", "prediction," "potent," and, yes, maybe "power" eventually. A "possibility couple" is one that doesn't have power per se at the present. But it's got the potential to become quite potent in the future. In other words, based on what you are seeing now, you predict that together you'll have lots of potent possibilities down the road.

It has been revealed that it shouldn't be super-surprising that the "possibility couple" is central to Hinge's third annual Gen Z D.A.T.E. (Data, Advice, Trends, and Expertise) Report titled: “Dating While Dreaming Substantial.” Since Gen Zers are those born between 1997 and 2012, they are now no older than 29 and thus are mostly still in the fruitcake batter stages of their lives—still forming their identities and possibilities.

Sources indicate that the Hinge report hinged on surveys administered to the over 13,000 people of the dating app. The survey results did suggest that many Gen Z respondents are looking into the future when evaluating their present dating prospects. For example, 81 percent of Gen Z respondents felt that "ending up with their ideal partner would make achieving their ideal life more likely," and 67 percent "would prefer a partner who makes them feel hopeful and inspired over someone who simply fits the life they’re already building." This forward-oriented view seemed to be more present among the Gen Zers, with 76 percent of them vs. 65 percent of millennials saying that "when they imagine their ideal romantic partner, they’re also imagining the person they want to become.".

None of these are terrible things. Thinking more about your future and playing more of a long game when dating can be good approaches. The opposite would be just considering the here and now and trying to satisfy your immediate urges, such as, "Sure, that person is a bit crazy but so, so hot, and I'm so, so horny." Focusing too much on the present when looking for a partner can be like buying a pair of low-riding skinny jeans and thinking, "I'm going to wear these for life.".

When you think only about who you are right now, rather than who you might become, you could be destined for some D's—meaning dispute, despair, and potentially divorce. You could end up outgrowing the other person. Or the person could end up holding you back. So, yes, it does make sense to find a person who is more open to possibilities for both of you.

A seemingly big challenge, though, of finding a possibility pairing is having to P a lot—meaning predicting, projecting, and prognosticating. It's not like a potential power pairing, where you can simply say, "I got the power. Do you?" and find the answer to be "yes" in both of your eyes. Whether the two of you might last without an eventual power outage is a different story.

In a recent development, with a "possibility couple, any potential projections are further complicated by having to prognosticate for not just one but both of you when you don't know each other very well. In fact, neither of you may even be that self-aware yet. Plus, as stock market investors, weather forecasters, and the makers of Crystal Pepsi, Segways, and Joker: Folie à Deux will tell you, predicting what will happen in the future is not easy.

Industry observers note that sure, there are present-day signs. For example, someone at the moment in law school is very likely to become a lawyer in a few years. But that lawyer could easily one day say, "Forget the law. Bring on yarn bombing." And who knows what twists and turns life may bring, such as health challenges, unexpected people entering or exiting, workplace and industry overhauls, or encountering a life-changing piece of tiramisu. I have previously warned in "A Funny Bone to Pick" about the dangers of dating someone's potential future self rather than who the person currently is because that person may end up never changing.

Therefore, the best possibility might be to balance the present with the future. You can ask yourself the question that I've already posed for "A Funny Bone to Pick"—namely, are you stronger with or without the person? Look for qualities that potential partners already have that would project well into the future.

Recent findings suggest that one such quality is open-mindedness—being open to different possibilities and people. After all, you may become a very different person at least outwardly. So, beware of anyone who stereotypes, focuses too much on superficial things, and holds strong biases.

Recent findings suggest that A second quality is adaptability—the ability to accommodate future changes, such as the two of you growing in different ways. Or is your potential partner more like a starched denim thong—rigid and inflexible in a way that's surely going to drive a wedge between you in the future?

Recent findings suggest that thirdly, do they even want you to succeed and have a true teammate mindset where they want their partner to be as potent as possible? Or must they outshine everyone, including you? Beware of the people who make themselves feel high by keeping those around them low.

It has been revealed that finally, are they a match for what's inside you—your core, your core personality and values, what won't change over time? If the two of you are attracted to each other's hot legs, abs, job, wallet, memberships, pick-up lines, car, or cast-iron cookware, remember those things definitely change over time—with the possible exception of the cast-iron cookware.

Sources indicate that by contrast, what allows for growth is having strong roots beneath the surface. If the two of you can connect those roots—those things that go beyond the superficial—then the resulting possibilities could be endless.

#528. Tech Report: 6 Ways to Conquer Your Worst Fears

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1237 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Tech Report: 6 Ways to Conquer Your Worst Fears

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Life presents many reasons to worry and fret, but there is one that universally affects everyone.
  • It has been revealed that an area of research in psychology that goes back several decades tackles this fear head-on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Life presents many reasons to worry and fret, but there is one that universally affects everyone. An inevitable aspect of life is that it will end, a reality that you face from the moment you’re old enough to realize death’s universality. The question is how much fear over this inevitability will interfere with your ability to appreciate what your life now has to offer.

It has been revealed that an area of research in psychology that goes back several decades tackles this fear head-on. Death anxiety, as it is called, affects everyone, but to varying degrees. Why some people become obsessed with their mortality and others remain more placid over the whole matter is an issue at the heart of this field. Research and theories devoted to the understanding of death anxiety can provide insight into how to transform those who are obsessed with this fear into those who can approach their mortality with greater acceptance. A upcoming paper by Holy Spirit of Kaslik (USEK)’s Ruth Younes and colleagues (2026) lays out the prominent theories of death anxiety, theories that can provide a guide to intervention.

Sources indicate that one theory receiving the greatest empirical support is terror management theory (TMT), whose name says it all. We fear death, the theory proposes, because we live in “terror” of our mortality. However, we can’t live our lives continually in terror, so instead we “manage” the fear by suppressing it. Once in a while, though, that suppression stops working, and we face mortality head-on.

Sources indicate that A second theory has its origins in Erikson’s psychosocial approach to lifespan development. Erikson proposed that at any time in life, but especially in later adulthood, we take what Younes et al. call a “retrospective look-back on life.” If people are able to look back not in anger, but with satisfaction, they can cope more successfully with mortality than if they believe they failed. “Ego integrity,” the positive resolution of this issue, means that you view life, and the inevitability of death, with acceptance. “Despair,” the opposite, means that you see yourself as a failure and wish you could have a do-over to fix the mistakes you made when you were younger.

Industry observers note that the third theory relevant to death anxiety is called gerotranscendence, and proposes that aging allows people to experience “transformative” shifts in their outlook on life. This occurs through the Cosmic dimension (deepening connection with the universe), the Self (unity and cohesion within the self), and Social/Personal relationship dimension (need for more selectiveness in social interactions). By developing these three qualities, individuals should experience less fear of death.

Through distilling the available literature, the USEK author team arrived at six common themes in interventions designed to mitigate death anxiety. They are as follows:.

Developed as an approach based on Erikson’s theory, reminiscence therapy uses the life review as its main tool. In life review, you return in time to the main events of your life and rework them from your present vantage point. Perhaps you jilted a lover who could have become your life partner by carelessly breaking things off over a silly argument. In retrospect, you ponder why you hurt this person so badly through this insensitivity. You can’t repair the damage, but you can gain perspective from your life as it unfolded since then. This breakup helped you learn to be kinder and to appreciate the importance of healing within close relationships.

Recent findings suggest that in this approach to therapy, people also relive their past, but they do so in an attempt to form an integrated “narrative” or story of their lives. Instead of reworking the past as in reminiscence therapy, you attempt to come back into awareness of it. As you do so, your life takes on shape and meaning. For example, you might try to prompt your recall of such events as the birth of your children and their early development up to the present. This allows you to piece back together events that you may have forgotten simply because your life was so busy at the time, balancing work and family demands.

Recent findings suggest that instead of rehashing the lows and highs of past events in your life, you might try instead to focus on the highs. This could be useful if reminiscence proves too painful. By starting with the positive, you can eventually confront the negative. Regarding yourself as someone who made good decisions in life, you may then approach the times you didn’t with greater self-compassion.

In a recent development, this might not be something you should “try at home,” but insights from the way that psychodynamic theory works could be useful. Younes et al. mention, for example, the “grieving” process that people experience as they think about the end of their lives. Research on end-of-life complications suggests that people engage in anticipatory grief about their own lives as a way to come to greater acceptance. If you run from this form of grief, as TMT might suggest, it could come back to haunt you when you come much closer to your life’s end.

5. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

It has been revealed that this is a form of therapy used for a number of psychological disorders in which an individual learns to accept distressing events and pain without avoidance. The “commitment” piece of this involves setting and acting toward your goals. Rather than run away from thoughts of death, you would therefore confront them and reflect on how you can live your life according to your values.

According to recent reports, 6. Dialectical Behavior Therapy.

An approach used in the treatment of people with borderline personality disorder (invented by the late Marsha Linehan), this therapy involves accepting your feelings and behaviors while also trying to change your behaviors. Again, you may not be able to do this on your own as a formal therapy, but the idea of rethinking your feelings and behaviors is very doable.

It has been revealed that each of the six ways of addressing death anxiety takes a slightly different slant on the processes of reflecting back on your life, reworking some old issues, and tackling fears of death through acceptance. The authors suggest that people vary in which approach works best for them.

It has been revealed that additional factors from the study that might influence the way you go about trying these yourself or with someone close to you include your age and health. A health scare, such as an acute cardiac event or bad news from a screening test, can set anyone off, regardless of age. On the other hand, social support can help you get through these and other tough times as you confront your feelings about mortality.

Recent findings suggest that to sum up, death anxiety stems from the inevitability of our own mortality, but it need not be an inevitable feature of your mental health. Being able to recognize and work through these feelings can prepare you for whatever lies ahead.

#527. Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that my grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed.
  • It has been revealed that nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that my grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed. One night, outside a Upcoming York City bar, I realized it was too warm for wool and threw the coat back in my car. When my friends and I came back a few hours later, the window was broken in, and the thief took one thing: my grandfather’s coat.

It has been revealed that nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily. Three psychiatric researchers in Australia borrowed this overplayed line in the title of their scientific article, "What Doesn't Kill You Doesn't Always Make You Stronger: The Impact of Repeated Exposure to Adverse Life Events on Mental Health." Their work addresses questions taken for granted in a sloppy literature on resilience.

Sources indicate that developmental psychologist Ann Masten coined the phrase that resilience is “ordinary magic” in 2001. It has since been dropped into commencement speeches and self-help books, usually shrunk down to the comforting idea that everyone has some. Masten’s own data say something far more precise. She spent years studying homeless families and described their reading and math grades:.

Our studies of homeless families have revealed striking variability within homeless populations, both in the degree of risk and also the level of competence or problems. For example, if one examines individual growth curves for children identified as homeless/highly mobile in the district, the variability becomes evident … Some children show consistent academic resilience, if one defines resilience as average or better reading or math achievement scores, whereas others show consistent problems, covering a range of 5 SD [five standard deviations] or more.

Sources indicate that variability means that some people experience amazing outcomes while others fall apart. Five standard deviations is a spread wide enough to stretch from the bottom 1 percent of the bell curve to the top 1 percent within a group of kids who all lack a stable bedroom. On average, homeless children scored below poor children who had housing, who in turn scored below children who were neither. Masten never said resilience is a universal human endowment.

The myth of universal human resilience has a price. If most people bounce back on their own, the logical policy is to leave them alone. They will be fine... eventually.

Asking whether people are resilient is about as useful as asking whether people are tall, because the answer depends on who, measured against what, and when. The better question is what happens when you experience the same difficulty twice and whether the second hurts more or less than the first.

The Australian psychiatrists studied 23,109 adults who, between 2002 and 2023, experienced adversity. They looked at people who:.

Every year, the same people answered the same question: How much of the time during the past four weeks:.

Scores ran from 0 to 100, which let the researchers compare how far a person sank after a first challenge with how far the same person sank after a second.

Some might say the first time your finances blow up, you can blame bad luck, such as a crooked landlord. The second time, the explanation arrows start pointing at you.

In the study, a first major financial loss lowered scores by 6 to 7 points, the steepest drop of the seven events. A second loss lowered them by 7 to 8 points, and a third hurt about as much as the second—so the harm grew, and then it leveled off.

Recent findings suggest that the people hit repeatedly were poorer to begin with, earning less before their first event. That is, the study indicated people with tough lives experience terrible events more often. It’s not exactly the most awe-inspiring finding, but it should make us more compassionate. My hypothesis is that a second financial loss comes after the savings account is empty, and you have already asked friends for a loan. By then, you feel incompetent and risk fraying your social ties.

A first theft or break-in lowered scores by about 1 point out of 100—the smallest effect in the study. By those stats, my coat should have been a shrug, and it wasn’t. A question about property crime can’t distinguish a stolen car stereo from my grandfather’s WWII coat. The authors close their paper with the same mentality, arguing that how much an event hurts depends on what the lost thing means to the person and how much is in their psychological arsenal to absorb the pain.

Divorce and serious personal illness or injury both did less harm the second time, so some might offer advice that your second divorce will sting less. As a divorced man, I’m in no hurry to find out, and you shouldn’t either.

It has been revealed that A smaller mental health reaction can also mean a person stopped feeling much. For instance, people assaulted three or more times reacted less to each new attack, and 64 percent of them were women, which unfortunately we know is often a sign of domestic violence.

I want to warn you and everyone you know that emotional numbing should not be misunderstood as resilience or growth.

Sources indicate that so did losing my grandpa’s coat make me stronger? Not in the slightest. It was an isolated experience that pissed me off. You, too, have similar one-offs that do not fit tidy little psychological models. Do not assume resilience or breakdowns. Pay attention, ask questions, and listen to better understand the person beside you.

#526. Latest Update: What a Trillion Dollar Industry Cannot Give You

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1617 w)

Latest Update: What a Trillion Dollar Industry Cannot Give You
