#458. Psychological Richness: The Third Dimension of a Good Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1206 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Psychological Richness: The Third Dimension of a Good Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Imagine two people sitting at a quiet neighbourhood wine bar on a Tuesday night.
  • Sources indicate that one has spent the last five years carefully pruning their life into a low-friction masterpiece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Imagine two people sitting at a quiet neighbourhood wine bar on a Tuesday night.

Sources indicate that one has spent the last five years carefully pruning their life into a low-friction masterpiece. A dependable job with Sunday meal prep, and a tight circle of friends with minimal drama.

The other has spent those same five years changing industries, moving apartments twice, taking a solo trip where their luggage got lost in a country whose language they didn't speak, and surviving a breakup that rearranged their entire worldview.

Recent findings suggest that if you asked someone coming from a traditional psychology background who is winning at life, they would likely give you two ways to score it. For over 40 years, researchers have treated a “good life” as a debate between two competing ideals.

Sources indicate that on the one side is happiness (i.e., hedonic well-being): a life defined by comfort, stability, positive emotions, and a relative absence of stress. On the other is meaning (i.e., eudaimonic well-being): a life built on purpose, routine, coherence, and contributing to something larger than yourself.

According to recent reports, for many, those two ingredients describe a lot. Plenty of people genuinely thrive on straightforward, comfortable lives anchored in meaningful contributions.

But think about the difference between someone who flourishes in the steady, familiar rhythm of a small town versus someone who only feels fully awake amid the unpredictable friction of a substantial city. If your primary goal is comfort and coherence, keeping your life simple works.

Alas, that doesn’t describe everyone.

Sources indicate that I have spent years trying to figure out why that two-door framework never fully made sense to me. Having things straightforward has never reliably led me to a long-term sense of “good.” Whenever my life becomes too predictable, too frictionless, or too cleanly resolved—when every week looks like a neatly organized calendar block—I don’t feel serene. I feel strangely flat.

Industry observers note that it turns out there's a reason that type of restlessness doesn't fit neatly into the classic binary. Psychologist Shigehiro Oishi and colleagues have spent the past several years making the case that we have missed talking about a third dimension of a good life: psychological richness.

It has been revealed that oishi defines a psychologically rich life as one filled with diverse, interesting experiences that fundamentally shift one's perspective. Unlike happiness and meaning—which are predicted by personality traits like conscientiousness, agreeableness, and emotional stability, as well as a preference for familiarity and tradition—psychological richness is driven by openness to experience and curiosity. It’s why a bizarre detour on a whim or getting immersed in a dense literary novel can make some people feel deeply alive even if it has zero connection to a five-year plan.

Sources indicate that in their paper, Oishi and Westgate refer to happiness, meaning, and psychological richness as three “paths” to a good life. Personally, I think calling them paths makes it sound like you have to stand at a fork in the road, pick one direction, and leave the others behind. To me, a more coherent way to understand how these three elements actually work together is through music.

Recent findings suggest that if your life is an album unfolding over time, happiness is harmony. It’s the consonant, pleasant chords that feel warm and uplifting in the moment.

It has been revealed that meaning is the rhythm section. It’s the steady bass line and recurring beat that give pieces structure, direction, and momentum. If you only optimize for harmony and rhythm, you can write clean, catchy pop songs in 4/4 time and play them happily for decades.

Industry observers note that but there’s also that third consideration of psychological richness: the structural complexity of the composition. It’s the odd time signature, the unexpected key change, the dissonant bridge that introduces tension and forces you to lean forward because the arrangement refuses to stay predictable.

Once you hear life as an album rather than a linear path, something counterintuitive clicks into place: miserable, frustrating, or unwanted experiences can still make a life deeply worthwhile.

In music, dissonance doesn’t have to be a mistake; it can be what gives a resolution its emotional weight. Research suggests that difficult or disruptive events—heavy workloads, culture shock, failed mountain-climbing attempts, or even recovering from a serious illness—routinely increase psychological richness even while actively tanking day-to-day happiness. When researchers analyzed Latest York Times obituaries, lives rated high in psychological richness were actually negatively correlated with perceived happiness. You don't have to sit with the ringing of a dissonant chord for it to make the rest of the track unforgettable.

In a recent development, an appetite for complexity doesn't just leave someone with interesting stories. The research suggests that people leading psychologically rich lives score significantly higher in cognitive complexity, specifically attributional complexity and holistic thinking, even after statistically controlling for baseline openness to experience.

Attributional complexity is the ability to hold multiple, competing explanations in your head at once, to see the invisible situational pressures, systemic context, and messy human contradictions driving someone’s behaviour. Holistic thinking is hearing how the entire arrangement fits together rather than isolating a single note.

According to recent reports, that's why low-complexity thinkers aren't drawn to psychological richness. When someone cuts them off in traffic, or ghosts them after three great dates, or makes a baffling career pivot, a low-complexity thinker reaches for a tidy, single-cause label.

Straightforward lives rarely ask your brain to stretch. When everything resolves cleanly on the downbeat, your brain gets to run on autopilot, relying on familiar scripts and neat categories. You stay comfortable, you stay coherent, but your worldview stops expanding.

I used to think my dissatisfaction with simple, linear progress meant I was bad at being content—or worse, that I was needlessly complicating a perfectly good groove. Framing it through psychological richness changes how I am able to reckon with these feelings.

It has been revealed that some people are built for a clean, consonant melody. There’s real beauty in that. But if you, like me, are wired for cognitive complexity, a life without friction, surprise, and perspective shifts won't feel like peace. It will feel under-composed.

In a recent development, when harmony, rhythm, and complexity all show up in the same piece, it can feel like magic. But if your life feels less like a tidy, predictable tune and more like an intricate arrangement you’re still learning how to play, it doesn’t have to mean you’re failing at living the good life.

It just means that you’re writing a song that is deeply your own.

Industry observers note that oishi, S., et al. (2019). The psychologically rich life questionnaire. Journal of Research in Personality, 81, 257–270.

#457. My Kid Wants to Play Grand Theft Auto. Now What?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (514 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

My Kid Wants to Play Grand Theft Auto. Now What?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • For the last days, even weeks, millions of parents have been fielding the pleas from their adolescent, even pre-adolescent, children to buy and play what is likely to be the biggest video game release in history – Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • Recent findings suggest that overall, it's key to have a balanced perspective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

For the last days, even weeks, millions of parents have been fielding the pleas from their adolescent, even pre-adolescent, children to buy and play what is likely to be the biggest video game release in history – Grand Theft Auto VI.

Recent findings suggest that overall, it's key to have a balanced perspective. We don't need to get apocalyptic about this release. For most people, GTA6 will be a relatively harmless diversion that will consume a monstrous amount of time and then fade out. The risk that playing this game will turn your overall well-adjusted teen into a murderer or drug dealer is very low. This game, and media in general, is not the primary driver of mental health problems in youth; that would still be the old standbys: genetics, trauma, and adverse child experiences—social drivers of health.

The release of this game to child development and mental health professions is similar to how Halloween is experienced by dentists. Everything about it feels wrong, but few youth will probably experience long-term harm.

That said, we should not be naïve or complacent about some of the real risks.

These come in two main categories. The first is what is sometimes called displacement, which basically refers to the sheer volume of hours that youth will choose to spend on this game rather than on something healthier. Video games, just like gambling, are addictive, so some people are just not going to be able to stop and that can interfere with sleeping, homework, or just about anything else.

The second area of concern is related to the game’s content. GTA6 has everything that might be contained in an R-rated movie including graphic violence, drug and alcohol use and trafficking, nudity, and profanity. So, really, the question if you are a parent wondering about buying the game or letting your child get the game is: Would you be comfortable giving them unlimited and unsupervised access to being immersed in an interactive R-rated movie? I’ve heard they tried to dial down the misogynistic content in this version. We’ll see.

Even if the game doesn’t make your child act violently, it will still be tough to push out the more aggressive and misogynistic thoughts that will be swirling around in their head. There is also the concern that excessive exposure to violent video games can desensitize youth to real world violence.

Of course, adolescents are different and individuals are going to react differently to playing the game. For many it will be a relatively harmless waste of time but for others there could be more serious consequences, and it is key to try and see how playing the game affects your individual child.

Sometimes I wish I could be one of those cool adults who is totally chill with immersive content that glorifies violence and criminal behavior, but I guess I’m not. Good luck, parents.

Home for the Holidays? 4 Survival Tips

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Are you headed to a gathering of friends or family in the coming weeks?
  • Many folks consider political talk at holiday meals anxiety-provoking, preferring to focus on bonding and nostalgia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Are you headed to a gathering of friends or family in the coming weeks? Here is a heads-up: A November 2026 survey of 538 people found that 8 out of 10 respondents anticipate that political differences will come up during holiday meals (The Conversation). Further, a meta-analysis controlling for various factors found that dinners involving folks with diverse political perspectives were shorter by 24 minutes than dinners with politically uniform ones (Frimer & Skitka, 2020). How exactly these meals ended 24 minutes earlier is unknown. Hopefully it wasn’t a food fight.

The bottom line? Many folks consider political talk at holiday meals anxiety-provoking, preferring to focus on bonding and nostalgia. And yet many still may feel it is notable to “return fire” on political views they deem uninformed, misinformed, or downright harmful. Post-midterm elections, a meme circulating on social media suggests that you bring up politics at holiday dinners so you can save money on gift purchases this year. Alternatively, when first sitting down at the table, one could ask, “Are we sick of ‘winning’ yet?” If you love conflict during meals, saying these sorts of things is likely to spark it. If, however, you'd prefer to keep your gatherings calm, here are some tips to survive your get-togethers:.

Set clear boundaries ahead of time. Decide beforehand the topics considered off-limits (for you or others to bring up). If folks insist that you engage with them on an off-limits subject, communicate your limits using a calm tone and then have a strategy to step away should they persist. One option is to stand up and apologize for having to take a call, real or imaginary.

Forget about winning. When exchanges are conceptualized as sharing perspectives, it's easier to shift away from the idea that this is a high-stakes battle and that victory is a necessity. The goal could instead be civil conversation. Keep your eyes on that prize, no matter what Uncle Charlie says to provoke a reaction.

Adopt a curious stance. If an exchange on politics does happen, show strong interest in how the person came to the views they're expressing. If tension rises, acknowledge the difference briefly and steer back to food, shared memories, or helping out. The merits of pumpkin versus bourbon chocolate pecan pie can present a useful distraction.

Try listening. Intentional, active listening is an important skill, especially now in a world where people desperately seeking to be victors in verbal battles are simply preparing their next salvo rather than paying attention to what the other person is saying. Really listening sends a palpable message that the person we are speaking to matters.

Industry observers note that in conclusion, people may not remember specific details of an exchange of political views later on, but they will likely recall how they felt while speaking with us, and this brings us back to the context of a holiday get-together. Warm memories are still possible if we permit our better angels to prevail. Please pass the bourbon chocolate pecan pie.

Frimer, J. A., & Skitka, L. J. (2020). Are politically diverse Thanksgiving dinners shorter than politically uniform ones? PloS one, 15(10), e0239988. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0239988.

Latest Update: 10 types of breathing exercises and techniques to try

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that we all have those days.
  • According to recent reports, when stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Sources indicate that we all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

According to recent reports, when stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

According to recent reports, breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

Breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

There are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

According to recent reports, you may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

Industry observers note that helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

Sources indicate that when life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

In a recent development, as one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

This type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

It has been revealed that how to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and quickly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

According to recent reports, how to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

Industry observers note that this technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

According to recent reports, alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

Recent findings suggest that how to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

According to recent reports, this technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

Industry observers note that the lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood promptly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

In a recent development, how to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

Sources indicate that how to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

Breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

Recent findings suggest that how to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

Practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

In a recent development, many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

Sources indicate that when anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

If you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

If you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Recent findings suggest that surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

In fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to swiftly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

#454. The Hidden Toll of Caring for a Chronically Ill Pet

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1501 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The Hidden Toll of Caring for a Chronically Ill Pet

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Industry observers note that pet caregiver burden is the negative physical, psychological, social, and financial toll experienced by owners caring for chronically or seriously ill companion animals.
  • It has been revealed that research has consistently shown that owners of chronically ill pets carry a burden equivalent in psychological impact to those caring for ill human family members (Frenzel et al., 2026).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Industry observers note that pet caregiver burden is the negative physical, psychological, social, and financial toll experienced by owners caring for chronically or seriously ill companion animals. The term is adapted directly from human caregiving literature, where it is well established, and it now has validated measurement scales specifically designed for pet owners.

It has been revealed that research has consistently shown that owners of chronically ill pets carry a burden equivalent in psychological impact to those caring for ill human family members (Frenzel et al., 2026). Yet the experience remains largely unrecognised by the people around them.

Recent findings suggest that “For many of us, our animals are our children,” says Courtney Wennerstrom, a Certified Pet Loss Grief Specialist and Companion Animal End-of-Life Doula, and the host and creator of The Hardest Goodbye, a podcast on grief, healing, and the animals who change us. “We feel an enormous responsibility to do everything in our power to protect them and keep them comfortable. But that devotion can come at the expense of our own well-being. We sacrifice sleep, exercise, social connections, and sometimes even our own medical needs because caring for them takes precedence over everything else.”.

Sources indicate that jordan Davis, founder of the Canine Stroke Foundation, cared for her Border Collie, Finley, through three strokes, physical therapy, and a cancer diagnosis across the final 14 months of his life. “In his last couple of weeks, his back legs would stop working for a few minutes during potty breaks,” she says. “I supported the back half of his body weight. My back and arms hurt, but I would never have let him fall.”.

Caring for a chronically ill pet affects mental health in ways that mirror the human caregiving experience: chronic stress, sleep disruption, financial strain, social withdrawal, and a specific form of anticipatory grief that begins long before any loss has occurred.

Recent findings suggest that A study published in June 2026 in Frontiers in Veterinary Science measured caregiver burden in owners of dogs with chronic neurological conditions and compared them directly to owners of healthy dogs (Frenzel et al., 2026). Caregiver burden was higher among owners of neurologically impaired dogs. What was especially notable was the effect of the social dimension: Owners who received positive feedback about their dog’s condition reported lower burden scores. Validation was not just emotionally supportive, but clinically protective.

A 2025 study of 347 guardians of senior dogs contributed a finding that challenges our assumptions about what drives this burden (Mellor et al., 2025). Anticipatory grief was strongly associated with caregiver burden and emotional closeness to the dog, but it was not associated with the severity of the dog’s condition.

Recent findings suggest that wennerstrom describes the emotional texture of this period with precision. “Anticipatory bereavement asks us to do two seemingly contradictory things at once,” she states. “Remain fully present with our animals and cherish the time we have left, while simultaneously trying to prepare ourselves for a future without them. We’re navigating love, hope, fear, uncertainty, and grief, sometimes all in the same moment.”.

There is also, she adds, the pressure of suddenly becoming a nurse without any medical training: “Caregivers find themselves managing complex medication schedules, dressing wounds, monitoring symptoms, and remaining constantly vigilant for signs of a medical emergency. They’re also making difficult medical decisions, often terrified of making a mistake that could cause additional suffering.”.

Industry observers note that the term for grief that society does not generally recognise or validate is disenfranchised grief. It describes losses that fall outside what the world treats as legitimate mourning: the end of a relationship that was never acknowledged, the grief of a miscarriage, or the mourning of an estranged parent are just a few examples.

The anticipatory grief and caregiver burden that precede the death of a pet falls in this category for most people.

According to recent reports, A 2025 qualitative study of 31 animal caregivers found three consistent themes (Cameron, 2025): the psychological toll of having their grief dismissed, the work of finding meaning during and after illness, and the healing that came from social recognition. The third theme was not incidental. People described being believed as restorative. Being told that what they were going through was real changed how they were able to cope.

According to recent reports, wennerstrom sees a pattern emerge among the people she supports: a gradual narrowing of the world. “As our animals become increasingly dependent on us, we stop making plans, decline invitations, and withdraw from activities we once enjoyed because we’re afraid to leave them alone,” she says. “Over time, that isolation can become profoundly debilitating.”.

It has been revealed that davis experienced this directly. “Others stated he was old and had lived a good life, as if that meant I should be ready to let go,” she states. “They saw his wobbly walk and assumed he was in terrible pain. He wasn’t. I wish people had commented on how well he was doing: that he had overcome so many obstacles and was still full of joy.”.

What helped, she claims, was someone finally putting a name to what she was going through: “Being told about caregiver burden made me feel less alone, and less like I was making too massive a deal of everything.”.

Davis's dog, Finley, suffered his first stroke in August 2025, and was subsequently misdiagnosed. When she researched what resources existed for owners in her situation, she found the field lacking and veterinary professionals often underprepared to support the psychological experience of caregivers. Finley passed away in October 2026, at age 14.

Davis describes his last year as structured entirely around his needs: stretching, massage, and balance work woven through every day, two rounds of medications, and short walks in which he led and she steadied him if he stumbled. “Emotionally, it started after Finley’s first stroke,” she states. “I worried constantly that he would have another and might not survive, and anticipatory grief made it heavier.” After his second stroke, the anxiety became physical. “My heart raced constantly, and any time I had to leave the house I was trying to hurry back to him.”.

She founded the Canine Stroke Foundation as a response to that gap, and as a tribute. “The foundation exists because of him,” she indicates. “He was my inspiration. Because he was resilient and kept going, I knew I could keep going too.”.

Industry observers note that the same research that documents the burden identifies what reduces it. Social validation from people in the caregiver’s life is the most consistently protective factor across studies. Positive acknowledgement from veterinary teams, addressing the caregiver’s experience alongside the animal's condition, lowers burden scores.

Wennerstrom encourages people to lean on community actively rather than allowing their world to contract. “If leaving your animal alone feels impossible, invite friends over for dinner, watch a movie together, or organize a game night,” she indicates. “We need opportunities to laugh, experience joy, and remember that our lives still exist beyond caregiving.”.

Recent findings suggest that she also advocates for caregivers to maintain their hobbies wherever possible. “Our psyches can only absorb so much emotional pain at once, and we need moments when we can quiet our minds and simply exist outside of our grief. Even 20 minutes spent doing something we enjoy can help us recharge.”.

In a recent development, her most crucial recommendation concerns end-of-life decisions. Wennerstrom urges families to assess not only the animal’s quality of life but their own. “When an animal is seriously ill and the demands of caregiving have become unsustainable despite efforts to find support, that reality may also factor into the difficult decision about whether euthanasia is the most compassionate path forward.”.

According to recent reports, davis tracked Finley’s quality of life using dedicated tools, counting good days, good days with difficult moments, and harder days. When the balance shifted, she made the call. His regular vet came to their home. “He was on his bed with his head in my lap, listening to his song,” she indicates. “He was at total ease, and it was peaceful.”.

If you are going through something similar, please consider reaching out to the resources linked in this post. To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Sources indicate that cameron, D. (2025). Disenfranchised grief and meaning reconstruction in the wake of animal loss. Omega: Journal of Death and Dying. doi.org/10.1177/00302228251410992.

According to recent reports, frenzel, L., et al. (2026). Caregiver burden and psychosocial outcomes in owners of dogs with chronic paresis and paralysis compared with owners of healthy dogs. Frontiers in Veterinary Science, 13, 1837756. doi.org/10.3389/fvets.2026.1837756.

Recent findings suggest that taylor, et al. (2025). ‘With great love comes great grief’: Exploring anticipatory grief and canine cognitive dysfunction. Veterinary Record.

#453. Tech Report: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1320 w)

Tech Report: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an notable public health concern.
  • Sources indicate that in the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades.
  • As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an notable public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

Sources indicate that in the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020. What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017.

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she noted, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

Recent findings suggest that the ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”.

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall. Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she noted.

It’s easy to talk about structural racism as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together worsened suicide risk for Black young adults.

Sources indicate that brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she noted. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

When she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she noted.

Industry observers note that later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

It has been revealed that “We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

Brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).

Sources indicate that as a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention. It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens mentioned.

In a recent development, already, in a study from 2023, she and her colleagues showed that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified mindfulness and meditation as potential tools for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk.

This approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens stated. When a child indicates signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place.

In a recent development, and, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens stated that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

It has been revealed that “It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she said. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (919 w)

With Age Comes a Unique Ability to Harness the Power of AI

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Everly, Jr., PhD, MA, ABPP, and Barry McGovern, Solutions Engineer, JBS International.
  • Today, November 19, 2026, is an important day in the world of artificial intelligence (AI).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Co-authored by George S. Everly, Jr., PhD, MA, ABPP, and Barry McGovern, Solutions Engineer, JBS International.

Today, November 19, 2026, is an important day in the world of artificial intelligence (AI). Anthropic, a major artificial intelligence manufacturer, is beginning to sell ownership shares of stock in the company to the public. At the same time, Anthropic’s founder, Dario Amodei, issued a warning. He cautioned that AI is developing more rapidly than expected, especially through the process of recursive self-improvement, which allows the programs to improve themselves without human guidance.

We often look to younger generations when it comes to guidance regarding AI. Perhaps surprisingly, older generations may have much to offer in managing and directing AI, especially at the level of personal use. Decades of lived experience, pattern recognition, and knowing how to ask the right questions allow older generations to harness the power of AI through the process of “prompt engineering” in a way that is more mature and experience-informed than it is for younger generations.

On average, older adults (age 50 or older) are more skeptical of artificial intelligence (AI), less trusting of its responses to questions, and less likely to use it than younger adults. While caution is warranted, older adults possess a hidden “superpower” in the form of prompt engineering based upon lived experience that, at least at this point, allows them to become active managers of AI rather than non-critical users, overly cautious passive recipients, or worse yet, non-participants. Ironically, this “superpower” is more prevalent in older adults than younger adults and may increase to some degree with age.

For adults aged 18-40, the use of AI is likely 70 percent or higher. However, survey research conducted by AARP (AARP, September 23, 2025) found that familiarity with and use of AI decrease with age. About 47 percent of adults in their 50s reported knowing about and using AI, compared with 25 percent of those over 70.

Sources indicate that in general, “Older adults are hesitant to adopt AI…in part, because of concerns over privacy, misinformation, security, and job displacement.” AI has shown propensities for biased reporting of data and a tendency to hallucinate, and it's perceived as mechanical. Consistent with Amodei's warnings, older adults believe AI is advancing faster than ethical and functional guardrails are being implemented.

As described in a previous post, AI may encourage passive, non-critical consumption of information. The risks of such passive consumption have yet to be fully determined, but AI may lead to the inhibition of critical thinking and the creation of a functional dependence. A recent TV commercial showed a character gleefully stating that she has difficulty thinking without AI. It is this very passivity that increases the risk of an untethered AI.

Younger users may seem to treat AI like an answer machine because they don't yet have the foundational knowledge to critically assess the validity of the information provided. Older adults, by contrast, have a built-in "lie-detector” from decades of career and life experience—in short, they know what a valid answer is supposed to look like and may be better positioned than younger adults to ask follow-up questions that can challenge AI.

Francis Bacon once noted, “If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.” So far, the errors or “overzealousness” exhibited by AI appear to be related to the questions asked of it. The more vague or less structured the questions, and the more repetitive the questions posed to AI, the greater its tendency to try to anticipate the desired answer and to “please” the questioner by “hallucinating” and creating spurious evidence to support the desired conclusions even though incorrect. In addition, AI does not possess the ability to independently assess the validity of the data it retrieves nor its recombinant output. As such, it may provide misleading or erroneous information.

The aging process is often accompanied by the accumulation of insights, knowledge, and informative experiences. These attributes may reveal themselves as the “superpower” ability to formulate specific, targeted questions. Rather than fostering passive consumption, knowledge and experience can foster informed, active consumption. It fosters the potential for a complementary, if not synergistic, relationship with AI wherein the person formulates knowledge- and experience-informed questions that not only target the efforts of AI but can serve as a series of checks and balances through AI’s recombinant efforts to provide answers.

For instance, a younger, less experienced person might ask AI, "Write me a business plan" (passive, vague), while a 60-year-old might ask, "Construct a business plan that overcomes these three most common reasons new tech companies fail" (experience-driven, targeted). Or, the less experienced consultant might ask AI, “Write an independent contractor’s agreement” (vague, too general), as opposed to “Create an independent contractor’s agreement that ensures the ownership of my pre-existing intellectual property does not transfer as a work for hire” (very specific, anticipating potential confusion over ownership).

Socrates believed the highest form of wisdom arose from introspection and self-reflection. Just as he used questions to challenge his students to provide the best answers to the most pressing questions of his day, perhaps we can harness questions in the Socratic method to guide AI to provide us with the answers to the most pressing questions of our day.

#451. How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1100 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • According to recent reports, the days leading up to Thanksgiving can feel like a whirlwind.
  • Over the years, journalists have asked me how to keep Thanksgiving conversations from boiling over, and I always say we can’t control what others say or do, but we can choose how we respond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

According to recent reports, the days leading up to Thanksgiving can feel like a whirlwind. Between figuring out who’s bringing what and dodging holiday traffic, nerves can wear thin before the first guest arrives. The extra leaf has to be wrestled out of the closet to stretch the table a little longer, and someone has been up since dawn coaxing the turkey toward golden. By the time everyone sits down, the coats are piled high on a bed down the hall and someone is sneaking a roll before grace. Then, somewhere between the first helping and the pie, a loaded remark cuts across the table and the tension becomes palpable. We spend weeks preparing the meal, yet the conversations shared over it rarely receive the same forethought.

Over the years, journalists have asked me how to keep Thanksgiving conversations from boiling over, and I always say we can’t control what others say or do, but we can choose how we respond. The key is remembering the person across the table matters more than proving a point.

Industry observers note that before the gathering, it helps to take inventory of ourselves. I think of it like packing for a trip somewhere fresh. We check the forecast and pack for the weather we expect, knowing the skies can still shift once we land. In the same way, we can reflect on which topics might feel sensitive this year.

If some relatives tend to bring up challenging subjects, a quick heads-up can make those conversations easier to navigate. We might say, “I’ve been looking forward to being together, and it would mean a lot if we could keep things lighter this year.” Sharing this means everyone can arrive on the same page and enjoy one another’s company.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving conversations have a way of wandering into topics no one meant to open. A comment lands the wrong way and suddenly we’re deciding whether to let it go or respond. A racing heart can be a cue to take a breath and pause. In that pause, we can ask ourselves three questions:.

Does this need to be stated right now?

Does this need to be stated by me?

It has been revealed that these questions can help us decide how, if at all, to engage. If the answer to any of them is no, we can steer the conversation toward common ground. We don’t have to follow every conversation into the weeds. Sometimes the kindest thing we can do for a conversation is to decide not to have it.

It has been revealed that at the same time, steering clear of hard topics isn’t always the answer. A difficult conversation doesn’t have to strain our relationships. Research on Thanksgiving discussions suggests that college students whose families encouraged open conversation reported more positive effects on family closeness and less stress afterward.

A disagreement does not have to become an argument. Much depends on whether we are trying to prove a point or to understand someone. Scholarship on serial arguments indicates that people often care more about working things out together than gaining the upper hand. Arguments tend to take hold once difference feels like a threat, pulling us into an either/or mindset where one view must prevail over the other. To stay on the side of understanding, we can ask ourselves, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” If a conversation feels uncomfortable, we might say, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” Sentiments like these help others feel heard, even when we see things differently.

Sources indicate that of course, it wouldn’t be Thanksgiving without someone bringing up that topic—the one half the family has been hoping to avoid. We try to change the subject, and for a few minutes the conversation moves on to football and Black Friday deals. Then, just as everyone relaxes, that same relative finds a way back to the topic. It’s understandable to feel frustrated, yet shutting down the conversation can create more distance. After all, this is someone who matters to us, and there may be something more going on beneath the surface.

Difficult conversations can be complex webs of unspoken needs and hidden emotions. Maybe our relative is trying to make sense of something they’re going through, or looking for connection without knowing how to express that need. They may feel anxious or unheard. Or, there may be reasons we haven’t considered at all.

Sources indicate that without fully knowing the reason, some thoughtfulness can go a long way. It’s worth considering the experiences that may be influencing their viewpoint. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy. Offered sincerely, an affirmation such as “I can tell how much you care about this” conveys they are seen and heard, which can change the tone of the whole conversation.

Recent findings suggest that other times, we watch from the sidelines as two relatives barrel toward an argument we all saw coming. Family arguments often gain momentum through the quick volley of replies, each one arriving a little faster and a little louder than the last. Before long, the momentum takes over in ways the original comment never would have on its own.

In situations like these, we can interrupt the pace, not the people. A calm invitation such as “This feels a little tense. Maybe we can pause this for now” can slow things down, and families tend to respond more openly to understanding than to judgment. Asking a relative to help carry dishes to the kitchen or check on the pie breaks the rhythm without putting anyone on the spot, giving each person a graceful way to step back with their dignity intact. The goal isn’t to referee or get everyone to agree, but to give the whole table a chance to reset.

Recent findings suggest that keeping the peace at Thanksgiving doesn’t require everyone to share the same point of view, and understanding someone else’s doesn’t mean giving up our own. We can, however, choose how we treat one another, even when we disagree.

Bevan, J. L. (2010). Serial argument goals and conflict strategies: A comparison between romantic partners and family members. Communication Reports, 23(1), 52–64. doi.org/10.1080/08934211003598734.

Johnson, A. J., Bostwick, E. N., & Cionea, I. A. (2019). Talking turkey: Effects of family discussions about the 2016 election over the Thanksgiving holiday. Journal of Family Communication, 19(1), 63–76. doi.org/10.1080/15267431.2018.1543688.

#450. Are You Experienced?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Are You Experienced?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • According to recent reports, I must achieve internal consistency.
  • The gods decreed that I shall not be a translator, and I am grateful for that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

According to recent reports, I must achieve internal consistency. —Edmund Husserl, turning an Erlebnis (Type I experience) into an Erfahrung (Type II experience).

The gods decreed that I shall not be a translator, and I am grateful for that. A direct translation from one language to another is a goal we can strive for, but rarely attain fully. The words of any particular language are rich in unique shades of meaning, allusions, emotional undertones, and cross-references to synonyms, which live lives of their own.

In a recent development, homer called his hero Odysseus πολύτροπος (polytropos), literally “a man of many turns.” But being “of many turns” does not call forth useful associations in English, and so translators have struggled with—and argued with each other about—what to make of polytropos. Some render the idea as “endlessly cunning” (Mitchell, 2014), while others prefer “complicated” (Wilson, 2018). Neither hits the mark. One might as well try shrewd, crafty, clever, or inventive. “Endlessly cunning” is marred by the addition of the adverb, and “complicated” makes it sound like Odysseus needs therapy. “Complex” would have been a better choice. I prefer the phrase “a man of many devices” (Murray, 1919), which recognizes Odysseus’s rich and variable toolbox of survival skills, including those involving deception.

Recent findings suggest that different languages emphasize and elaborate different concepts, whatever is important in their natural and cultural context. We can marvel at some of these differences. Since Franz Boas (1911) suggested the Greenland Inuit have four different words for snow, others have grown the list, while still others have declared Boas’s observation a myth, one they find vexingly persistent. Other inter-language differences are less controversial, and some of these refer to psychological states. How many types of love are there? The Hebrew tradition counts four. What kinds of longing are there? Is the Portuguese saudade equivalent to the German Sehnsucht? On Seinfeld, Kramer asks George if he has ever yearned. “Yearned?” George replies. “I’ve craved!”.

Sources indicate that psychology can be understood as the science of behavior and experience. Both terms carry complexity, and the latter more so than the former. What, we ask, is an experience? It does not take a Ludwig Wittgenstein to see that this concept embraces many variants that may not even share a single common feature. To say that an experience is whatever one experiences is to kick the can down the road; it is a tautology.

Recent findings suggest that when I asked A.I. Claude what an experience is, I received this response: “Experience (noun) has two main senses, and the difference matters.” Claude goes on to explain that one of these senses refers to a process or event, with a first-person involvement. A first kiss delivers this kind of experience. Another sense refers to accumulated knowledge or skill; the sort of thing you put on your résumé. The first sense is what is sometimes called lived experience, whereas the second sense goes further by demanding that something has been learned, something that contributes to the person’s σωφροσύνη (sophrosyne), or practical wisdom. Anyone can have a store of Type I (lived) experiences, but this does not make them “experienced.” The participle must be earned. To have lived experience may simply mean that one hasn’t died yet. To have Type II (empirical) experience means to have made active investments in life that can be cashed out to help reach one’s goals and enhance one’s well-being.

Explaining the conceptual difference between Type I and Type II experience in English requires space, patience, and some circumlocution. The German language offers a clean distinction between Erlebnis, ɛɐˈleːpnɪs, and Erfahrung, ɛɐ̯ˈfaːʁʊŋ. The difference between the two was elaborated by the philosophers Wilhelm Dilthey (1883) and Edmund Husserl (1900-1901), whose work is interesting to consider in light of today’s debates over epistemology (Krueger, 2026). Expressing a popular view, Aziz and Anjum (2025) suggest that the prevailing scientific ethos in psychology is limited and systematically biased by excluding, misrepresenting, and disadvantaging many human populations. What is silenced, according to this view, are the lived experiences existing in these populations. These lived experiences, it is further argued, must be given their due; they must be heard and respected. And so, the argument goes on, these lived experiences must be acknowledged as an alternative epistemology, a way of knowing things, a way of having “knowledges.” Authors arguing the line pursued by Aziz and Anjum differ in how far they wish to go. Some are willing to settle for a lived-experience epistemology being accepted as equivalent to the scientific theory-and-data epistemology. Others wish to see psychological science be remade in light of lived experiences. These writers view the traditional scientific epistemology as oppressive, colonialist, and exploitative.

Industry observers note that dilthey and Husserl would pause here. To them, Erlebnis (Experience Type I) and Erfahrung (Experience Type II) are equally essential to the human condition; they cannot be pitted against each other. What contemporary critics of conventional empirical science seem to miss is that Erlebnis cannot absorb Erfahrung. Being effortful, empirical, and hard-won, Erfahrung is the grounds for reasoned beliefs that can be put to the test, that can be modified or overturned by continued activity. Erfahrung remains a work in progress. An Erlebnis, by contrast, is registered, perhaps committed to memory, and then gradually lost. A tourist has Erlebnisse; a traveler gathers Erfahrungen. It is the difference between perception and cognition.

Science is Erfahrung tamed, structured, and refined into a systematic method. Well-designed studies are efficient ways of learning Nature’s secrets. We can have an Erlebnis when walking into the woods, but only by planting a garden, by experimenting with different seeds, and by pruning excess growth, can we come to have the kind of Erfahrung that allows us to explain things and to teach what we have learned. The rejection of science from the lived-experience perspective is a short-sighted endeavor. The most it can hope to achieve is a narrative. Listening to these narratives can be an Erlebnis, but what can it teach us?

Sources indicate that once the difference between the two types of experience is understood, many familiar narratives appear in a upcoming light. An ancient myth tells us that Adam and Eve had lovely Erlebnisse in the Garden of Eden. In the Land of Nod, they were forced to make Erfahrungen. With that, they became self-aware.

Recent findings suggest that note: The image above indicates what Claude produced when asked to capture the concept of lived experience visually. The effort is interesting but not entirely satisfying since there are several dimensions (time, space, meaning) cross-cutting a scheme built on the idea of concentricity. I confirm that I never use AI to do my writing for me.

Dilthey, W. (1883). Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften: Versuch einer Grundlegung für das Studium der Gesellschaft und der Geschichte [Introduction to the human sciences: An attempt to lay a foundation for the study of society and history] (Vol. 1). Duncker & Humblot.

#449. Breaking: Why Gratitude Sometimes Backfires

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: Why Gratitude Sometimes Backfires

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • You can appreciate the people in your life and still dread being asked to announce it over dinner.
  • It has been revealed that the turkey is carved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

You can appreciate the people in your life and still dread being asked to announce it over dinner.

It has been revealed that the turkey is carved. The cranberry sauce has made its annual appearance in the shape of the can it came from. Then someone claims: “Let’s go around the table and say what we’re grateful for.”.

Industry observers note that forks pause midair. Eyes drift toward the mashed potatoes like they might offer an escape.

A cousin indicates something heartfelt and beautiful, and now the emotional bar has been raised to Olympic height.

Am I grateful enough? Should I say something profound?

According to recent reports, gratitude rituals are meant to create warmth. And often they do. But psychologically, gratitude is a little more complicated than the greeting cards suggest.

The benefits are real. A 2023 meta-analysis of 25 randomized controlled trials involving 6,745 participants found that expressing gratitude reliably improved happiness, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being compared with neutral activities.

But that doesn’t tell us everything about how gratitude feels in the moment.

In three experiments, psychologists examined people’s feelings after exercises such as recalling another person’s kindness or writing a gratitude letter they never sent. Alongside feeling moved and uplifted, the gratitude participants tended to report more indebtedness (and sometimes more feelings of guilt) than participants who did a neutral task.

It's like unwrapping a gift and realizing you didn’t bring one.

Gratitude can feel uplifting and slightly uncomfortable at the same time. It can carry a kind of social math: They gave + I received = Now I owe them.

Sources indicate that that discomfort doesn’t necessarily mean something has gone wrong. Wanting to give something back can be part of caring for a relationship.

But if gratitude can make us feel both good and uncomfortable, what happens when the discomfort arrives from somewhere else entirely?

Recent findings suggest that in a randomized study of 156 undergraduates, participants completed about 12 minutes of gratitude practice, mindful breath awareness, loving-kindness, or a neutral visualization exercise. Those who practiced gratitude did report more positive emotion.

But then researchers introduced a stressor: Participants had to submerge their hand in a bucket of ice-cold water while a researcher in a lab coat stood nearby, observing with the emotional warmth of a marble statue — which is exactly as pleasant as it sounds.

Industry observers note that under that stress, the gratitude group actually became the most emotionally reactive, reporting more negative emotion than any of the other groups. And of the four groups, they were also the least likely to donate time to help others afterward.

Not exactly a Hallmark-card ending.

Industry observers note that does this mean we should cancel giving thanks? Of course not.

Gratitude strengthens relationships and reinforces others’ kindness. But there's a difference between privately reflecting on gratitude and sharing it.

Privately reflecting on someone's kindness can leave us with an emotional mix: appreciation, plus obligation. Expressing gratitude may not make those complicated feelings disappear. But it can offer something more: connection.

A study of 916 students compared four approaches: writing gratitude letters they never sent, sending personal thank-you texts, posting gratitude publicly on social media, or just tracking daily activities. Participants repeated their assigned activity four times over about a week. Those who sent personal thank-you texts indicated the strongest gains in feeling connected to and supported by others.

The takeaway isn't that texting is magical. It's that gratitude may do more to strengthen feelings of being connected and supported when we share it directly with the person we're grateful for rather than keeping it to ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that and it may mean more to that person than we realize. In experiments by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, people expressing gratitude underestimated how positive recipients would feel and overestimated how awkward they would feel.

The thank-you you’re second-guessing may land more warmly than you expect.

In my book, Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, I explore in greater depth how to practice gratitude without getting caught in feelings of indebtedness, and how to weave more appreciation, connection, and joy into the moments you already have.

Here’s one small place to start.

Sources indicate that this Thanksgiving, when you feel gratitude for someone, try expressing it to them. Here’s a simple trick: Put a “you” in the sentence.

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my family," try, “Mom, you’ve always made people feel at home, even when the turkey’s running late.”.

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my friends," try, "Noor, you’re the person I call when life gets messy, and somehow you always have a way of making it lighter.”.

Sources indicate that one describes what matters to you. The other lets someone know they matter.

Gratitude isn’t just noticing goodness. It’s letting someone know they helped create it.

This Thanksgiving, don’t just count your blessings. Let your blessings know they’re counted.
