#434. Tech Report: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
  • In a recent development, the scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. New research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

In a recent development, the scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an vital role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," noted Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Recent findings suggest that rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

Recent findings suggest that for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

After the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

In mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This demonstrated that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

It has been revealed that the more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

According to recent reports, this prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than rapidly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

Sources indicate that however, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

According to recent reports, dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

It has been revealed that another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

This result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The new results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another key part of this process.

For recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Recent findings suggest that rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he right now works as a researcher.

Sources indicate that additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

Recent findings suggest that the team is now participating in a upcoming international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

#433. Breaking: When Your Cofounder Isn’t Who You Vetted

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: When Your Cofounder Isn’t Who You Vetted

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • You’re driving home from the pitch, replaying the way your cofounder talked over you in front of the investor.
  • Sources indicate that most founders I work with put time and energy into selecting their cofounder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

You’re driving home from the pitch, replaying the way your cofounder talked over you in front of the investor. The part that stings is that you did this carefully. You went through the cofounder dating questions together. You spent more time vetting them than most other founders you know. But you still ended up frustrated and disappointed, thinking to yourself: How did I choose wrong?

Sources indicate that most founders I work with put time and energy into selecting their cofounder. Many used Gloria Lin’s 50 questions, published by First Round Review. These questions are useful, but the problem is often that the answers were true when you gave them, and people change, especially under pressure.

Two founders I worked with demonstrated this clearly.

In a recent development, one of them was leaving an established company to start the business. Sarah was worried about what failing would do to her reputation and felt concerned she couldn't simply re-enter her role if she left. So she set a condition. She'd only make the leap if her partner, Tom, was willing to give up everything for the company: his sleep, his health, his marriage. Tom said yes, and he meant it (at the time).

In a recent development, then Tom's wife got very sick. His priorities shifted, and he no longer wanted to prioritize the company above his marriage. He worked fewer hours. Sarah saw that as a breach of contract. Tom hoped that Sarah would change her mind and the two of them could keep building. But Sarah wasn’t willing to budge. She was quite clear on the level of sacrifice and commitment to the business she required, and they ultimately parted ways.

Looking back, the warning signs were present in their first conversation.

In a recent development, sarah's demand was extreme. It highlighted unconscious anxiety about her inability to recover the prestige of her previous manufacturer and corresponding rigidity about sacrifice and commitment. The partnership agreement was also too inflexible. When Tom's life changed, they didn't have the capacity to change the terms.

I find it useful to separate aspirational values from lived values. Aspirational values are the ones you’d list if someone asked you. Lived values are what someone watching your behavior would see.

When cofounders answer each other’s questions before they start, they’re mostly reporting aspirational values. They mean them. They just haven’t had to live them yet.

A core idea in psychoanalysis is that we’re of many minds, and that the conscious mind doesn’t always win.

Partnerships within a startup environment prove that point. Founders are often exhausted, sick, and under pressure, and in my experience, people regress under that kind of load. They fall back on older, less flexible ways of coping. It’s easy to say you’ll stay calm in a disagreement. It’s much harder when your heart is pounding, your revenue isn't growing, and you’re frustrated with the person across the table.

In a 1995 review in Psychological Bulletin, the psychologists Benjamin Karney and Thomas Bradbury drew on 115 longitudinal studies covering more than 45,000 marriages and proposed what they called the vulnerability-stress-adaptation model.

In their model, how a marriage fares depends on three things working together: what each partner brings into the relationship, such as personality and family history; the stress the couple faces; and how the two of them treat each other under that stress.

A couple can look steady when life is calm and struggle once the pressure rises. I see the same thing with cofounders, and a startup supplies plenty of pressure.

Two other cofounders I worked with had been colleagues at a previous company. Before starting, they agreed to a chart spelling out who was responsible for each area and who would be consulted or just informed on each decision.

According to recent reports, the technical cofounder signed off on being informed about areas outside his own. What he actually expected was to be consulted, because to him that’s what being a cofounder meant. His partner saw the cofounder title as little more than extra equity. What mattered to her was running separate areas and moving fast. Nobody asked what “informed” meant, and the mismatch only surfaced once they were building.

It has been revealed that gaps like this tend to get pushed aside, because they feel less urgent than shipping a product or landing customers. Founders tell themselves they’ll talk once the demo works, then once they have more customers.

Sources indicate that in my experience, the tech giant usually grows faster than the partnership does. Whatever got skipped early comes back later, often at a bad moment, like the middle of a fundraise, when you’re also deciding who’ll be the face of the company to investors.

Recent findings suggest that the questions are a starting point. The test is working together long enough, ideally several months, to say yes to two things: We’re aligned on what we’re building, and I know how you act under stress. It helps to think in milestones rather than a set number of weeks.

The first yes covers the practical side: where you want the business to go, how you’ll fund it, what financial outcome each of you wants, how much risk each of you is taking on, and how much time and sacrifice each of you can give.

Recent findings suggest that the second yes is about the two of you. Have you seen how your partner responds when things get hard, and do you still enjoy working with them? Can you give each other feedback in both directions? Have you had a genuine disagreement and come back from it?

It has been revealed that that last one carries a lot of weight. In my work, trust between partners tends to grow through repeated cycles of rupture and repair, and the honeymoon period doesn’t offer many of those.

Before you sign anything, agree on how you’ll adjust equity, compensation, or roles if that were needed, and write it down. Most people’s life circumstances and values change at some point. What hurt the founders in my story was having no agreed way to adjust when that happened.

If you are successful, you'll spend the next 5 to 10 years with this person. Building resilience in a relationship requires going through hardship together and coming through aligned on the other side. There's no question that can preempt that.

Sources indicate that karney, B. R., & Bradbury, T. N. (1995). The longitudinal course of marital quality and stability: A review of theory, method, and research. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 3–34. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.118.1.3.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
  • A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results indicated that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, said:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very key to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This said, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially crucial, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Just beyond the bridge, there’s a man in the middle of the roadway. He’s standing there on the thin divide between coming and going, speeding up to make the light and slowing down when it turns red, entering the city and getting out of town.

Recent findings suggest that my daughter and I are leaving. The sun is sinking on another long day of work and school. If only my car could fly like the Jetsons’, we’d be home instead of inching along in this clogged line where the drivers’ aggravations rise like exhaust fumes into the twilight.

As we edge closer to the man, it’s the sign that grabs my attention. Simple. Clever. To the point.

Not High, Not Drunk, Just Hungry.

Recent findings suggest that that’s what it indicates as he waits, message in one hand, and a Whole Foods shopping bag in the other. Standing there on the thin divide between a warm car and a cold street, a full tank and an empty stomach, a way out and no way out.

If traffic were moving, I could just drive by. I wouldn’t have to look. I wouldn’t have to think. Stuck here in this jam, it’s not that easy.

He knows this. He’s smart. His little roadside marketing campaign has all the right elements. Know your audience. Address their concerns. Eliminate their objections. Appeal to their needs. Basic human needs. Food, water, that sort of thing.

Sources indicate that the Whole Foods bag is a nice touch. Without a word, he’s telling us his intentions are good. Organic, pure and wholesome. And to think we might have suspected otherwise.

According to recent reports, motor running. Car stalled. Mind racing. Time suspended. I reach for my purse.

“Mom, you’re not going to give him money?”.

According to recent reports, my daughter’s words, yes. But they come from me, from what I’ve taught her over the years. Don’t talk to strangers. Don’t stop. Don’t get involved. You never really know who they are. You never really know where they come from. You never really know what they’re doing there in the middle of the roadway.

Recent findings suggest that especially now. In these hard times when the rules have all changed.

According to recent reports, I roll down my window. The wind whips against my face as I hand the man a few crumpled bills I might have used for a cappuccino. He smiles. I search his eyes for something. Reassurance? About him? About me? The light turns green. We drive away.

But in my rearview mirror, I catch a glimpse of him alongside another car, another rolled-down window, another arm extended into the night.

Standing there on the thin divide between doubt and faith, cynicism and optimism, despair and hope.

Even if it is just one small ray.

#430. We’ve Been Getting “Alpha” All Wrong—Here's What It Really Means

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (887 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

We’ve Been Getting “Alpha” All Wrong—Here's What It Really Means

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Think of the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the term “alpha male.” Maybe you picture a John Wayne type or a Douglass MacArthur; maybe a "jock" or the captain of the football team; maybe even a criminal like Tony Soprano of the television show The Sopranos or Frank Underwood of House of Cards.
  • Popular belief has largely aligned with these archetypal depictions of the “alpha.” This view of masculinity as dominant, aggressive, and hyper-independent is widely held across the globe, from the concept of the “man box” in Australia, which describes seven principles of being a man (self-sufficiency, acting tough, physical attractiveness, rigid gender roles, heterosexuality and homophobia, hypersexuality, aggression and control) to the “manosphere,” a loosely connected network of online communities that promote rigid, often unhealthy, views of manhood that align with the “alpha” concept (MensLine Australia, 2022).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Think of the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the term “alpha male.” Maybe you picture a John Wayne type or a Douglass MacArthur; maybe a "jock" or the captain of the football team; maybe even a criminal like Tony Soprano of the television show The Sopranos or Frank Underwood of House of Cards. When we think of the concept of the “alpha male,” we tend to imagine it having to do with rugged independence, aggression, and dominant behavior.

Popular belief has largely aligned with these archetypal depictions of the “alpha.” This view of masculinity as dominant, aggressive, and hyper-independent is widely held across the globe, from the concept of the “man box” in Australia, which describes seven principles of being a man (self-sufficiency, acting tough, physical attractiveness, rigid gender roles, heterosexuality and homophobia, hypersexuality, aggression and control) to the “manosphere,” a loosely connected network of online communities that promote rigid, often unhealthy, views of manhood that align with the “alpha” concept (MensLine Australia, 2022).

In a recent development, but ironically, natural science contradicts this rigid interpretation of the “alpha” concept. While popular culture and media have depicted the “alpha male” in a way that has become widely accepted and unchallenged, zoology directly contradicts the notion that alphas are aggressive, dominant, and isolated. Early research on animal behavior spawned the concept of the “alpha male.” When zoologist Konrad Lorenz studied animal behavior in the 1960s to understand aggression in the natural world, he concluded that there were three hierarchical categories found in the animal kingdom:.

Lorenz’s conclusion implied that most animal behavior was predicated on aggression and dominance, and that animals were classified by either being dominant or submissive. This early animal research laid the foundation for what gradually became a widely held (yet oversimplified) belief about male behavior, with the “alpha” being seen as preferred and elite.

It has been revealed that in the 1970s, however, biologist and expert on wolf behavior David Mech drew a very different conclusion than had Lorenz: the idea of the “alpha” had been oversimplified and misapplied in earlier research. Mech’s research revealed that wolf packs acted as family units, relying on cooperation and caregiving, rather than on fighting and aggression. The alpha role was actually taken on by both wolf parents, not just the male, to protect wolf cubs, ensure survival, and establish a family hierarchy (Mech, 1970).

Recent findings suggest that society often perpetuates myths that simplify more complex ideas: in this case, it is easier and simpler to view “alpha” as a singular personality type than to see it as a collaborative model that cannot be rigidly defined. The “alpha” concept has become so oversimplified that the way we tend to view it today is light years from its actual meaning in the animal kingdom. And the collateral damage of this misattribution has profound implications: A 2025 survey concluded that “young men ages 16 to 25 consuming online masculinity influencers’ content reported higher rates of emotional distress,” including feelings of worthlessness, nervousness, and sadness (Fischer, et al., 2025). A 2023 survey found that men in America are five times lonelier than they were in 1990, and, while finding a community is a necessity, not all communities—such as those like the “manosphere” are helpful or psychologically healthy (Bledsoe & Smith, 2025).

It has been revealed that despite the scientific debunking of the “alpha” myth, by the late 20th century, the idea of the “alpha male” had seeped into society and become widely accepted, as it remains today. We still hear this term used, and it is still thought by many to accurately describe “preferred” male behavior. Though it is often seen as describing qualities of leadership and success, the “alpha male” idea actually holds no scientific credence and is more a social construct than a fact of nature.

Sources indicate that survival in the animal kingdom is predicated upon collaboration, not isolation. A wolf pack is a “pack” for a reason—it would not survive without its collaborative dynamic. A “lone wolf”—though romanticized in popular culture and media—would actually struggle to get by without the support of a collaborative environment. It is no wonder, then, that when we rigidly view the “alpha” personality as being preferred, we run into countless problems, which can result in serious societal fissures such as a normalization of aggression, isolation, and unhealthy behaviors and responses. Taking a cue from nature might help us to reframe our often toxic definition of what “alpha” really means.

Sources indicate that lorenz, K. (1966). On aggression. New York, NY: Harcourt, Brace & World.

#429. Why Kids with ADHD Get Stuck in the Screen-Time Loop. And How to Break It.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1032 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Additudemag

Why Kids with ADHD Get Stuck in the Screen-Time Loop. And How to Break It.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games.
  • Screen addiction is not the problem.
  • Once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games. Learn why ADHD brains get hooked on these “other stimulants,” and how to protect them.

Screen addiction is not the problem. Your child is not hooked on their phone, but rather the endless loop of novelty, stimulation, and unpredictable rewards streaming through it. It’s the dopamine; not the device.

Once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one. Here’s the central point: Phones and video games weren’t as addictive before they got connected to the Internet. A standalone game that you can beat has an ending. A connected game like Fortnite, Roblox, or Minecraft never ends.

For a kid with ADHD, whose brain runs on a dopamine deficit, the Internet is impossible to resist – by design. We hand the most addictive delivery system ever built to the most vulnerable brains, and then ask them to show self-control. That’s not a fair fight.

Adolescents and teens with ADHD find screens irresistible, and it’s no wonder why. The ADHD brain is dopamine-deficient, and screens deliver dopamine instantly, reliably, and without effort. Almost everything else in life – school, sports, chores, homework – delivers dopamine slowly, inconsistently, and with lots of effort. The brain always chooses the path of least resistance to its dopamine.

This isn’t a character flaw or a discipline problem. It’s neurology. The dopamine hit from a connected screen is more powerful and more reinforcing for an ADHD brain than it is for a neurotypical one because the ADHD brain is always hunting for dopamine.

[Download: Managing and Safeguarding Your Child’s Screen Time].

A 2023 meta-analysis of more than 81,000 children found that two or more hours a day of screen time were associated with significantly elevated ADHD risk compared with less than two hours.1 Large longitudinal data from a separate study, which tracked more than 10,000 kids for two years, found that more screen time predicted increased ADHD – and that changes in brain structure helped explain the link.2.

Imaging research has tied greater screen time to altered development in the orbitofrontal cortex, lateral prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex – the regions that govern attention, cognitive control, and reward.

Back in the 1950s, the psychologist B.F. Skinner discovered something the entire tech industry would later weaponize: The most powerful way to drive a behavior isn’t to reward it every time, but to reward it unpredictably. It’s called a variable-ratio reinforcement schedule, and it’s the most addictive reward pattern known to behavioral science.

It is why slot machines are built as they are. You pull the lever, and you might get nothing, or you might hit the jackpot. Not knowing is what keeps you pulling.

[Read: How Can I Help My Teen Better Manage Screen Time?].

The same mechanism is now built into the games and apps your child uses every day. The loot box that might contain something rare. The next Roblox round that might go better. The Snapchat notification that might be from someone who matters. The Fortnite match that might end in a Victory Royale. The brain releases dopamine in anticipation of the reward, not when it arrives. This is why your child can’t stop.

But disconnect the device, and the compulsion largely collapses: the variable rewards stop, the social pressure disappears, and the relentless loop finally ends. You don’t have to eliminate every screen, but you must control the connection.

The brain’s prefrontal cortex (the executive function center) isn’t fully developed until around age 25, and perhaps later in an individual with ADHD. Every year you delay access to the Internet is another year of maturity for your child’s executive function system before it’s asked to regulate the most dysregulating product ever made.

It has been revealed that this is why a growing chorus of researchers is now urging parents to delay smartphones until at least high school (around age 14) and social media until at least age 16. The logic is simple: Let the most vulnerable period of brain development happen before your child can access the loop.

Here’s the empowering part: You control the devices, the accounts, the passwords, the router, and the timing of introduction. The strategy below is about exerting that control through environmental design – not nagging, not negotiating, not hoping a dysregulated brain suddenly regulates itself.

STEP 1: Make a pact. Counter the “I’m the only one without a phone” argument by encouraging three or four other families to agree to delay access together. Ask the parents of your child’s friends to make the pact. It’s easier to hold the line together than alone.

Sources indicate that STEP 2: Stop competing with the screen. Control access to the dopamine source through environmental design, not willpower. Screens go in a central location after a certain hour. Devices charge outside bedrooms, every night, no exceptions.

STEP 3: Build “earn-access” systems. Screens become available only after the non-negotiables are done. Homework must be completed, then Xbox. Follow the simple, consistent rules every single day. The structure does the work so you don’t have to issue the reminder.

Michael McLeod is the founder of GrowNOW ADHD and the author of The Executive Function Playbook.

#428. Industry News: When Anger Makes ADHD Harder to Manage

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (799 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Industry News: When Anger Makes ADHD Harder to Manage

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • It has been revealed that anger can lead to increasing symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
  • At work, Stan interrupts others and talks too much, leading to difficulties with others when his colleagues oppose his proposals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

It has been revealed that anger can lead to increasing symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). When a person is angry, it’s hard to sit still, which is already a symptom that many people with ADHD experience. When you’re angry, your mind can become clouded, leading to careless mistakes and not listening to others because you are distracted. Stan’s anger leads not only to problems in his relationship but also to impairments in functioning in the workplace.

At work, Stan interrupts others and talks too much, leading to difficulties with others when his colleagues oppose his proposals. His anger leads him to quickly blame others, and before he knows it, he’s accusing others of dropping the ball. What follows next might be called an “ADHD triple play.” Instead of a pitcher getting three players out on base, he alienates three of his colleagues in vital roles for ensuring timely completion of a project.

Industry observers note that stan’s anger, in part, creates the ADHD symptoms of talking too much and not waiting his turn or listening to others. These are symptoms of ADHD, showing how ADHD can exacerbate anger. He interrupts Rob without listening to him (not waiting his turn), insults Clara rather than listening to understand her perspective (not listening), accuses Lena of not responding to emails (talking too much), and doesn’t give her an opening to explain her higher priorities and apologize for the delay.

In a recent development, so, how do ADHD symptoms lead to anger? In Stan’s case, his ADHD often sets the backdrop for instigating his anger. At work, he doesn’t always listen closely to updates about current projects during check-ins with his colleagues. Because he missed information, he is more likely to accuse his colleagues of things they didn’t do or of dropping the ball on things they actually did do.

You may feel forgetful at times. You might be guilty of hearing what a colleague mentioned but then forgetting who said it, and you may find yourself getting angry at someone who wasn’t even involved. Or maybe you have a habit of butting in on others' conversations. Impulse control is a defining feature of ADHD, so butting in on others can lead to harsh comments from others, which can make them more angry. Then, as your anger alienates others, you might increasingly find yourself on the outside of conversations. You may sense the walls others put up, which can increase your anger at feeling left out. People might tiptoe around you to avoid your anger. It can only take one blow-up for others to have their radar up in every interaction, creating uncomfortable dynamics. This can lead to not being able to let go of the anger, which interferes with focus and listening to others.

Recent findings suggest that one way to stop this vicious cycle is to learn skills for feeling the anger without taking it out on others. A simple principle of practicing radical acceptance starts with knowing you can’t control other people’s behavior.

In a recent development, the recommendation to choose acceptance is fundamentally hard. Trying to change the other person means you have not accepted the person or the stark reality that while you can influence other people, you can’t change them.

This is so hard that it can take a lifetime to learn this lesson. There are stages of life where there are grey zones. If you have a rebellious teenager, how much can you accept behavior that can lead to serious consequences? There are clearly areas where you have influence and can work to change the other person, such as parenting, teaching, and coaching, where your job is to identify blind spots and work for change.

It has been revealed that research demonstrates that radical acceptance helps people to reframe negative events, which likely strengthens their coping skills (Segal et al., 2023). Keep in mind, radical acceptance does not mean approving of other people’s behavior. You may have valuable contributions to make, but your ADHD symptoms may cause others to dismiss you as a hothead. If this leads to failing to be persuasive, you may begin to feel ineffectual, like no one is listening to you, which can fuel more anger and resentment. Radical acceptance can help you acknowledge how frustrating it is to feel dismissed and choose a response that gives your ideas a better chance of being heard.

According to recent reports, segal, O., Sher, H., Aderka, I. M., & Weinbach, N. (2023). Does acceptance lead to change? Training in radical acceptance improves implementation of cognitive reappraisal. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 164, 1–9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brat.2023.104303.

#427. 3 Signs Your Adult Child's Problems Are Draining Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (671 w)

3 Signs Your Adult Child's Problems Are Draining Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that during a recent presentation for a local chapter of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, I spoke about the emotionally taxing challenges of overcoming helplessness when parenting struggling adult children.
  • For sure, challenges like serious mental illness, chronic avoidance, substance use, personality factors, and other challenges can limit what adult children can realistically handle on a day-to-day basis.
  • According to recent reports, as I discuss in my book—ou Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!—parental guilt and excessive rescuing create a powerful one-two punch that results in a relentless, emotionally exhausting cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recent findings suggest that during a recent presentation for a local chapter of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, I spoke about the emotionally taxing challenges of overcoming helplessness when parenting struggling adult children. I emphasized a central theme I see play out in the parents I coach, those contending with the overwhelming realities of seeing their grown children struggle in heartbreaking ways. By this, I mean how easily it is for parents to ironically lose themselves when they attempt to help their adult children find their way.

For sure, challenges like serious mental illness, chronic avoidance, substance use, personality factors, and other challenges can limit what adult children can realistically handle on a day-to-day basis. From working with so many parents in these situations, I appreciate these challenges. But no matter what difficulties parents face, they deserve a quality of life that includes moments of calm, serenity, self-nurturing, and pursuing activities that give them some joy, too.

According to recent reports, as I discuss in my book—ou Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!—parental guilt and excessive rescuing create a powerful one-two punch that results in a relentless, emotionally exhausting cycle. Here are three signs that you may be caught in this cycle.

Industry observers note that the parents of struggling adult children I coach often tell me they can only relax when their child is having a good day. For many parents in these situations, their state of mind is hypervigilant, constantly waiting for the next outburst, demand, or emotional push-pull cycle from their adult child.

Industry observers note that one of my parent clients remarked: "When my daughter is angry or disappointed, it's like a pit in my stomach." What does this mean for parents in these circumstances? The effects I hear: Checking their phones when out with friends or being otherwise internally preoccupied about when the next ball is about to drop. Related, one distinction I emphasized during my recent presentation was caring versus carrying. By this I mean reminding yourself that you can care deeply about your adult child's struggles without emotionally carrying all of them.

Do you open your laptop and research job or volunteering possibilities, look for therapists, provide money, try to discuss finances, and offer what feels like seemingly endless suggestions? If this is you, you are not alone. Nor are you alone if you end up feeling depleted and even resentful. It is so seductive to fall into the rescue trap, but remember that rescuing today to relieve distress may come at the cost of your adult child's self-confidence. Alternatively, even small accomplishments can help your adult child feel less helpless.

When you feel that compelling urge to offer solutions to your adult child, instead of rushing in wearing your "first responder" uniform, try asking, "What's one small step you feel capable of taking?" And to help this land well, be curious rather than critical about what your adult child can realistically manage.

It can feel maddening when your adult child accuses you of being selfish or reminds you of mistakes made when raising them. Many parents confide in me that they back down in these situations because they fear losing the relationship. Well, I have some really significant news for you. You can acknowledge your past parenting setbacks and mistakes without spending the rest of your days feeling like you have to keep paying emotionally or financially. Your adult child can validly feel disappointed in things you did as a parent, but that doesn't automatically mean you did everything wrong.

I hope you can come away from this post realizing that reclaiming your life does not mean abandoning your adult child. You have spent much of your life trying to support and help your struggling adult child. You are still entitled to build, live, and enjoy your own life as well.

#426. When Being the Strong One Makes It Hard to Ask for Help

When Being the Strong One Makes It Hard to Ask for Help

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • There's usually someone in every family, friendship group, or workplace whom people know they can count on.
  • It has been revealed that you have probably heard the advice to take care of yourself before caring for others, or "put your own oxygen mask on first".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

There's usually someone in every family, friendship group, or workplace whom people know they can count on. When problems in life arise, that person often gets called to support and fix the problem. Can you relate to being that person?

It has been revealed that you have probably heard the advice to take care of yourself before caring for others, or "put your own oxygen mask on first". For a lot of people, being the dependable one becomes central to their identity. But sometimes, being the person everyone counts on comes at the expense of taking care of yourself.

Reliability stops being a habit at some point and becomes who you are. You may start measuring your worth by how much you do for others and how little you need from them. Once that's set, asking for help may feel like breaking character.

In a recent development, that label, "strong one," can ultimately impact your self-image. It may make it more challenging to reach out when you need support. According to a 2025 review of caregiver experiences, participants reported that individuals, due to the pressure to stay strong and reliable, may feel that they are not living up to their role if they seek psychological help.

You may be the person that others call when they need advice or that people turn to when life gets difficult. But when someone asks how you're doing, you change the subject or say “I'm good.”.

In a recent 2025 study, experts examined people's beliefs about seeking and receiving help. They found that some people believe accepting help makes them less themselves or threatens their independence. Those beliefs were connected to how people experienced receiving help and to their well-being. Accepting help can be hard, not because support isn't there, but because it can impact how people see themselves.

You're probably used to running things and fixing problems on your own. Letting someone support you means admitting what's actually going on, and that gets uncomfortable when your whole identity is built on being the one who handles everything. To engage in vulnerability, try to ask yourself, "When did I last let myself be vulnerable?" Did it bring relief, or did it leave you reluctant to open up again? Letting someone help sometimes means letting go of control and showing them a side they don't usually see.

Industry observers note that it can be even harder when you feel pressure to appear "successful" and seem like you have everything under control. For instance, a recent study introduces another factor that can make asking for help difficult: competition. When employees viewed professional success as a contest, where one person's win meant someone else's loss, they were less likely to seek help from colleagues.

If you always identify as "the strong one", here are a few ways to become more comfortable accepting help:.

Sources indicate that you don't always have to be the person who has it all together. It's okay to have a bad day, ask someone for help, or admit that you don't know what to do. You spend so much time showing up for others that you sometimes forget you need support too.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

#425. Latest Update: Finding Solace and Comfort in Listening to Trees

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1265 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: Finding Solace and Comfort in Listening to Trees

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Recent findings suggest that as we approach the holiday season, each of us needs to find ways to take time for ourselves to recover from the activities and responsibilities of the season.
  • Industry observers note that listening to trees is one contemplative, meditative practice that invites us to slow down, become more attentive, and be more fully present in our everyday lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Recent findings suggest that as we approach the holiday season, each of us needs to find ways to take time for ourselves to recover from the activities and responsibilities of the season. Attention restoration theory, proposed by Kaplan and Kaplan (1989), suggests that if we are able to spend time in natural spaces, we can feel rested, renewed, and better able to cope with the stressors and demands of the season. Listening to trees is one healing practice that offers such a possibility by calming the mind and body. Through this practice, we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves, where we are in life, how we feel, what is vital to us, and what we need during this season.

Industry observers note that listening to trees is one contemplative, meditative practice that invites us to slow down, become more attentive, and be more fully present in our everyday lives. At the same time, spending quiet, contemplative time in natural spaces can lead us to experience feelings of transcendence. Transcendent experiences deepen our sense of connection to ourselves, to the natural world, to other people, and to something larger than our individual lives.

In a recent development, each person experiences transcendence differently. For some, it is connected to religious beliefs and spiritual practices; for others, it emerges through mind-body practice; for others, creative engagement can lead to transcendence. Experiencing transcendence does not involve the withdrawal from the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Instead, it helps us to be more deeply engaged with life by opening ourselves to a greater sense of connection, meaning, and belonging. Transcendent experiences serve dual purposes. They help us not only to ground ourselves more fully in the moment but also to connect to something that surpasses the immediate moment.

According to recent reports, the theory of transcendence (Tornstam, 1977) suggests that as we age, we tend to shift our perspective toward more spiritual and cosmic concerns. According to this view, transcendence includes a shift in meaning by recognizing that time is limited, and understanding and accepting the past while at the same time being more fully in the present. It also includes integrating and accepting all aspects of the self, and placing greater emphasis on connections and relationships (social transcendence), and the well-being of the planet. Transcendence in later life, or gerotranscendence, encompasses all three dimensions and focuses on a deep connection with the natural flow of life, with natural spaces, with the future of the planet, and future generations. As we acknowledge that our time is limited, transcendence can help us heal from loss, cope with bereavement, and navigate day-to-day expectations. Transcendence prompts us to shift our focus more fully to what truly matters, while at the same time connecting us to something beyond our individual lives.

Recent findings suggest that one therapeutic way of promoting transcendence is to regularly engage with nature — to listen to trees. Natural spaces provide solace, comfort, and healing, particularly in later life as aging adults contemplate the world they will leave behind. We also know that our individual well-being and happiness are intricately connected to the well-being of the planet. Listening to trees, walking through forests, spending time in parks and on beaches, or simply viewing nature are all physically and psychologically restorative and healing. The Biophilia Hypothesis (Wilson, 1984) even suggests that our connection with nature and natural spaces is fundamental to our survival. Natural immersion, even a few minutes daily in natural spaces, can also deepen our sensory awareness and draw our attention beyond our worries and anxieties toward a transcendent view in which we reflect on who we are, our place in the world, and what will be left when we are no longer here.

Certainly, human beings are not able to survive if nature does not. Our connection to nature is deeply rooted in our biology. Consciously or unconsciously, we have psychological, emotional, and physical connections to the natural world. I first learned about biophilia, our innate human tendency to be connected to nature and living organisms, in graduate school, when I studied the work of psychologist Erich Fromm. Fromm used the term in relation to a love of life and all that is alive (Fromm, 1973). This view has continued to inform my work and my personal life. In my ongoing work on well-being in later life, it has often been evident that our relationship with nature can sustain us throughout our lives, particularly during periods of vulnerability and loss.

According to recent reports, in a culture of haste, in our busy lives, and particularly during the winter holidays, when the days are short and light is limited, burnout is an ever-present possibility. Psychological theories have suggested that if we can find the time to connect with natural spaces during this time, we can manage our stressors and demands more effectively and feel more restored. Attention restoration theory (ART) states that time in natural spaces can replenish our ability to manage our attention, concentrate, and be mindfully present in our daily lives and in our holiday gatherings — and in the process help prevent feelings of loneliness and isolation.

Industry observers note that the American Psychological Association has stated that the healing and therapeutic benefits of spending time in natural spaces are available even after only spending two hours each week in nature. By setting aside less than 30 minutes a day to walk, unplug, breathe deeply, and mindfully take in our surroundings, we can begin to experience the restorative energy that nature has to offer. Even limited exposure to nature can be beneficial. Simply viewing nature can have a calming and positive influence on both physical and emotional well-being (Tahmaseb McConatha et al., 2023).

As the holidays approach, one way to stay grounded and prevent burnout is to reconnect with natural spaces. One simple practice is to listen to the trees. This experience can be deepened by finding a comfortable place near or beneath a tree and sitting quietly for a few moments. Even five minutes can help calm the mind and body.

There is no need to find the perfect spot or the perfect tree, or to set expectations or goals for your practice. Instead, give yourself permission to pause, be present, and take in the world around you. Simply engage your senses by noticing the sounds, scents, colors, textures, and gentle movements of nature. Allow yourself to become more aware of your surroundings and embrace the quiet of the moment.

When you are ready to move on, thank your tree for being there and offering stillness, comfort, and a place to simply be.

Renewing transcendence can be a regular practice. It does not require anything other than slowing down, connecting with nature and senses, and allowing ourselves to be fully present.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry. “Every mortal loss is an Immortal Gain,” William Blake wrote two centuries before her in his beautiful letter to a bereaved father.

We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.

And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.

That is what Judith Viorst explores in her 1987 consolation of a book Necessary Losses (public library) — an inquiry into the profound and far-reaching relationship between our losses and our gains, revealing renunciation as a fulcrum of growth. She paints the vast landscape of loss upon which life plays out:.

When we think of loss we think of the loss, through death, of people we love. But loss is a far more encompassing theme in our life. For we lose not only through death, but also by leaving and being left, by changing and letting go and moving on. And our losses include not only our separations and departures from those we love, but our conscious and unconscious losses of romantic dreams, impossible expectations, illusions of freedom and power, illusions of safety — and the loss of our own younger self, the self that thought it always would be unwrinkled and invulnerable and immortal.

These necessary losses… we confront when we are confronted by the inescapable fact… that we are essentially out here on our own; that we will have to accept — in other people and ourselves — the mingling of love with hate, of the good with the bad;… that there are flaws in every human connection; that our status on this planet is implacably impermanent; and that we are utterly powerless to offer ourselves or those we love protection — protection from danger and pain, from the in-roads of time, from the coming of age, from the coming of death; protection from our necessary losses.

These losses are a part of life — universal, unavoidable, inexorable. And these losses are necessary because we grow by losing and leaving and letting go.

As a sculpture is shaped by what is chiseled off from the block of stone, so too are we shaped by what we lose — by choice, with all the complexities and difficulties of letting go, or by the scythe of chance, which takes away as impartially as it gives. Viorst writes:.

The road to human development is paved with renunciation. Throughout our life we grow by giving up. We give up some of our deepest attachments to others. We give up certain cherished parts of ourselves. We must confront, in the dreams we dream, as well as in our intimate relationships, all that we never will have and never will be. Passionate investment leaves us vulnerable to loss. And sometimes, no matter how clever we are, we must lose… It is only through our losses that we become fully developed human beings.

Industry observers note that we enter the realm of loss the moment the umbilical cord is cut to sever what Viorst calls the “blurred-boundary bliss of mother-child oneness” — the primal loss that sets off the ongoing task of becoming ourselves. From this origin point, she traces the lifelong vector of losses and gains:.

According to recent reports, exchanging the illusion of absolute shelter and absolute safety for the triumphant anxieties of standing alone… we become a moral, responsible, adult self, discovering — within the limitations imposed by necessity — our freedoms and choices. And in giving up our impossible expectations, we become a lovingly connected self, renouncing ideal visions of perfect friendship, marriage, children, family life for the sweet imperfections of all-too-human relationships. And in confronting the many losses that are brought by time and death, we become a mourning and adapting self, finding at every stage — until we draw our final breath — opportunities for creative transformations.

In a sentiment the poet Mark Doty would echo — “you need to both remember where love leads and love anyway,” he wrote in his beautiful reckoning with love and loss — she adds:.

We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go.

Complement Necessary Losses, which goes on to explore the many regions of loss in human life and how they can become frontiers of growth, with Hannah Arendt on learning how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, Thoreau on living through a loss, and Alan Watts on learning not to think of gain and loss, then explore two uncommon lenses on loss: fractals and chlorophyll.

#423. Latest Update: Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2357 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Themarginalian

Latest Update: Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances… that’s what life is all about, that’s its task,” the young Dostoyevsky exulted in a letter to his brother just after his death sentence was repealed — death, that great clarifying force for what it means to be alive, what the stakes and sanctities of living are.
  • In the two centuries since, our understanding of what it means to be human, to be mortal and imperfect and ablaze with feeling, has altered dramatically as we have entrusted the cold logic of computation with answering the soul’s cry for connection, for creativity, for meaning — something Dostoyevsky’s contemporary Samuel Butler anticipated in his far-seeing admonition against the dehumanization of humanity in the hands of our machines, something that has metastasized in today’s technocratic cult of posthumanism.
  • In Jung vs Borg: Finding the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age, Glen Slater bridges ecology, depth psychology, systems theory, and various post-Cartesian philosophies to explore how this civilizational cult has effected “a widening divide between fabrication and authenticity, a loss of more self-aware and soulful modes of living, and an increase in anxiety and depression,” and what we can do to rewild the psyche and reclaim the soul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances… that’s what life is all about, that’s its task,” the young Dostoyevsky exulted in a letter to his brother just after his death sentence was repealed — death, that great clarifying force for what it means to be alive, what the stakes and sanctities of living are.

In the two centuries since, our understanding of what it means to be human, to be mortal and imperfect and ablaze with feeling, has altered dramatically as we have entrusted the cold logic of computation with answering the soul’s cry for connection, for creativity, for meaning — something Dostoyevsky’s contemporary Samuel Butler anticipated in his far-seeing admonition against the dehumanization of humanity in the hands of our machines, something that has metastasized in today’s technocratic cult of posthumanism.

In Jung vs Borg: Finding the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age, Glen Slater bridges ecology, depth psychology, systems theory, and various post-Cartesian philosophies to explore how this civilizational cult has effected “a widening divide between fabrication and authenticity, a loss of more self-aware and soulful modes of living, and an increase in anxiety and depression,” and what we can do to rewild the psyche and reclaim the soul.

He begins by drawing an analogy between the catalytic impact of Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring on awakening the modern ecological conscience and the need for a conscious awakening from the dangerous dream of posthumanism into which Silicon Valley has lulled us. Just as the industrial capitalism of Carson’s era commodified our planet’s ecosystems and elemental resources, Slater observes that digital capitalism has “turned our habits of mind into the earth’s most valuable commodity”; just as Carson pioneered the holistic view of ecology that may be our only path to saving Earth, her contemporary Carl Jung pioneered the holistic view of psychology that might, just might, save the human soul from death by commodification.

Whether or not we have turned the ecological corner, there is more consciousness about the way we relate to the world around us and the actions required to avert a climate catastrophe.

However, the world within us, the inner life of thought and emotion, is another matter. Here integrative understanding has been resisted. The human psyche, the ecosystem of the mind, with its own structures and dynamics, our relation to which is surely as significant as our relation to the outer world, now faces its own significant disruption, one that essentially parallels the syndrome Carson described… The depths of human nature are becoming harder to recognize and protect. Abundant information has furthered scientific knowledge but not human understanding. It has instead left us dazed, confused, and disoriented. Attention, motivation, identity, self-image, and the capacity to reason clearly and imagine deeply are all impacted… While the advantages of digital technologies are impressed upon us at every turn, the rapid entry of these technologies into every aspect of life is evidently impacting our ecology of mind.

With an eye to the urgency of “moving beyond objectification of the earth and of the bodies and minds that inhabit it,” he adds:.

In a recent development, the technosphere now overlays the ecosphere and we cannot help but inhale its post-industrial gases. Virtuality has begun to displace reality, making the ground of human existence hard to discern… The human psyche and the nature of the whole person are not only suffering in this technospheric environment, the suffering has itself been given over to technological solutions, resulting in a vicious cycle.

Industry observers note that the penchant for digital ways of relating, expanding faith in AI, and the one-sided education designed to service these things are combining to generate reductive conceptions of psychological life. We are, in particular, discounting the deeply human… the essential qualities of human experience, which extend from the instinctual patterns that shape basic behavior to the timeless values that mold the cultural imagination. The deeply human anchors the vertical axis of inner understanding; it grounds the ecology of mind. It is also what connects us to the more-than-human. In our era, however, an almost exclusive dedication to a horizontal axis of data gathering threatens this verticality and grounding. This is leading to a world drowning in information and thirsting for understanding.

At the heart of this civilizational crisis is the systemic compartmentalization of our experience, evident in the core polarities and dichotomies of Western culture — past and future, inner and outer, matter and spirit. Pulsating beneath it all is our dissociation from the life of the body, which connects us to the life of the Earth and the life of the universe. Everything beautiful that we touch and see and hear — birdsong, a sunrise, a kiss — is a bittersweet reminder that we have a body and are therefore mortal. Dissociation thrives on the denial of death that began with our ancestors’ mythologies of immortality and is culminating in Silicon Valley’s lurid and lucrative dreams of redesigning human nature, of downloading the mind onto disembodied machines and reducing the soul to a datum.

Pointing to Jung’s timeless cosmogony of the unconscious as the antidote to this damaging delusion, Slater writes:.

Jung’s comprehension of the depths of human nature constitutes an incisive counterpoint to the assumptions of posthumanism and to the dissociative bubble that presently fosters these assumptions… Jung sheds light on the self-regulating nature of the psyche and the archetypal forms behind this — forms we may choose to overlook but cannot ultimately dismiss. These forms pertain to brain structure, anatomy, and evolved patterns of perception and behavior. But they also reflect the larger rhythms of the cosmos and are seemingly woven into the fabric of life itself. Jung pointedly demonstrates that even as we have embraced reason and science, the archetypal world of non-rational impulses and religious ideas have continued to unconsciously influence our thoughts and actions.

Recent findings suggest that jung’s crowning contribution was to invite an understanding of the psyche as the foundation of all perception, experience, thought, feeling, and action — the wellspring of our humanity. In exploring the psychology of the unconscious with all of its interlaced convolutions — archetypes and complexes, projections and introjections — Jung illuminated the way our dreams and fantasies unconsciously shape the course of our lives, the way our arts and sciences cohere into a vast collective unconscious that shapes the course of our civilization. With an eye to Jung’s legacy, Slater writes:.

It is the psyche that contains the pursuit of the angelic, the claims of the animal body, and the structures and dynamics that join the two. It is the psyche that generates and insists upon the symbolic expressions of culture, which are often based on the transformative and aspirational power of ordinary, even elemental, things — mountains and rivers, suns and moons, fire and rain — thereby reminding us of the inextricable bond between mind and world. If cosmic matter has given rise to consciousness, and we are now called to grasp the nature of consciousness, realizing that thinking about our thinking is the necessary companion of any exploration and understanding of the universe that surrounds us, our grasp of the inner world becomes just as vital as our grasp on the outer world — perhaps even more so.

Nearly a century after the Swiss poet, philosopher, and linguist Jean Gebser made his exquisite case for the evolution of consciousness, Slater reflects on Jung’s legacy and writes:.

It has been revealed that godlike power necessitates godlike responsibility. This begins with self-awareness, which is rooted in a sober consideration of the human psyche, the most critical part of which is shedding light on the shadow side of our willful pursuits… Will and reason alone cannot form a seat of wise agency — a far more expansive consciousness is required.

Recent findings suggest that an expansion of consciousness is imperative if we are to make responsible use of the transformative power in our hands… With divine guidance largely beyond our secular vision, we are left to look within for something deeper than our controlling inclinations and to look without to perceive the guidance of nature’s intelligence. Guidance must ultimately come from dialogue with these marginalized sources of knowledge and from the cultural imagination, which shapes this dialogue. The result will be a “co-creation” — a partnership between innovation, self-knowledge, and a cosmology befitting this age. Such a co-creative process will mitigate and shape our technologies as well as generate opportunities for spiritual renewal.

Such co-creation, Slater argues, demands a reanimated view of existence — one that “counters the commodification of all things that is right now consuming us,” one that “conveys a confluence of spirit and matter — the very means by which a sense of soul is generated.” He writes:.

It has been revealed that A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent. The great task of this late modern era is thus to bring together what the spiritual preoccupations of the old world and the material focus of the new world have torn apart. The psyche demonstrates us this dependency whenever a person or group attempts to embrace one without the other, in the way the neglected side begins to rule the unconscious… But the earth process itself suggests we rediscover nature as spirit as well as understand it as matter — nature as presence, intelligence, and root source of inspiration and imagination… Both mind and earth are calling for perspectives capable of marrying these dimensions of reality.

Countering this fragmentation of reality requires, above all, learning to resist our dissociative tendencies and trust our emotions — for, as philosopher Martha Nussbaum observes in her masterwork on the intelligence of the emotions, “emotions are not just the fuel that powers the psychological mechanism of a reasoning creature, they are parts, highly complex and messy parts, of this creature’s reasoning itself.” Slater considers the building blocks of this self-trust:.

Sources indicate that such trust begins with a natural appreciation of emotional intelligence and the guiding potential of this intelligence, which can feel like it emanates from a will of its own. This trust may grow over a long time or it may come as a sudden life-lesson. But few things beyond the contemplation of emotional responses open the door to the deeply human and the awareness of having an inner partner [that] operates apart from conscious, rational direction. To be full of emotion is to be animated by something in spite of ourselves; perhaps this is why we end up regularly conversing with the sadness or anger that grips us. Emotions like these stand in need of negotiation, mollification or perhaps just more attention. Often, when we want to keep moving on, the emotions will not allow it. And sometimes when we would choose to hold back, emotions charge ahead.

In a recent development, because our emotions are a fundament of our human nature, which is itself a fractal of Nature, they are the raw material for the co-creative process that offers an antidote to the dehumanization of humanity. Slater writes:.

We are affected by desire for more satisfying ways of being, outrage about all that is regularly exploited and destroyed, fear of what stresses and overwhelms, and shame about participating in the machinations of it all. To consider the way emotion comes upon us, from a nature we call “ours,” all the while being a branch of Nature itself, calls into question whether these emotions even belong to us or to the sufferings of the world, and we are being directed to feel and respond on its behalf. In other words, our animation may be the world’s way of speaking to us, and thus be an indispensable dimension of the co-creative process. Recognition of the autonomous intelligence of these deep emotional responses may be an invitation to attune ourselves to the presence of the earth’s own intelligence — or intelligences.

It is the psyche that bridges these regions of intelligence, the inner and the outer, the human and the cosmic, death and life. Slater writes:.

The psyche, which is obviously grounded in nature, also leads us beyond this ground, into a concern with destiny and leaving some trace of ourselves in service to humanity… We neither have to lean on notions of a spirit that literally departs the body, nor on fantasies of downloading our minds. Rather, we accept that the substance of psychic experience, accumulated over a lifetime, marks everything we do and everyone around us. And such a marking can be dreamed on. Life and death thus intertwine to produce defining qualities of being.

In a passage evocative of James Baldwin’s soulful insistence that “it is necessary… to know that in oneself, waiting to be found, there is a light,” and that “everything in our lives depends on how we bear the light,” Slater adds:.

The wonder of psychological life is that this dimming of the ego-light allows the perception of another light, one that has been in the background all along… Posthumanism brightens the ego-light, the light of the intellect and will that blankets the light of natural consciousness the wise ape presents to us. It fails to reconcile our spiritual reach and our instinctual ground. It cracks cultural vessels that have always incubated this reconciliation and truncates rather than extends the human experiment.

Lensing Jung’s legacy through the light of thinkers as varied as Hannah Arendt, William James, Yuval Harari, and Oliver Sacks, Slater goes on to explore and celebrate the countercultural movement in the margins of this techno-trance — ways of seeing and of being that, unlike posthumanism, refuse to exclude beauty, eros, and transcendence from the human story, a story told in the language of the soul, irreducible to data. Complement Jung vs Borg with Iain McGilchrist on how we render reality, James Bridle on rethinking intelligence, and Pierre Teilhard de Chardin on bridging the scientific and the sacred, then revisit Jung himself on the most key paradigm for living.

#422. Tech Report: Did a Narcissistic Boss Cost You Your Career?

Tech Report: Did a Narcissistic Boss Cost You Your Career?

💡 Key Takeaways
