📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Prada was a 29-year-old registered nurse when she came to my office in tears, saying she hated her job and was having panic attacks. Sharon, the hospital’s human resources director, perceived that the trauma exposure in her work in the emergency room was the source of the panic attacks and sent her to specialized resilience training.

It has been revealed that devin, a 42-year-old software architect, came to my office with concerns about depression. He feared losing his job because he was too old and believed that newly introduced artificial intelligence programs were replacing him.

It has been revealed that at first glance, their struggles seemed understandable, given the unique demands of their professions. The trauma exposure, aging concerns, and technological pressures were real. But more conversations revealed something deeper and more destabilizing: a high-achieving, abusive, and narcissistic boss.

According to recent reports, the challenge is that organizations often view a high-achiever as the goose that lays the golden egg, making them revered and supported. But when that high-achiever also commits narcissistic abuse, they can be untouchable. And the fallout of their abusive tactics resides in the long-term wounds of countless victims.

In It's Not You: Identifying and Healing from Narcissistic People, Ramani Durvasula describes how many therapists are trained to address the person’s isolated symptoms and often miss the larger impacts of narcissistic relationships. She also echoes what Lundy Bancroft explained almost 25 years ago in Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men—the abusive person is a master of disguise and actually gains footing with the therapist, while the abused person who shows up as anxious and closed can get further gaslit and retraumatized by the therapist. Moreover, interventions focused on appeasement or better communication can reinforce and escalate manipulation and abusive tactics.

Now imagine that third party is HR, an executive coach, or an organizational consultant.

And imagine that the abusive person is exceptionally accomplished, charismatic, influential, and valuable to the organization.

Sources indicate that who gets believed? Who gets coached? Who gets labeled difficult? And who quietly disappears from the organization?

Given these complex dynamics, I was surprised to read an article in the Journal of Business Ethics suggesting that clear codes of conduct and consequences could help address narcissistically abusive supervision. The authors’ research revealed that leaders high in narcissistic rivalry employ abusive supervision when they perceive employees as deviating from their authority or organizational rules; yet they suggest: “It is essential that organizations recognize the importance of fostering a supportive environment in which both leaders and followers are equipped with the skills and knowledge to interact respectfully with each other” (Gauglitz & Schyns, 2024).

While rules for conduct can establish best practices and delineate what is prohibited, they may fail to address the hidden dynamics of manipulation, coercion, and stealth sabotage.

In Ten Keys to Staying Empowered in a Power Struggle, I explain how manipulative tactics often operate through confusing double-binds, intermittent praise, shifting expectations, selective memory, and gaslighting. These patterns can leave people questioning their judgment while the person causing harm appears credible and composed.

I have witnessed people who left jobs—and entire careers—without understanding how an abusive workplace dynamic eroded their confidence, health, and sense of agency.

If something like this happened to you, or someone you know, consider these five questions:.

In contrast, healthy workplace dynamics and leadership allow disagreement without humiliation, accountability without retaliation, and growth without diminishing someone's dignity.

Sometimes, recognizing what happened is the first step toward healing, which involves reclaiming what you lost, honoring what you endured, and breaking the cycle of abuse that continues long after the abuser is gone through self-blame, shame, and the transformation of someone else’s cruelty into your own inner voice.

Sources indicate that gauglitz, I. K., & Schyns, B. (20240801). Triggered Abuse: How and Why Leaders with Narcissistic Rivalry React to Follower Deviance. Journal of Business Ethics, 193(1), 115–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-023-05579-7.

#421. Breaking: Where the Joy Is

Breaking: Where the Joy Is

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of the most important things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair.
  • Joy is not difficult to find, but it can be difficult to trust — partly because the merchants of pseudo-morality have sold us the dangerous myth that, in an unjust world, despair is an emblem of our solidarity with justice, and partly because in this age of grandiosity, we have forgotten that joy is a plurality of smallnesses: a function of what Hermann Hesse called “the little joys” that light up a life with presence.
  • Sources indicate that we need them, these reminders that joy is not a denial of suffering but the fulcrum of our resilience in its midst; that it comes to us not with horns and cymbals but as a distant whisper from the birthplace of the ordinary, not like a bouquet of roses offered with champagne but like the lovely little weed blooming through a crack in the sidewalk of the quotidian.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the most important things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair. “Experience of conflict and a load of suffering has taught me that what matters above all is to celebrate joy… Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, precisely because it is so easy to do so,” the artist René Magritte wrote in his timeless manifesto for the courage of joy in the wake of the second World War of his life. “We’ve all had too much sorrow — now is the time for joy,” Nick Cave sang an epoch later as he contemplated the paradox of joy against the backdrop of unimaginable loss.

Joy is not difficult to find, but it can be difficult to trust — partly because the merchants of pseudo-morality have sold us the dangerous myth that, in an unjust world, despair is an emblem of our solidarity with justice, and partly because in this age of grandiosity, we have forgotten that joy is a plurality of smallnesses: a function of what Hermann Hesse called “the little joys” that light up a life with presence.

Sources indicate that we need them, these reminders that joy is not a denial of suffering but the fulcrum of our resilience in its midst; that it comes to us not with horns and cymbals but as a distant whisper from the birthplace of the ordinary, not like a bouquet of roses offered with champagne but like the lovely little weed blooming through a crack in the sidewalk of the quotidian. And that is precisely what artist-philosopher Maira Kalman offers in her book Joy (public library) — a love letter to the sweet strangeness of life, to its unboastful wonderland of small miracles, to the way it expands and expands and expands the moment we contract the aperture of attention onto a single unit of gladness.

that suffering and sorrow envelop our planet and our little lives.

And then it goes where we, short-termists of the present, rarely go: into the lives of some of her heroes who lived through times and turmoils far more unimaginable than ours: She paints Alfred Dreyfus sitting in his prison cell on Devil’s Island; she paints the bedroom in which Beethoven, fully deaf, wrote “Ode to Joy”; she paints Virginia Woolf and her “surprisingly colorful” sitting room just before she filled her coat pockets with stones and waded into the River Ouse; she paints Kafka under the black hat he wore as a helmet of despair, his hand rested tenderly on his beloved dog.

As if to remind us that we are always in relationship with those whose lives have touched ours, whether living or dead, whether or not we have ever met them, she paints her imaginary conversations with Gertrude Stein, with James Baldwin, with Vladimir Nabokov.

Dog punctuate this love letter to joy, cradled in arms and curled in corners, peeking from the pages with their searching eyes and their uncomplicated sweetness: “Isn’t that the answer to everything,” she writes with an eye to a friend who tends to her four dogs “with unlimited care and love.”.

And people, of course, so many people with their strange and soulful faces, each a universe of feeling conjured up with just a few brush strokes.

What might happen if you could leave gloom (pervasive) and perils (lurking) for just a little bit?

What solace might you find if you turned your gaze to a thing of beauty.

She reverences trees, “kind and strong and loving,” and a medieval painting of “a saint with a terrific hairdo” at the Met, and a beautiful man with a porkpie hat at the bookstore, and the fig tree in a friend’s backyard, and people singing, and a young man playing Bach on his violin under the cherry tree, and Pablo Casals playing Bach on his cello while smoking a pipe.

And isn’t it true we are lost without music?

Do children not give us our reason?

Page by page of these small reveries — birdsong, a summer breeze, books and libraries, a woman “lost in thought basking in the morning sun with her little dog by her side,” the bowl of fresh berries on a dying friend’s table, the way a garden, any garden, “can fill you with elation,” the way sitting by the ocean, any ocean, is “enough to make your spirits soar,” the way holding a child’s gaze can make you “forget all the sorrows of the world” — you discover that any moment of joy contains “the essence of what it means to be alive.”.

And don’t I know, and don’t you know, how one sublime instant, one sublime, fleeting instant, changes everything and makes the world right?

It isn’t nothing, that instant — this atom of time, this unit of eternity, the only thing we ever have that is ours for the keeping. “Time is a reality confined to the instant and suspended between two voids,” philosopher Gaston Bachelard wrote. Because attention is what fills the instant with reality, how we spend our attention is how we spend our lives. Emerging from these painted pages is a beckoning to train our attention on joy in all its variousness, its unassuming abundance, its sacred smallness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • We get a lot of things wrong about one another.
  • Recent findings suggest that psychologists have spent decades documenting the many ways our perceptions of others can be distorted; we are frequently wrong about others and even ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

We get a lot of things wrong about one another. We often think we understand what other people think of us, and assume that the handful of actions we observe tells us something meaningful about their personality as a whole. Someone behaves rudely, and we conclude they are an unpleasant person. Someone struggles to find work, and we wonder whether they are trying hard enough. We interpret other people’s behaviour through our own experiences, expectations and beliefs, often with considerable confidence and remarkably little information1.

Recent findings suggest that psychologists have spent decades documenting the many ways our perceptions of others can be distorted; we are frequently wrong about others and even ourselves. These biases have consequences far beyond our interpersonal relationships. They shape whom we trust, whom we blame, what we believe people deserve and, ultimately, the institutions and policies we create and sustain.

Many of us feel we are living through unprecedented times. Particularly since 2020, rapid technological change, political polarisation and growing uncertainty about the future have made the world feel increasingly difficult to understand. But people have felt similarly at other points in history, and often with good reason.

In nineteenth-century Britain, the Industrial Revolution was transforming almost every aspect of society. Population growth, industrialisation and urbanisation brought extraordinary economic opportunities alongside increasingly visible poverty, overcrowding and disease. Governments were faced with social problems on a scale that existing institutions were poorly equipped to manage.

One response was the Poor Law Amendment Act of 18342.

For centuries, responsibility for assisting people experiencing poverty had rested largely with local parishes. Someone who became ill, lost their employment or could no longer support their family might receive money, food or other assistance without having to leave their home. The system was inconsistent, often ungenerous and increasingly expensive, but it afforded local authorities some discretion to respond to individual circumstances.

The 1834 reforms sought to make poor relief more efficient, less costly and less attractive to those thought capable of supporting themselves. Administration was reorganised, and assistance was increasingly tied to entering a workhouse. Relief outside the workhouse continued in some circumstances, for the sick and elderly, but even then, many elderly and disabled people still ended up in the workhouse.

It has been revealed that workhouses were deliberately designed to be places people would enter only out of desperation2. We are familiar with these institutions through Charles Dickens, whose Oliver Twist depicts a world in which poverty is often treated as a moral offence. Families were often separated, food really was gruel, and residents were subjected to arduous work and strict discipline. The severity was not an unfortunate consequence of inadequate resources but part of the intended deterrent.

The reasoning was straightforward enough: If assistance was too easy or readily available, people might become dependent upon it rather than seek employment. In fact, educating children was, in theory, supposed to be part of a workhouse remit, but in practice the standard varied considerably. Make assistance sufficiently unpleasant, and those capable of supporting themselves would presumably find a way to do so.

Of course, this reasoning depended on a particular understanding of why people were poor in the first place. A person unable to find employment, earning wages insufficient to support a family, or living with illness could not necessarily improve their circumstances through the threat of punishment. But policies built around assumptions about individual motivation often failed to account for precisely those conditions.

Sources indicate that I don’t think the nineteenth-century reformers were simply cruel or stupid. They were attempting to manage substantial social and economic changes with the knowledge, institutions and political priorities available to them. Some were undoubtedly concerned with improving administration and reducing costs, while others had a more punitive understanding of poverty. The reforms also served the interests of those who wanted to reduce their contributions towards poor relief.

But the consequences illustrate something important: Our explanations of human behaviour influence the solutions we consider reasonable, even when those explanations are incomplete or mistaken.

Nearly two centuries later, we are living through another period of extraordinary transformation. Technology has changed how we work, communicate, form relationships and participate in society. Our scientific understanding of the world has expanded beyond anything nineteenth-century reformers could have imagined.

And, unlike our predecessors, we now possess the knowledge and technological capabilities to address many problems that once seemed insurmountable.

We have developed effective technologies that can substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions3. Advances in agriculture have enabled us to produce enough food globally to feed the world’s population, despite its extraordinary growth4. Vaccines, public health measures and medical research have given us tools to prevent and respond to devastating diseases.

But climate change continues, millions experience hunger, and preventable diseases still cause enormous suffering.

These problems are complex, and scientific and technological limitations remain. But increasingly, the question is not simply whether humanity possesses the knowledge or resources to improve people’s lives. The obstacles are frequently social, cultural, economic and political. They involve how resources are distributed, how institutions operate, whose interests they serve, and whether people can cooperate towards shared goals.

And underlying many of these obstacles are the explanations we give for why people believe and behave as they do.

Consider a more recent example of advocacy for punitive measures. Over several decades, psychiatrist James Gilligan studied violence in American prisons and sought to reform the way prisoners were treated5,6. In Massachusetts prisons, where violence, humiliation and abuse were commonplace, he developed reforms that emphasised treating prisoners with respect, providing psychological treatment and creating opportunities for education7.

Gilligan reported significant reductions in violence, and his research into prison education found extraordinarily low rates of reoffending among prisoners who completed college degrees. Even those regarded as among the most violent could, under different conditions, behave quite differently. But when William Weld became governor of Massachusetts in 1991, he opposed providing prisoners with free college education, arguing that people who couldn't afford university might start committing crimes just to get a degree in prison. His administration subsequently withdrew much of the state funding and undermined education delivery, despite reported drops in recidivism7,8. Sound familiar?

Recent findings suggest that neither understanding nor policy exists independently of the other. Our beliefs influence the systems we support, while those systems shape the circumstances and behaviours we subsequently observe. The resulting outcomes can then appear to confirm the assumptions that helped produce them—making the system self-reinforcing.

Institutions are also shaped by competing interests, and some people benefit considerably from arrangements that disadvantage others. Those with influence may understand perfectly well what a particular policy or economic incentive is likely to produce.

But the interests of a relatively small number of powerful actors can become difficult to challenge when much larger populations are persuaded that the existing arrangements serve their interests too, or that the problems those arrangements create are simply the fault of the individuals experiencing them.

This is where our understanding of one another becomes immensely consequential.

The way we explain another person’s circumstances influences how willing we are to help them, what we consider fair, and whether we recognise a problem as something that requires societal intervention. These explanations become part of our cultural understanding of how the world works, and help determine which institutions we defend and which we are prepared to change.

Recent findings suggest that this blog is about those explanations: How we come to understand other people’s behaviour, why we so often get it wrong, and what the consequences are for the societies we live in. I’ll draw on research across psychology, biology, anthropology, and the social sciences to explore how individual behaviour interacts with the environments in which it develops. Sometimes that will mean examining the assumptions we make about our friends, strangers and, most importantly, ourselves. At other times, it will mean considering how those same assumptions influence our attitudes towards responsibility, inequality, politics and the institutions that govern our lives.

Understanding these processes is only part of the task. If we want different outcomes, we also have to use that understanding to change the conditions that produce them.

The nineteenth-century workhouse offers one illustration of what can happen when our assumptions about human behaviour inform our attempts to solve social problems. Seeing the same way of thinking manifest centuries later, despite all our accumulated knowledge, tells us something important about the real barriers to solving our problems.

One of the great challenges of our time is learning how to use knowledge to build societies that work better for the people living within them.

Perhaps a useful place to begin is by examining how much we still get wrong about one another and ourselves.

#419. Breaking: Should I Let My Child Play Grand Theft Auto?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1383 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: Should I Let My Child Play Grand Theft Auto?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • According to recent reports, tomorrow, the biggest video game of all time will be released.
  • It has been revealed that the Grand Theft Auto games are an extremely violent, darkly satirical exploration of American culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

According to recent reports, tomorrow, the biggest video game of all time will be released. The latest game in the blockbuster Grand Theft Auto series took 13 years and over a billion dollars to make. It’s predicted to be the biggest opening of any entertainment product in history.

It has been revealed that the Grand Theft Auto games are an extremely violent, darkly satirical exploration of American culture. Currently, the game will only include a single-player story, but a multiplayer version is slated for release next year. I wrote previously about how to keep your kids safe while playing multiplayer games here.

Sources indicate that it is unclear what content this game will include, as no one has discussed it publicly. If leaks are to be believed, the game will feature full nudity, including visible genitals and sex scenes. Based on previous entries, it will certainly feature drug use, offensive language including racial slurs, and frequent gun violence, including the ability to shoot police officers.

Industry observers note that the game will absolutely not be meant for children. It is rated “M for Mature,” which means it is designed to be played only by people age 17 and older. However, many young people, especially high school boys, want to play it. I have worked with a number of young people who regularly play the previous game in the series, some of whom started as young as nine years old.

Industry observers note that some parents might decide to make an exception for their children, as they do with some R-rated movies. My parents let me watch some R-rated action movies like The Matrix as a young teenager, but they definitely would not have let me watch movies with explicit sexual content or graphic violence.

Parents understandably have questions about whether the game is appropriate and whether it will influence their children like the media suggests.

In a recent development, GTA games are extremely violent. I likely killed thousands of computer-controlled characters in the process of completing GTA V. They are not meant for children.

According to recent reports, however, there is no evidence that the game, or any other violent media, will make players violent in the real world. The studies that purport to show a connection between violent video games and aggression often have serious methodological problems. Further, despite what the news media suggests, school shooters are actually less likely to enjoy violent video games than their peers. I wrote about this in more depth in a previous article.

Although video games are unlikely to make children violent, there is some evidence that our opinions and values can be shaped by the media we consume.

According to recent reports, for example, people who live in the Nadroga province of Fiji had traditionally viewed larger bodies as healthy and desirable. This began to change starting in 1995 when they started receiving outside television signals. Researchers surveyed a group of teen girls within a month of American television reaching their region and again three years later. Historically, dieting was rare in this area, and none of the girls reported vomiting to control their weight in 1995. But by the second survey, 69 percent of these same girls had started to diet, and 11 percent had begun intentionally vomiting to control their weight. That is, just three years of exposure to Western media seems to have fundamentally altered how the entire region viewed body image.

Importantly, GTA is not alone in featuring problematic elements. Each can be found in other movies, games, and even the news on TV. It is unlikely that this game will be the first time an older teenager hears racial slurs or sexual language, or sees nudity or violence. Most recent R-rated crime movies feature all of the above. Modern horror movies like Saw or Hereditary feature much more graphic violence than GTA does. Ultimately, this is why the series’ satire is relevant; the games are simply a more extreme version of the culture in which many of us have grown up.

It is therefore unlikely that simply playing this game will have more of an effect on its players’ values than their other daily cultural experiences. The aforementioned girls in Fiji, whose body image was drastically changed, were being exposed to a foreign culture they had not experienced before. American teens are already saturated with media showing extreme violence, sexuality, and crime.

In a recent development, however, people who consume more violent media tend to believe that the world is more dangerous than it really is. Researchers who have studied this “mean world syndrome” have found that people who consume more media are more likely to fear violence and trust others less. If playing this game drastically increases the amount of time an individual spends consuming media, it is possible that they will believe themselves to be in more danger in the real world than they did before playing.

In a recent development, parents who do not want their children to play this game should know that their children can simply download the game independently. Nearly all game consoles and computers now permit users to purchase the game digitally with a credit card or console-specific currency. To prevent this, concerned parents can set parental locks on game devices, including preventing purchases of games rated “M for Mature” (similar to blocking all R or NC-17 movies), or requiring a password before any digital purchases.

I also recommend that parents who are unsure whether their children should play such a game supervise their children or play along with them. As I wrote previously, this not only provides the opportunity to bond with children through their interests, but also lets parents talk about the game’s content and provide valuable context to what the children are experiencing. When the multiplayer version is eventually released, make sure that your kids are not chatting with strangers by turning off public chat.

Industry observers note that whether to let your children play a game like this is a personal decision. Reasonable parents can choose to ignore the recommended age if they understand the content of the game and believe their children are emotionally mature enough to consume it.

Below is a non-exhaustive list of questions parents should consider before purchasing the game for their children:.

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto VI will have a number of elements which most parents would find extremely objectionable. These are not likely to psychologically harm people who are mature enough to manage the subject matter and understand it in context.

It has been revealed that however, the game’s content is highly inappropriate for most young people, and parents should proceed cautiously. If parents decide to buy it for their children, I recommend supervising them while playing and having open conversations about what their children are witnessing and experiencing.

#418. Should Parents Genetically Enhance Their Children?

Should Parents Genetically Enhance Their Children?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a world where everyone is healthy, intelligent, long-living, and happy.
  • Sources indicate that in 2001, when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) enabled parents to select from multiple embryos, Julian Savulescu introduced the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB), arguing that parents have obligations to choose the child expected to have the best life.
  • It has been revealed that savulescu, Sandberg, and Kahane jointly propose the following definition for human enhancement: “[a]ny change in the biology or psychology of a person which increases the chances of leading a good life in the relevant set of circumstances.” According to this welfarist definition, a conception of normality is not needed to define enhancement, as we do not define an enhancement as being better than normal, but simply being better full stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Imagine a world where everyone is healthy, intelligent, long-living, and happy. Intuitively, this seems wonderful, albeit unrealistic. However, recent scientific developments in genetic engineering, namely CRISPR-Cas, bring the question into public discourse: how the genetic enhancement of humans should be evaluated morally. This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

Sources indicate that in 2001, when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) enabled parents to select from multiple embryos, Julian Savulescu introduced the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB), arguing that parents have obligations to choose the child expected to have the best life. In this post, I argue that accepting the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP) that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par commits one to accepting the parental obligation to genetically enhance their prospective children—that is, embryos—a position Savulescu doesn’t explicitly endorse but I argue is committed to.

It has been revealed that savulescu, Sandberg, and Kahane jointly propose the following definition for human enhancement: “[a]ny change in the biology or psychology of a person which increases the chances of leading a good life in the relevant set of circumstances.” According to this welfarist definition, a conception of normality is not needed to define enhancement, as we do not define an enhancement as being better than normal, but simply being better full stop. Medical treatments are therefore just a form of enhancement. If a genetic alteration in an embryo is not expected to lead to a better life for that human, then it is simply not an enhancement.

Recent findings suggest that consequentialists are only concerned with outcomes; how these outcomes are achieved is morally irrelevant. Killing and letting die are thus ceteris paribus morally equivalent. To formulate my argument:.

(1) Those who want to be parents have the obligation to select the child that is expected to have the best life, or at least as good a life as the others, based on the relevant available information (= the PPB).

(2) Application of the PPB leads to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without the application of the PPB, based on the relevant available information.

(3) If act A and act B have the same expected consequences, then they are morally on par. (= the CP).

(4) Genetic enhancements in embryos lead to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without genetic enhancements, based on the relevant available information.

(5) Therefore, those who want to be parents have the obligation to genetically enhance embryos.

The ‘slippery slope’ is genuine.

According to recent reports, an objection often put forward is that genetic enhancements have risks that are too high or unknown and would make the life of the person targeted worse. However, when genetic alterations are expected to be more harmful than beneficial, they do not count as genetic enhancements and are therefore ruled out. Demanding a risk of zero to the targeted agents is over-demanding; otherwise, medical treatments would never be at the point they are today. In 2015, Chinese researchers released an article showing that the gene editing of human embryos is technologically possible.

In a recent development, still, many therapies and treatments in medicine are often deemed obligatory, even though there is no consent, for example, vaccination. Also, everyone should be familiar with parents sending their children to school, even though their children might not have given their consent. As a child, I certainly wondered who gave my parents my permission to do so. Just as education makes us more autonomous, genetically increased intelligence would serve the same purpose. Genetic enhancements aim to increase rather than limit one's possible choices in life.

In a recent development, there is a rather famous critic against genetic enhancements from Mehlman and Botkin, that is, being too expensive and therefore even when all parents follow their obligation, the children of rich parents will be far more enhanced or those of poor parents won’t get any enhancements at all. Concerning the worry of unequal access through wealth, Savulescu argues that this is not an objection to the PPB, hence genetic enhancements, but to all purchases of benefits like better education or healthcare. If equality matters, then these benefits should be available to all.

That is to say, those who accept the PPB and the CP must bite the bullet and accept that parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. As a consequentialist, Julian Savulescu should have no problem doing so.

If you enjoyed this short essay, you might enjoy the much longer version, on which it is based, where I go into much more detail: click here.

#417. Latest Update: Rethinking Relationships Through the Lens of Asexuality

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)

Latest Update: Rethinking Relationships Through the Lens of Asexuality

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • This post was co-written with Paula Bange and Laura Botzet, Ph.D.
  • The belief that sexuality is a universal and essential part of the human experience is deeply ingrained in our society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

This post was co-written with Paula Bange and Laura Botzet, Ph.D.

The belief that sexuality is a universal and essential part of the human experience is deeply ingrained in our society. In pop culture, this assumption is especially visible. Reality TV shows like Too Hot To Handle are entirely built around the premise that people cannot resist sexual temptation. At the same time, these shows reflect the common idea that sexual attraction is closely tied to the beginning of romantic relationships. Accordingly, much of relationship science has been anchored in the idea that sexual attraction is a key mechanism guiding partner choice with the ultimate goal of having and raising children (1).

Industry observers note that asexuality, the lack of (or limited presence of) sexual attraction, challenges this long-held assumption. Looking at relationships through the lens of asexuality raises crucial questions: What do we really need for intimacy and connection? And does a fulfilling life necessarily require sexual attraction or a romantic partner?

It has been revealed that if sexual attraction were a necessary condition for romantic love and relationships, asexual people must not want relationships. Right? This couldn’t be further from the truth. Research clearly shows that many asexual people seek emotionally intimate, close relationships but prefer not to engage in sexual intimacy (1, 2, 3, 4).

According to recent reports, this highlights that romantic and sexual attraction don’t always go hand in hand. The split attraction model (5) distinguishes between different types of attraction, particularly sexual and romantic attraction, which do not always align. While many people experience both together, asexual people may experience romantic attraction without sexual desire. In other words, they might not desire sexual intercourse, but they fall in love, seek companionship, and build committed relationships.

Sources indicate that at the same time, asexual people are less likely to be in romantic relationships (6) compared to allosexual people (individuals who experience sexual attraction). In addition, in our own work, we found that asexual women are more interested in being single in the future compared to heterosexual women (2). Given that decades of research have shown that being in a romantic relationship, especially a satisfying one, is linked to greater happiness, better health, and reduced loneliness (7), this seems like bad news.

Contradicting this assumption, being in a romantic relationship does not seem to protect against loneliness for asexual people in the same way it does for heterosexual, bisexual, and homosexual people (6). Even when asexual people are in a good relationship, it doesn’t reduce their loneliness as much as it does for other groups. Yet, being in a bad relationship doesn’t increase their loneliness as much either. In short, asexual people seem to be less affected—positively or negatively—by relationship quality compared to others. Dovetailing with these results, asexual singles are most satisfied with being single compared to other sexual orientations (8).

Together, these findings challenge the common belief that everyone wants and benefits from a romantic relationship. For asexual people, there may be even more good reasons to stay single. While some asexual people may prefer being single because they anticipate difficulties in finding a partner and maintaining a relationship that fits their needs, other asexual people do not experience romantic attraction and may not want any romantic relationship at all. Yet other forms of connection, such as friendships, may offer an notable source of intimacy.

According to recent reports, indeed, emerging research highlights that asexual people are more interested in, for example, alternative committed relationships than heterosexual people (2, 3, 4). These could be close friendships but may also take the form of emotionally close, committed, yet platonic partnerships. These so-called queer platonic partnerships are often described as deeply meaningful bonds that go beyond conventional friendship, while not necessarily involving romantic or sexual attraction (4). For asexual people in particular, queer platonic relationships may offer a way to experience closeness and commitment without the expectations tied to romance and sex.

Overall, asexual people seem to prefer constructing their ideal relationships outside of “traditional” scripts, yet more closely around their identity and needs. For example, asexual people may often date someone who experiences sexual attraction and wants to engage in sexual activities (3, 4). The couple will have to negotiate ways to meet both partners’ needs. Sometimes this may lead to consensually opening up relationships so that sexual needs can be met outside the relationship (2, 3). At the same time, research suggests that asexual people are less interested in becoming parents than allosexual people, indicating that having children may be less central for them or perceived as less normative (2). This further challenges key assumptions of research on partner selection that typically see reproduction as the ultimate goal.

Together, these findings highlight that asexual people are open to a variety of relationship structures and life paths.

In a recent development, human experiences are diverse and so are asexual experiences. Differences in romantic and sexual attraction are just one piece of a much more complex picture of how people form relationships and define intimacy. Asexuality includes many different identities. For example, some asexual people do experience sexual attraction but only after they have formed an emotional bond with another person (demisexual), and others fall somewhere in between asexual and allosexual (graysexual) (9). All these nuances of (a)sexual experiences likely play a role in shaping what kind of relationship we are searching for.

Sources indicate that looking through the lens of asexuality reveals that there are different pathways to emotional connection and well-being. Relationships do not need to include sexual intimacy, not even romantic feelings, and can take on a multitude of forms. What asexuality teaches us is to rethink what intimacy and partnerships can look like and to recognize that a fulfilling life may not necessarily include a (romantic) partner altogether.

#416. Industry News: Failure Has Value in the Right Context

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1081 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Industry News: Failure Has Value in the Right Context

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • According to recent reports, conventional wisdom says that we learn more from failure than success, and our culture tends to support this, often romanticizing failure as a noble precursor to accomplishment.
  • Recent findings suggest that we know that globally, around 70 to 80 percent of business start-ups fail within 10 years, varying by industry and region.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

According to recent reports, conventional wisdom says that we learn more from failure than success, and our culture tends to support this, often romanticizing failure as a noble precursor to accomplishment. Business literature encourages us to “fail forward” or “fail better”—phrases that have become as ubiquitous as they are clichéd.

Recent findings suggest that we know that globally, around 70 to 80 percent of business start-ups fail within 10 years, varying by industry and region. But wherever you go, the chances of failure of a start-up are overwhelmingly greater than the probability of success. Take the example of 80 in 100 latest businesses ultimately failing—that means there are 20 recipes for success and 80 for failure. If you succeed, you have discovered one of the 20 routes to success, whereas if you fail, you have experienced one of the 80 routes to failure.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, in the case of a start-up business, experience of success is four times more valuable than experience of failure. Success will always be more instructive than failure when the probability of success is less than that of failure, which is virtually always the case in endeavors of impact and scale. They are never easy.

Recent findings suggest that we are told that failure breeds resilience. Winston Churchill famously remarked, “Success is going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.” While that made sense in the bleak early days of World War II, when successes on the battlefield were rare, overall failure is overrated as a staging post on the path to success.

To be clear: I am not saying we can’t learn from failure, or that bouncing back from it isn’t hugely commendable and character-building. Importantly, the courage to fail emboldens people to try, and this is the bedrock of entrepreneurship and ultimately economic growth. But at an individual level, success is a better teacher.

At Discovery, we have learned from both success and failure, but our most profound lessons have come from learning what went right.

Recent findings suggest that in 2008, we exited the U.S. health insurance market after eight years of trying to gain traction. Despite our efforts, we couldn’t attract enough members to create the scale to compete with incumbent giants. It was a very painful and instructive failure. And yes, we learned lessons that helped propel us onto the global stage. Today, instead of competing head-on, we partner with global insurers.

Industry observers note that but what has been the biggest cause of our progress? Is it learning from our failure in the U.S.? Or is it the insights drawn from our success in incentivizing healthier behavior and turning that into a scalable global model known as Vitality?

Both have been vital. But in my view, the lessons from success have been more transformative.

Sources indicate that the reasons why we learn more from success than failure lie in our psychology. Emotionally, failure is difficult to absorb. It feels bad. And when something feels bad, we tune out and don’t absorb the lessons as deeply.

Industry observers note that behavioral science shows that people tend to avoid personal bad news. For example, various studies show that up to 54 percent of individuals who undergo an HIV diagnostic test will not collect their results.

Industry observers note that cognitively, failure yields less useful information than success. Whereas success reveals patterns and principles that can be replicated, failure tends to be less instructional—it tells us what not to do but rarely illuminates what we should do.

It has been revealed that research by American motivational psychologists Lauren Eskreis-Winkler and Ayelet Fishbach, who aim to better understand the nature of success by studying failure, found that failure undermines learning. In their 2019 paper, “Not Learning from Failure—The Greatest Failure of All,” they reported on five studies with over 1,600 participants, who were asked a series of binary choice questions. For example: How much money do U.S. companies lose annually due to poor customer service? They were given only two possible answers to choose from: $60 billion or $90 billion. They were then given the correct answers to all questions and re-tested. Given that there were only two possible answers in each case, participants ought to have been able to remember the right one. But those who got the answer correct the first time did better on re-testing than those who got it wrong the first time. Why?

Industry observers note that “Our society celebrates failure as a teachable moment,” they wrote. “Yet in five studies, failure did the opposite: it undermined learning. Why does failure undermine learning? Failure is ego-threatening, which causes people to tune out.”.

Sources indicate that in the field of medicine, a fascinating study from Harvard Business School—“Learning From My Success and From Others’ Failure”—tracked 71 cardiothoracic surgeons over 10 years and 6,500 operations. The research, by KC Diwas and colleagues, found that surgeons learned more from their own successes than from their own failures—and more from others’ mistakes than others’ successes. Why? Because others’ failures don’t trigger the same ego threat, so we tune in more readily.

Ironically, while failure demands resilience, it doesn’t always build it. Success does. It reminds us that winning and progress are possible.

According to recent reports, of course, there are times when failure is immensely instructive. Plane crashes happen so rarely that when they do, they present rich opportunities for learning. If you are flying a space shuttle, you are only as strong as your weakest link, and studying these allows you to avoid the same catastrophic outcome twice.

But in complex networked systems, where processes are not linear, and where the chances of failure are greater than the chances of success, it is success that teaches best.

How to Wash, and Boost, Your Brain

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the glymphatic system contains glial cells, non-electrical cells in the lymphatic system that protect and cleanse.
  • Industry observers note that plaque clearance happens twice as fast at night when you sleep well.
  • Sources indicate that since this clearing occurs primarily in deep (delta-wave) sleep and not the other sleep stages, quality sleep is more key than quantity for the brain's night cleaning—more sleep does not mean better, and less sleep is not always harmful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

According to recent reports, the glymphatic system contains glial cells, non-electrical cells in the lymphatic system that protect and cleanse. In 2012, a team of researchers (Maiken Nedergaard and others) proposed that this system primarily clears waste and is most active during deep sleep. (also called delta-wave sleep, a type of non-REM sleep). The glymphatic system is mostly made up of cerebrospinal fluid that clears waste such as amyloid-beta plaques and tau proteins. These waste particles are commonly found in clusters in the brains and other organs of people with neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington’s disease, as well as mood disorders (Zhang and colleagues, 2022).

Industry observers note that plaque clearance happens twice as fast at night when you sleep well. That's the good news. The bad news is that if your sleep is disturbed, waste is not cleared as efficiently. The natural ebb and flow of fluid is interrupted, and more waste particles accumulate.

Sources indicate that since this clearing occurs primarily in deep (delta-wave) sleep and not the other sleep stages, quality sleep is more key than quantity for the brain's night cleaning—more sleep does not mean better, and less sleep is not always harmful. The type of brain waves during sleep matters more than the eight hours you’ve heard about. The timing also matters. It is better to have deep (non-dreaming) sleep in several chunks toward the first half of the night. During a 90-minute sleep cycle, your brain dips into shallow sleep, then deep, then to shallow again.

Stop alcohol use. Dr. Qinghua Liu and his team found that even moderate alcohol use reduces cerebrospinal fluid from entering and clearing plaques and proteins (Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, 2020). They also found that chronic moderate alcohol use led to increased activation of astrocytes—star-shaped cells that reactively try to address the extra inflammation from alcohol, thus reducing glymphatic function.

It has been revealed that there is also a widespread loss of proteins that can polarize (shift across membranes) to move fluid and waste out. Over time, this loss is very difficult to reverse. Alcohol can clean a lot of things outside of our body, but it does not help cell function inside the brain or body. Stopping alcohol may be the single most important thing to begin cleaning your brain. Other depressant medications, like opioids, when used chronically, may also inhibit the flow and cleaning process of cerebrospinal fluid.

You may have already guessed that what helps keep cerebrospinal fluid moving and cleaning your brain also supports general health. However, knowing why can be helpful to keep you motivated. Here are four other things you can do and why:.

#414. 5 Steps to Prevent and Recover From Burnout

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1555 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

5 Steps to Prevent and Recover From Burnout

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • It has been revealed that it’s the number one question I get: “How can I cope with the feeling of overwhelm from all the stress and complexity in my life?” Sometimes the symptoms are physical or emotional.
  • Sources indicate that stress and burnout are widespread.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Burnout is today’s number one concern.

It has been revealed that it’s the number one question I get: “How can I cope with the feeling of overwhelm from all the stress and complexity in my life?” Sometimes the symptoms are physical or emotional. For others, the problem manifests in difficulty focusing, cognitive fog, and impaired performance. My experience validates the data indicating we are in a national crisis around burnout and the impact of how life is speeding up.

Sources indicate that stress and burnout are widespread. A 2023 APA survey, “Work in America,” revealed that 77% of workers reported experiencing work-related stress in the previous month (American Psychological Association, 2023). A similar Gallup poll reported that 27% of U.S. full-time employees felt burned out either very often or always (Gallup, 2026). There isn’t much consolation in knowing that you are not alone, other than that this indicates there are good reasons for your predicament.

Recent findings suggest that this trend that continues to accelerate is due to the gap between our ability to adapt and the exponential changes taking place in our society, along with how childhood survival learning freezes our ability to adapt. I’ve written about this previously: The 4 Horsemen of Stress: Why Managing Stress Is So Difficult | Psychology Today.

It’s crucial to make sure that the symptoms you are experiencing are not held as a badge of honor or proof of how hard you work. They are signals of deep physiological dysregulation and that something needs to change. In this essay, I want to encourage you by presenting the first five steps you can take on The Path to recovery or prevention, and turning this into a challenge to reconnect with your biological ability to adapt. This is a route toward healing, recovery, greater resilience, and an adaptive biology better able to meet the world’s accelerating pace of change and complexity.

Sources indicate that begin by honestly recognizing where you are, along with being willing to put energy into this process; such as with my resilience assessment to help you identify the patterns, pressures, and symptoms that need attention. It is important to acknowledge your starting point, so you accept that the road to greater resilience will take time and thus require your patience.

In a recent development, there is also a bigger role for acceptance in a world where so much is outside your control. This is a key to resilience. Everything you do requires energy. Yet, you have a limited amount of what I refer to as personal energy. Every time you hear about a tragedy in the media, or deal with a person who is unconsciously bothering you, it can easily trigger an emotional and physical stress response. Your mind-body goes into the stress fight-or-flight response, which drains your energy. But there is no benefit to this use of your energy, and at the same time, it takes away from your body’s ability to heal and recover. Solution: begin by recognizing that every stress you engage with drains your energy. Start making better choices about where you choose to send that energy. Decide to use your energy only where it can be of benefit.

Sources indicate that at the foundation of recovery is self-love: the belief that you deserve to be healthy and happy. Self-love includes accepting yourself – blemishes and all. My use of the word “accepting” doesn’t mean you like everything about yourself, but simply an acknowledgment of reality: This is where I’m at right now. The paradoxical theory of change states that growth begins with accepting where you are in this moment – because you can’t be anywhere else.

According to recent reports, judgments such as “I should be further along” or “I shouldn’t have made that mistake” ignore your reality and the truth in this moment. This carries the unconscious message that you are not good enough and is undermining. That interpretation often begins in childhood and can push you in the direction of burnout. Give yourself 30 days to follow this suggestion of radical self-acceptance. Then notice if it results in greater calm and peace, and perhaps a lessening of your symptoms. Note: the qualities of a healthy internal voice include loving yourself, being accepting and compassionate with yourself, as well as being supportive and caring. Treating yourself to this grounding will result in your fastest recovery and growth.

You arrived here, in part, because you have been trying so hard. You want to do well; you put pressure on yourself and may have judged yourself too harshly. Recognizing that you are here not because you are defective, but because you have been striving so intensely, can make recovery easier. You are removing the stigma of inadequacy while owning your capacity. Take this challenge to be your best positive coach.

Industry observers note that how can you translate your hard work and motivation to support your own self-care? Identify a practice of recovery, such as the use of meditation, a relaxation exercise, or biofeedback, that engages the parasympathetic branch of your nervous system. Think of this as a training that reengages your innate ability to adapt and recover.

We get stuck in old patterns. These patterns are a barrier to adaptation and growth. In fact, whenever you get close to breaking through to new ground, it can trigger uncomfortable or awkward feelings. (Tied to some form of “this isn’t me”.) These feelings then interrupt progress and cause you to pull back.

Industry observers note that to break this pattern, I invite you to focus on your many accomplishments. You may already appreciate your successes, but it’s the identification of your skills and temperament that led to those achievements that translate results into belief in yourself. For success not to feel like it was magic, identify your unique ingredients that led to your successes. The hard work, the ability to set goals and focus, the persistence and the courage, and the skills that they demonstrate about you. These can be applied for success with fresh challenges. Use these to trust yourself to grow and establish a new pattern of balance and recovery, rather than burnout.

A key ingredient here is a willingness to sit with – to tolerate - the discomfort that comes from entering new territory. This is called, “growing pains”. A belief in your capacity to learn, recover, and respond differently based on a more accurate assessment of your achievements, creates the foundation for new habits and greater resilience. What you are simply doing is shifting your focus away from your shortcomings to your successes – and the skills and abilities you have already demonstrated.

Recent findings suggest that this shift in focus will result in less fear or anxiety. And this is the foundation for regaining your ability to adapt. We have been conditioned to over-extend our stress response, while short-changing the opposite, the recovery response. Acknowledging your abilities creates the psychological space to take time to engage in the necessary recovery practices mentioned above.

One entryway to the healthy path forward is adopting a growth mindset. My previous steps led to this umbrella concept of how to engage with the world. It means that when you encounter something difficult and want to give up or distract yourself, instead, you remind yourself that this is a situation that is challenging you to grow and learn. I know that it’s easy to feel overwhelmed in this process. So many things to do and change and address. The key here is to have a map of the territory. This begins with knowing what The Path forward is. It is based on my 9 pillars of resilience. It’s a blueprint. Thus, whenever you take steps based on any of the 9 pillars, this puts you onto The Path. When you are on The Path you don’t have to worry about what you are not doing, as you are already achieving success for that day. (Focusing on what is, rather than on what isn’t.) This creates a powerful and practical framework that will consistently move you towards resilience, adaptation and away from burnout. In this article, I’ve already identified the first pillar – having a loving and accepting relationship with yourself; the fourth pillar – physical balance and mastery (engaging the recovery branch of your nervous system; the fifth pillar – mental balance and mastery – having a growth mindset; and the sixth pillar – emotional balance and mastery – tolerating the emotional discomfort of growth.

Resilience is about the ability to “bounce forward”. Not simply to return to your old baseline or pattern, but to use each stress to challenge yourself to learn, grow and move forward with greater awareness, flexibility and resilience.

According to recent reports, challenge yourself to follow these five manageable steps that put you on The Path and then appreciate the effort. And remember, successful recovery and adaptability will happen one step at a time.

#413. The Psychology Behind “Overreacting”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (918 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The Psychology Behind “Overreacting”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • According to recent reports, couples don’t break up because they argue.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever thought, “We just can’t communicate,” you might be asking the wrong question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

According to recent reports, couples don’t break up because they argue. They break up because they feel alone while arguing.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever thought, “We just can’t communicate,” you might be asking the wrong question. The real puzzle isn’t why couples fight. It’s this: Why do people who love each other deeply end up triggering each other so consistently?

It has been revealed that emotionally focused therapy (EFT), an empirically-supported model of couple therapy grounded in attachment science, offers a clear answer: Love is not a negotiation problem; it's a bonding problem (Johnson, 2020). More than three decades of research have established EFT as an effective, evidence-based approach for helping couples move from distress to secure connection (Johnson, 2020). And bonding is biological.

Industry observers note that attachment theory, originally developed by Bowlby (1969, 1982) and extended to adult relationships (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007), conceptualizes close relationships as emotional bonds that regulate safety, distress, and connection. In this framework, romantic partners become primary attachment figures; people we turn to for reassurance, comfort, and security in moments of stress (Johnson, 2019).

According to recent reports, when your partner turns away mid-argument, your brain doesn’t process it as a small irritation but as a threat. From an attachment perspective, humans are wired to seek emotional closeness in moments of distress. When connection feels unavailable, the nervous system activates what researchers call protest behaviors: anger, criticism, defensiveness, or withdrawal (Johnson, 2008).These responses don't reflect character flaws; they're adaptive survival strategies. Attachment research shows that these emotional reactions are part of an evolved system designed to keep us connected (Bowlby, 1969, 1982; Johnson, 2019). What looks like “drama” is often attachment fear.

In a recent development, we often tell couples to improve their communication by using “I” statements, remaining calm, and compromising. This advice can help but it's not enough. Communication skills do not regulate an activated attachment system. When someone fears abandonment, logic does not soothe them. When someone fears inadequacy, confrontation feels threatening.Lasting change in relationships doesn't occur in arguments. A growing body of EFT outcome research indicates that it occurs through emotional responsiveness—the experience of reaching for a partner and having them respond (Johnson, 2020).Secure love develops when the answer to the question “Are you there for me?” is consistently yes (Johnson, 2008). Without that, technique feels empty.

Attachment unfolds within social systems. Couples live inside structures shaped by race, gender, immigration status, class, sexuality, and power. These contexts shape how safe, or unsafe, connection feels.Recent developments in EFT and related relational frameworks highlight that attachment experiences are deeply influenced by sociocultural realities, including trauma, marginalization, and systemic inequality (Johnson & Campbell, 2022). When one partner has experienced chronic marginalization, their attachment system may be more easily activated. What appears as “oversensitivity” may reflect accumulated threat. Emotional safety is not only created within the relationship; it is also shaped by the world outside it. Dismissing a partner’s lived experience can represent rupture.

The turning point in attachment-based therapy occurs when partners risk vulnerability instead of protection. Instead of saying, “You never care about me," they say things like, “When you walk away, I feel scared that I don’t matter.” Instead of telling a partner they're "too sensitive," they say, “I didn’t realize you felt alone. I don’t want you to feel that way.” These are vital communication—and attachment—shifts.

According to recent reports, process research in EFT reveals that when vulnerability is met with responsiveness, the attachment bond reorganizes, creating a sense of safety and reducing emotional reactivity (Johnson, 2020). The nervous system learns that closeness is safe, and love becomes a regulator rather than a trigger.

Industry observers note that we live in a culture that glorifies independence. We are taught that strong adults should not “need” anyone, that reliance is weakness, and that self-sufficiency is maturity. Attachment science tells a different story: Humans are wired for interdependence. Emotional closeness is not regression but regulation (Johnson, 2019). And secure relationships are built on accessibility, responsiveness, and engagement. Needing a partner is not dysfunction; it's biology.

Love falters when fear replaces responsiveness. The research is clear: Secure love isn’t built on turning toward each other when it would be easier to turn away (Johnson, 2020). In a culture that prizes independence, emotional responsiveness may be one of the most radical acts we can practice.

It has been revealed that carlota Azpiazu Osorio, is a registered marriage and family therapist associate at Pacifica Group in San Francisco, California. Her clinical work is grounded in emotionally focused therapy (EFT), attachment theory, trauma-informed care, and family systems approaches, with a particular focus on helping individuals and couples strengthen relationships and develop more secure emotional connections.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

In November, at the WHO Health Pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, a packed room of climate scientists and policymakers got to their feet and danced. On stage, a collective of women musicians played songs built from the sounds of water: melting glaciers, swollen rivers, rising seas. After two weeks of talk about emissions, clean energy, and finance, the climate crisis stopped being something we discussed and became something we felt, together, in our bodies.

Many of us know the opposite feeling: another headline about record heat or flooding, a jolt of dread, and we scroll on, more alone with it than before. Climate anxiety is a reasonable response to a real threat, but carried alone, it paralyzes us. In that room, something moved.

In a recent development, most people do not experience climate change as a graph. It is intense heat, difficult breathing, and worries about water: too little, too much, or whether it’s safe to drink. Women often carry the heaviest load, as do indigenous peoples, long keepers of these waters.

This COP also put health on the agenda by opening with a health day. The numbers explain why: The Lancet Countdown links fossil fuels and climate change to an estimated 3.3 million deaths a year from air pollution and extreme heat alone. The toll on our minds is harder to count, but it is just as real. Heat disrupts sleep and attention, and the slow dread of what is coming shows up as anxiety and paralysis. A WHO Europe report released during the summit, Strengthening Mental Health in a Changing Climate, links floods and wildfires to anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress, and calls for mental health to be part of climate policy.

Recent findings suggest that what helps? The WHO report looked at 20 interventions in 15 countries. Most aimed to build resilience and agency close to where people live. Agency is exactly what the arts can help people find. Art speaks human.

As a drama therapist and scientist, I am interested in how art can help us—projects using music, storytelling, and film to amplify the climate emergency. This isn’t therapy per se, but it draws on the same processes that creative arts therapists use with clients: giving form to hard-to-name feelings, and sharing them so they become bearable. It does two things that research and practice keep pointing to.

In a recent development, it invites people in as authors. Each artist found her own way into water. People engage differently when they are recognized as experts in their own lives.

Sources indicate that it turns feeling into connection. In a survey of 10,000 young people in 10 countries, 59 percent were very or extremely worried about climate change. In my clinical work and in the classroom, I see people shut down when fear and grief have nowhere to go. Music gives those feelings a shared rhythm.

There is good reason to think this helps. Eco-anxiety is closely tied to difficulty regulating emotions, and a meta-analysis of controlled studies found that listening to music reduces anxiety. In a study that followed adults over three years, those who increasingly turned to music to manage their emotions also became more likely to tackle problems head-on. Music doesn’t only soothe. It can help us act.

"When we are emotionally and empathetically tied to the natural world, we are reminded at a more profound, instinctive level of our interdependence with it."—Yo-Yo Ma, in Music and Mind, edited by Renée Fleming.

According to recent reports, this echoes what my colleagues and I found in developing the WHO Europe-Jameel Arts & Health Lab policy brief on the role of the arts and culture in addressing the health impacts of climate change, and it reinforces findings from the first Culture Global Stocktake for Climate Action, also released at COP31. Culture and cultural practices reflect and shape what we value, and it can build the trust and belonging that help people act on what they know.

Industry observers note that listen to these sounds of nature. Then ask yourself: what is your relationship to water where you live? What would it take to protect it, together? Then let the listening lead somewhere. Review these six acts for water that help us move from feeling to understanding to action:.

● Learn how much water your daily life uses.

● Adopt a few water-saving habits.

● Go deeper with films and talks from communities living with water crises.

● Join a group protecting rivers and oceans.

● Find out how you can help restore local wetlands, streams, and soils.

It has been revealed that ● Share your story. Make something with what comes up: a sketch, a few lines, a song. It doesn't have to be good.

If you work with young people or adults, try that last act as a group. Try a simple structure: open in a circle where people name what they feel; write a short song together from a local challenge, a mood, and a beat; perform it; then reflect on creating together rather than alone.

What I saw in Antalya gives me hope: a room full of committed people discovered they could still be moved, and could still move together. In my experience, hope is less a feeling we wait for than something we practice with others. The futures we can feel together are the ones we begin to build.

How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents
