#377. Tech Report: The Family Table: Finding Your Place as an Elder

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (878 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Tech Report: The Family Table: Finding Your Place as an Elder

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Note: This post may stir feelings of grief, estrangement, and old wounds.
  • With the holidays approaching, many of us think about our actual family tables and where everyone will sit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Note: This post may stir feelings of grief, estrangement, and old wounds. Not every family table was safe, and that distance or estrangement can be a valid, even necessary, choice.

With the holidays approaching, many of us think about our actual family tables and where everyone will sit. The idea of a family table is also a metaphor for our relationships. For example: Who sets it? Who is served first? Who sits at the head? Who was not invited? Over the course of our lifetimes, our place at the table shifts and rearranges itself, often because of losses, marriages and divorces, grandchildren, aging siblings, distance, and the chosen family members who have pulled up a chair.

We begin our lives at the children’s table; then we are perhaps the chef and server; and as elders, we might be lucky enough to become guests at our children’s or chosen family’s tables.

In a recent development, lately, many people in middle age and beyond have spoken about the changing dynamics of their relationships with their adult children. These feelings can be magnified during the holidays. Things are simply not what they used to be. When our children were young, their world revolved around us and our world revolved around them. Many of us have read books on parenting children and teenagers, but few of us were offered books or conversations about navigating life with our adult children. For many parents of adult children, there’s a deep ache in realizing that their role isn't what it used to be.

In a recent development, we move from managing our children’s lives to being something of an outsider. We are no longer involved in their everyday activities, and sometimes we don’t even know what they’re up to. We might have taught our children the power of independence, and now there is a lot of holding on and letting go.

According to recent reports, becoming a mother-in-law is another challenging role shift. Sharing our children with spouses and in-law families is not always an easy transition, especially if the partner is different from what we imagined for our child and/or if the couple lives far away.

Another shift is that children might begin worrying about their parents rather than the other way around. Perhaps the parents have physical or psychological health problems that call for their children’s intervention and care. It’s vital for elders to accept help while maintaining their dignity. At the same time, many elders are still caring for aging parents or grieving them.

Sadly, estrangement has become increasingly common. Perhaps more common than people care to admit. Very often, because of shame, it’s carried in silence, which can be very painful.

It has been revealed that one woman shared the story of organizing a holiday with her three adult children and four small grandchildren at a beautiful resort. One minute they were a happy family, and the next minute they were estranged. She still isn’t sure what happened, but on the last day of the trip, one of her adult children picked a fight about something that had happened years earlier, leaving the grandparents speechless. Everyone went home, and the adult child who picked a fight simply cut off contact and never really understood why.

Recent findings suggest that those who were close with their grandparents understand how vitally vital this relationship can be. I am the daughter of immigrants, and my parents worked very long hours to make ends meet, so my grandmother was my primary caretaker. Because I remember the closeness of that relationship, I was eager and excited to become a grandmother. I thought long and hard about what kind of grandmother I wanted to be and how I would handle certain situations.

Recent findings suggest that one thing grandparents learn swiftly is the importance of keeping their opinions to themselves. They realize this is vital, especially if they want to keep the lines of communication open with their adult children. This can be difficult, especially when they reach a stage of life when they might have—at a stage of life when they may hold strong opinions that their children don’t want to hear. Many elders say that their children really don’t want their advice. The truth is, younger generations can find most of what they want online, especially now that AI has become an integral part of our lives. The challenge is knowing when to speak and when to stay quiet.

It has been revealed that for those without children, with distant children, or whose friends have become their truest family, the holiday table might look different from what they imagined. Holidays remind us that change is always happening. Sometimes there are empty chairs at the table, sometimes upcoming faces, and sometimes more than one table. Some people might choose new or different traditions, and change requires acceptance. Change calls for acceptance, which leaves room for something new. Remember, nobody ever promised that things would stay the same. Enjoy whatever gathering you're part of. There will always be new stories to tell.

#376. Breaking: What Your Doctor Fails to Tell You Can Definitely Hurt

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1376 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: What Your Doctor Fails to Tell You Can Definitely Hurt

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • When you think about your physical health, it’s natural to think of all the ways a physician or similar healthcare provider should be able to help you.
  • Industry observers note that as it turns out, a number of medical conditions and treatments have crucial psychological connections that are equally important to promote healing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

When you think about your physical health, it’s natural to think of all the ways a physician or similar healthcare provider should be able to help you. If you or a loved one have developed a chronic disease that requires monitoring, surgery, or a switch in medications, you’ll probably feel that this is enough to get things back on track on the road to recovery.

Industry observers note that as it turns out, a number of medical conditions and treatments have crucial psychological connections that are equally important to promote healing. Whether it’s depression, cognitive changes, or anxiety, you may not realize that these are natural outcomes of various types of interventions. Unfortunately, healthcare professionals aren’t always either (a) aware of these connections or (b) prepared (or have the time) to address them.

It has been revealed that in a review of studies “at the intersection of psychiatry and cardiology,” Medical University of Silesia’s Kamila Klimek-Ociepka and colleagues scanned various databases to identify publications over the 15-year period of 2010 to 2025 in which findings were reported on the conjunction of cardiac device implantation (such as pacemakers) and assessment of patient symptoms in the domains of depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and cognitive disorders. A total of 44 studies made it to the final set used to analyze the main findings.

According to recent reports, key to understanding these studies is “heart-focused anxiety (HFA).” As you might imagine, having a procedure done to your heart, even if it is meant to reduce your risk of dying, is hardly a minor episode in your life. Anxiety and depression are reported in as many as 44 percent of patients treated with internal devices meant to keep the heart beating regularly.

In particular, HFA occurs when people experience “excessive anxiety related specifically to cardiac sensations, symptoms, and anticipated cardiovascular events.” People with certain types of implants, the ones that perform internal defibrillation (to get the heart started, are particularly likely to have HFA, fearing being harmed by the voltage from the shocks the device performs. Instead of engaging in what would be heart-healthy exercise, they instead decide they could hurt themselves by making the heart overwork, leading to an actual worsening of their condition.

It has been revealed that depressive symptoms, for their part, can also become highly prevalent among cardiac patients, with estimates ranging up to 64 percent, especially when they first learn of their diagnosis. Their depression can be expressed as sleep disturbances and loss of energy, or in the emotional realm as hopelessness and pessimism about the future.

Industry observers note that finally, PTSD can also develop in patients who experienced sudden cardiac events or invasive therapies. There are probably few traumas that can occur in daily life as frightening as having your heart literally stop for a second or two. But because they don’t remember the event, their PTSD may be expressed as “hypervigilance, anxiety, and avoidance behaviors rather than intrusive memories or flashbacks.”.

Recent findings suggest that in reading about these psychological consequences of cardiac events and treatment, you might be wondering why you’ve never heard anyone speak about them in the context of treatment. Shouldn’t you (or your relative) have been warned or at least educated about these risks? Considering all the precautions listed on any kind of medical consent form, you would think that it might be worth adding these—along with an explanation.

Additionally, as pointed out by Erzurum Bolge Training and Research Hospital's Murat Özmen, physicians may not realize that depression can be associated with the low physical activity, high stress, obesity, and hypertension that are part of the disease picture. Just as physicians and other healthcare professionals instruct their patients about implanted devices themselves, the authors claim they need to educate them about the importance of sleep, developing coping methods to reduce stress, and participating in exercise as warranted by stage of recovery.

The experience of cardiovascular disease is clearly life-threatening and scary, but even more ominous is a diagnosis of cancer. Considering how highly prevalent cancer is within the population, it’s likely that someone you know (or you) has received this diagnosis.

In a recent development, it may seem almost self-evident that the uncertainty of a cancer diagnosis, along with the stress involved in tests, procedures, and therapy, would be enough to lead a patient’s mind to travel to existential questions about the possibility of surviving into the future. Fortunately, those who treat cancer patients are tuned in to the psychological risks. University of Houston’s Haejeong An and Yoonjung Kim note that this “general understanding is expanded by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), which specifically defines distress as a multifaceted concept covering physical, psychological, social, or spiritual discomfort that emerges during cancer survivorship, which affects how survivors think, feel, or act.”.

Unfortunately, though, the concept of distress is not well-defined in actual practice. Therapeutic approaches fail to separate distress from anxiety, depression, and stress, meaning that interventions will fail to target this piece of the cancer journey separately and effectively. Starting with a database of more than 2,700 studies, the authors analyzed the final 14 that met all the rigorous criteria for inclusion.

The methods used in these studies were all over the map, ranging from standard psychological interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to virtual reality, mindfulness, and hypnosis. As a result, there were inconsistent findings regarding effectiveness, a problem made worse by lack of a clear definition of distress.

Compared to cardiac disease, the scope of psychosocial interventions for cancer patients is far more advanced. However, the U. Houston findings suggest that practitioners do not have clear pathways for reducing the distress of their patients, if they indeed decide to implement some type of intervention.

According to recent reports, these examples of research in the area of psychological symptoms and serious disease should alert you to the idea that if you (or a loved one) are headed for some type of intervention, it’s crucial to be aware of possible emotional consequences. In an era of overburdened healthcare providers, where you may feel lucky to get an appointment at all, finding ways to receive this support may seem impossible.

According to recent reports, however, if it’s not from the provider itself, consider seeking support from other sources. There is a wide number of support groups associated with specific diseases, but if there isn’t one in your community, you can also draw from online resources. You can even start your own group.

Industry observers note that an added piece of irony in the equation is that behavioral medicine often focuses on ways to help patients adopt healthier lifestyles. Less often does the field seek connections between physical disease and mental health. The An and Kim article suggests some causes of optimism given the large number of intervention studies in the area of breast cancer. The problem in this area is not lack of recognition, but lack of definitions and clear methodologies, leading to the exclusion of most available research.

According to recent reports, to sum up, the next time you draw up your list of questions to ask your healthcare provider before going in for an appointment, think about whether your stress, anxiety, and depression might also be important to mention. Your mental health and your physical health can only stand to gain.

#375. What's in a Label With Neurodivergence, and Why You Should Care

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (807 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

What's in a Label With Neurodivergence, and Why You Should Care

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Recently, I was having coffee with a few colleagues when the topic of labels came up.
  • As someone who's part of Generation X, when I was a child, there were far fewer labels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Recently, I was having coffee with a few colleagues when the topic of labels came up. One of our clients said they self-identified as an “autistic person" versus a "neurodivergent person." This is a distinction worth noting since neurodivergence can be viewed as a broad term. Everyone's eyes turned to me in anticipation of my response because, of course, I'm known around the office for having what my children call "hot takes." Without hesitation, I shared mine: "I support specific labels across the neurodivergent community, as long as they don't define an individual's entire identity." My team was divided, but let me explain my stance.

As someone who's part of Generation X, when I was a child, there were far fewer labels. No one was diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or learning disabilities. If there was an academic challenge, the kids figured it out or didn’t. As for me, I was a fun, fearless, and resilient child. No one told me who I was, and I embraced that way of thinking, often finding solutions along the way. Fast forward to today, this isn't the case at all in any aspect of our society. Labels are a way people identify themselves, especially those within the neurodivergent community. And within these labels, there is identity-first language and person-centered language, which we've touched on in the past. See here for more background if you’re too busy to scan through my previous blog posts.

These terms aside, if you're not working in the field like me, and labeling your child makes you uncomfortable, that's a good thing. It means you're thoughtful and sensitive. But I'll be clear: A label stating an actual diagnosis is imperative. In my line of work, I create programs for people with disabilities, and many clients have ADHD and/or autism. I often find myself using a label to support client advocacy and secure supports. In cases like this one, a label is vital. If a client doesn't have a formal diagnosis of autism, they might not receive services from a school system, disability development services, or health insurance. For them, the lack of a label means no consideration for applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy; the answer is simply "no.".

Sources indicate that over the years, I've met many clients who proudly share their diagnosis: "This is who I am, and accept me for me." They identify with a label because it helps them explain how they differ from the general population, and, in some cases, that label becomes a central part of their identity. This is where it can get tricky.

One strong example is Asperger's syndrome, once a widely used diagnosis, which has largely faded from everyday use and has been absorbed into the diagnosis of autism. Many people with Asperger's still use the term and feel that the shift erases part of themselves and others' history. Without a distinct category, their needs may even be overlooked. Some believe they’ve lost a sense of self, and I really feel for them. I can't imagine someone telling me something I've connected to for years essentially no longer exists.

A great way to find a healthy balance when approaching labels within neurodivergence is to find a community of people who share your child's background. When integrating, your child will likely see that, yes, they share a label and some similarities, but they have their own unique personality and interests. This realization can also help a child who might feel isolated by fostering connections.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, every person is an individual, and yes, labels are a necessary part of life and play a huge role in our healthcare system. However, again, I'm not the one labeling my clients; I ask them to tell me, and if that's challenging, I work with their parent or caregiver for insight. Ask, don't assume.

Sources indicate that after working for so many years with families with children with disabilities, I can assure you that as a parent, you can deeply impact the way your child sees themselves and trust and believe they're so much more than the label they might currently identify with. Encourage them to accept who they are, know that they bring something special to the world, and continue to find the wonderful qualities and characteristics that go far beyond a label because that's what makes them special and unique. The diagnosis is just one part of who they are. I know my younger self would be shocked by my new acceptance of labels, but she was never defined by one thing, and neither is your child.

#374. Three Key Behaviors of Highly Creative People

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1058 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Three Key Behaviors of Highly Creative People

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • It may well be one of the most frequently asked questions by people from a wide range of occupations: “What do I need to do in order to become more creative?” Suffice it to say that there are several intertwining characteristics of those deemed to be innovative and imaginative.
  • The mysteries of the universe have always been an impetus for us to peek and poke and prod for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

It may well be one of the most frequently asked questions by people from a wide range of occupations: “What do I need to do in order to become more creative?” Suffice it to say that there are several intertwining characteristics of those deemed to be innovative and imaginative. But, for our purposes, let’s take a look at three of the most-cited and most-recommended behaviors that positively influence our creative expression.

Curiosity is ingrained in our DNA. The mysteries of the universe have always been an impetus for us to peek and poke and prod for.

Industry observers note that answers - learning something new about our surroundings as well as about ourselves. We want to know more than we know; we want to expand our horizons, try out the new and undiscovered, and pursue experiences that deepen our comprehension (and appreciation) of the world in which we live.

But curiosity is much more than a simple search for answers. It is also the generation of possibilities. When we look at the world from multiple perspectives, we give ourselves permission to examine a wider range of resolutions and remedies. We open up our minds to explore the unexamined and unknown. Curiosity becomes a propellant for upcoming opportunities and new options. Ian Leslie explains it this way: “…curiosity is essential to an exploring mind; it opens our eyes to the new and undiscovered, encouraging us to seek out new experiences and meet new people.”.

It was Albert Einstein who famously mentioned, “I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.” For Einstein, curiosity was the engine that drove his creativity. Curiosity was his catalyst for questioning, and questioning is what propels us to seek out the unfamiliar and the unknown. For, without curiosity, knowledge becomes stagnant and immovable. It does not move us forward, nor does it have sufficient power to examine what may lie just beyond our experiences.

According to recent reports, in conducting research for my latest book (see below), I came across some compelling insights underscoring the fact that creative thinkers tend to ask more open-ended questions. For example, a 2023 study in the Journal of Creativity took a look at the types of questions posed by 165 undergraduate students during select creative-thinking tasks. Individuals whose responses indicated greater originality and fluency tended to ask more open-ended questions. The researchers also discovered that questions involving possibilities (rather than absolutes) were associated with originality in various tasks.

Consider the difference between these two questions: “Is this a good idea?” (This type of query invites a yes-no response. As such, it encourages evaluation before any exploration takes place.) and “What are some different ways this particular idea could be improved?” (This type of question, on the other hand, invites alternatives, experimentation, and the possibility of multiple solutions.) Additionally, there is evidence to indicate that open-ended questions may support creativity through several inter-related processes:.

Perhaps most compelling are the open-ended questions we ask ourselves. These inwardly-directed queries often shape what we pay attention to, which alternatives we may conjure, and how we interpret our experiences. They give us a framework to muse, ponder, and think in several different directions. For example, contemplate these possibilities: “What could I learn that would help me improve?” “What did this attempt teach me, and what could I try next?” “What are six possible solutions, including unconventional ones?” and “What other approaches might work just as well – or better?” Note that these examples illustrate divergent ways of thinking – contemplations of what might be rather than what is. Or, in the words of Eugene Jonesco, “It is not the answer that enlightens, but the question.”.

It has been revealed that taking risks is essential in our overall growth and development. We all took some risks when we learned how to walk. By the same token, we took a risk when we got our driver’s license and took the family car out for a spin, and many of us took a risk when we joined up with another individual and said that we would spend the rest of our lives with that person. Basically, taking risks is an essential element of our learning curve. Yet, what we often practice in the real world may be altogether different—minimize the risk, and you can minimize the potential defeats. But what results is often stunted creative expression. Innovation is all about taking a chance; all about venturing into unfamiliar territories with the possibility of discovering something fresh or something different. That’s not possible without risk-taking.

Creative individuals are known for taking chances. They examine the unknown – not necessarily because it will lead to something successful but rather because it’s fresh (Cue Leonardo da Vinci, Marie Curie, Pablo Picasso and Steve Jobs). Those individuals were happy to move beyond what they knew in order to play with unexplored ideas. Most importantly, they often envisioned the inevitability of failure as a creative learning opportunity…a chance to regroup and refocus.

By and large, creativity involves the freedom to move into uncharted territories and unfamiliar vistas. As such, risk-taking is an essential element of the creative life simply because it gives us license to step outside our comfort zone, challenge how we think, and explore a plethora of possibilities. When we give ourselves permission to experiment (and make mistakes), we open a door to unexpected discoveries and innovative ideas. Or, as Erich Fromm so eloquently put it, “Creativity requires the courage to let go of certainties.”.

What is most important – especially for those who wish to enhance their creative spirit – is to constantly pursue, refresh, and master the three attributes above. Every day!

#373. Childhood Trauma and Grief: Lessons From Batman and Two-Face

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Childhood Trauma and Grief: Lessons From Batman and Two-Face

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • The difference between a heroic caped crusader and a criminal mastermind may come down to who was waiting in the doorway after a very bad childhood.
  • Industry observers note that harvey Dent (Two-Face) and Bruce Wayne (Batman) both carry the weight of living losses: grief from a traumatic childhood that never fully ends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

The difference between a heroic caped crusader and a criminal mastermind may come down to who was waiting in the doorway after a very bad childhood.

Industry observers note that harvey Dent (Two-Face) and Bruce Wayne (Batman) both carry the weight of living losses: grief from a traumatic childhood that never fully ends. Bruce becomes Gotham’s protector, while Harvey becomes Two-Face, a sadistic supervillain who mirrors the abuse he internalized as a child. Their stories show how loss is shaped by the context in which it occurs.

In a recent development, we usually think of grief as something that follows a death, but some of the deepest grief comes from what never was, such as a safe, loving, and reliable family. Grief researchers call this nonfinite loss, or living loss. It is re-experienced throughout life and keeps demanding adjustment.1.

Recent findings suggest that in "The Dark Knight," Harvey is a driven, idealistic district attorney who becomes Two-Face after violence takes the woman he loves.2 The comics reveal an earlier story: a father who abused him, with outcomes decided by the flip of a coin.3,4 Long before that night, Harvey had lost security, trust, innocence, and a sense of his own authenticity. These are intangible losses, which are symbolic, invisible, more existential, and easy to bury under professional achievements.

Industry observers note that his story is also less rare and outlandish than it seems. The World Health Organization estimates that about six in ten adults in North America and four in ten in Europe have had at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE).5 ACEs are correlated with increased risks of being involved in the criminal justice system, health-harming behaviours, poor psychological health, and poverty or homelessness, and higher mortality rates, in addition to chronic illnesses.

It has been revealed that early relationships teach us how to regulate ourselves and what to expect from the world.6 When caregivers become a source of threat, a child adapts. Parts of our psyche hide, go numb, or freeze. Freeze is a psychobiological conservation strategy that results in having fractured developmental egoic states; we adapt by hiding, repressing, or emotionally isolating certain aspects of ourselves, analogous to how we have been made to feel by others.7.

Jungian analyst Donald Kalsched describes how a traumatized psyche will survive in pieces when it is not safe to be whole.8 Two-Face is what happens when that adaptation becomes literal and hardens into identity: a polarized psyche, split between idealism and rage. He demonstrates how unexpressed grief does not disappear, and how traumatic loss can tear us apart from the inside.

In a recent development, bruce has his own devastating losses.9 The difference is Alfred, a secure attachment figure who is consistent, attuned, and present when it matters. With Alfred, Bruce could grieve beside someone instead of alone, and being able to access the right support allowed Bruce to engage in his grief in a more integrative way than Harvey.

While Bruce nonetheless demonstrates his own childhood attachment injury from the death of his parents, his relationship with his parents is portrayed as positive in the Batman films and comics. This highlights how Bruce had internalized what it means to be protected, co-regulated with when distressed, and supported by loving attachment figures in expressing his own autonomy or interdependence at a young age.

In a recent development, this illuminates how loss experiences are always shaped by the various relational contexts in which they occur. In practice, that means finding our own Alfred, as we all need a trusted and caring person who can help us tend old losses. It also means cultivating an inner Alfred within our own imagination—a steady, compassionate aspect of ourselves that helps us stay grounded when the pain surfaces, even when it is not possible to find such a person externally to us.

This piece draws on my book chapter, Shadows in Context: Two-Face, Batman, and Losses Associated with a Traumatic Childhood in Superhero Grief and the Multiverse of Loss: Considerations and Case Studies edited by Jill Harrington and Darcy Harris (2026), which is a new collection published by Routledge that uses superheroes and the multiverse to explore the impact of non-death loss on our psychology.10.

#372. Tech Report: How to Motivate Children for Success in School

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1094 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Psychologytoday

Tech Report: How to Motivate Children for Success in School

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • In a recent development, parents in America and around the world agree on this: We want our children to succeed in school.
  • In a recent development, american students, however, are not doing well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

In a recent development, parents in America and around the world agree on this: We want our children to succeed in school. Intense pressure for academic achievement now dominates the lives of many American families.

In a recent development, american students, however, are not doing well. Perhaps even more concerning, they seem to have less interest in learning. High school and college teachers across the country now assign less reading to their students, and students still complain that this is more than they can manage. Many American high school and college students no longer read books!

There are several possible causes for our children's loss of interest in learning, and different causes for different children. The impact of screens is certainly notable. Children no longer have the attention span for reading. Instead, they are scrolling and watching short videos. They may even believe that, in this way, they are learning.

Industry observers note that 1. Express enthusiastic interest in your child’s interests, even if these are not the interests you would choose. Learning begins with interest. Children's instinctive interest and curiosity about the world are the starting point for their motivation and enjoyment of learning. As soon as children begin to talk, they are constantly asking questions, seeking information, and wanting to know “why.” Too often, in our understandable effort to help improve their skills, we neglect this essential aspect of children’s motivation.

In a recent development, make note of moments of interest and talk with your children about what interests them. Ask questions. Do "research" together. Help them develop their interests into projects and goals.

According to recent reports, the promise of rewards or the threat of punishment may lead to some short-term improvement in a child’s effort. But rewards and punishments cannot create interest, enjoyment, or long-term goals.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Find the source of their anxiety, frustration, and discouragement. Parents often ask, "Why doesn’t he put more effort into his schoolwork? Why doesn’t he care?” The answer to these questions is almost always, “Because he is discouraged.”.

Recent findings suggest that children may mask their discouragement with defiant or rebellious attitudes, and they may pretend that they don’t care. But they do care. If we look hard enough, we will find in every child some interest and a desire to do well.

Undiagnosed attention and learning disorders are a common source of discouragement and lack of sustained effort in children and adolescents. It is essential for parents and teachers to understand the impact of these difficulties. Even mild or moderate learning problems can be a source of anxiety, frustration, and low self-esteem.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Make note of every improvement, not every mistake. To solve the problem of discouragement, children need more encouragement and less criticism. Of course, to improve their skills, children need criticism. But they need encouragement even more. Encouragement is not false praise. We all need encouragement, even as adults, with every latest challenge and skill we attempt to master.

Industry observers note that 4. Help them cultivate a growth mindset. Praise effort, not intelligence or talent. Praise learning, not grades. Then, on this foundation, we can set high standards and challenge children to work harder. But we will have to do this less often, because they will more often challenge themselves.

According to recent reports, 5. Appreciate their strengths. Students who seem unmotivated are often focused on their weaknesses, not on their strengths.

Recent findings suggest that when I talk with “unmotivated” children, I often find qualities of intelligence, creativity, effort, and character that their parents and teachers have overlooked and that they may also fail to appreciate. When I point out these qualities, many children and adolescents feel deeply understood. For some, this is a transformative moment. Years later, these affirming statements are what they remember and value most about our work.

6. Make learning meaningful. Individual achievement alone—getting good grades in school—is a fragile source of motivation and effort, with a high cost in anxiety and stress. If we define achievement, however, as making a contribution to our families, our communities, our country, and the world, we offer children a much better goal and standard for success. We should help them become involved in projects that help their community, and we should be involved with them.

7. Have conversations. Every moment of dialogue with our children and grandchildren adds meaning and relevance to learning. Talk with your children about what they are studying—about civics and history, science, literature, and religion—and the importance of these subjects to our current lives. Talk with them about how others help us, about the good work that many people are doing, and what they can do to help others.

In a recent development, conversation is a (partial) antidote to the addictive pull of screens. Before you ask, “Have you done your homework?” ask them about what they have been learning in school.

8. Establish "library hours" in your home. Even when children are highly motivated to do well in school, they still need to establish good work habits. They need to put away their devices, do their homework, and get enough sleep.

Sources indicate that I encourage parents to set aside a specified time, early in the evening, as a homework or “library” hour. During the library hour, all electronics should be turned off (except for computers or tablets children need for schoolwork) for the entire family. No television, no video games, no phones.

Homework should be done in a communal place (as in a library), at the kitchen or dining room table. Especially with younger children, parents are present and available to help, offer encouragement, and answer questions. Then, when homework is done, there is time for play.

According to recent reports, most families have found these guidelines helpful for students of all ages. The result is an important lesson in self-discipline, fewer family arguments, and more success in school.

Sources indicate that west, M. R. Student Test Scores Keep Falling. What's Really to Blame? Education Week, September 9, 2025.

Horowitch, J. The Elite College Students Who Can't Read Books. The Atlantic, October 1, 2024.

In a recent development, dweck, C. (2007) Mindset: The Fresh Psychology of Success (2nd Edition). Ballantine Books.

Can Buying Your Childhood Home Bring Back the Past?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • In a recent development, think of the home where you spent your childhood.
  • It has been revealed that some people go beyond remembering their childhood homes and decide to buy them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

In a recent development, think of the home where you spent your childhood. You may still remember the room you slept in, the conversations you had there, the sound of someone calling you for dinner or the family and friends who came to visit on special occasions. Even years after leaving, that house may remain closely connected to your memories and sense of self.

It has been revealed that some people go beyond remembering their childhood homes and decide to buy them. But can recovering a childhood home also bring back the life once lived there?

Below, I explore that question through the experiences of three people who did exactly that. What made them want to reclaim these properties, and what did they discover when they returned? Their stories invite us to consider what it means to return to a place that remains so much a part of who we are.

Sources indicate that eddie Dilleen is one of Australia’s largest residential landlords; he owns more than 200 properties. But there was one property he could not buy. For more than 12 years, he waited for his childhood home to go on the market.

As he has written, ‘You can set reminders and stuff like that, but when I was on my phone messing around, I would randomly check it literally every one or two weeks for the past 12 years.’ When the house finally came on the market, he noted, ‘I just bought it sight unseen.’ The price was just under $1 million. The house had been sold 25 years earlier for $97,000 following his parents’ divorce.

In a recent development, eddie’s childhood home remained notable to him throughout his adult life, even after he achieved financial success. His constant checking on it suggests an enduring emotional attachment to a place associated with loss and family separation. His decision to purchase the house without viewing it indicates a desperation to reclaim something he felt he had lost.

His experience also may be understood in the context of cognitive immobility, which can occur when an individual is unable to stay put in an intended place due to the absence or presence of certain restrictions or circumstances beyond their control, which may originate in their present or desired location, inside themselves, or in the external world.

Circumstances beyond Dilleen’s control made him leave his childhood home but some part of him remained in it.

Jenaca Rogers lived with her grandma but was also raised from infancy by her family friends, Pat and Jerry. Their house held many of her childhood memories, from family celebrations to everyday moments spent with her grandparents. When Pat and Jerry died, the house was sold following probate proceedings. As Jenaca recalled, ‘We were all heartbroken. Your whole life you hope for something and then it’s just taken away’.

Years later, in 2025, Jenaca unexpectedly discovered that the house was for sale, and called the estate agent. When he failed to answer, she said, ‘I just started crying because I was like, I’m not going to get it’.

Recent findings suggest that she then found the agent’s mobile number online. She recalls, ‘I called him and he got us out there, and I cried in the driveway, I cried touring the house’. During the visit, she discovered her toy car in the backyard shed, which overwhelmed her further. She eventually bought the house and surprised her grandma, Connie, with a viewing. It was a homecoming for them both.

Industry observers note that buying the house brought Jenaca peace and comfort, but it did not erase her grief. Her experience suggests that reclaiming a meaningful place may help us feel emotionally connected with loved ones who have died but does not necessarily help with the loss.

It has been revealed that moving from Bogotá to Miami brought Colombian singer-songwriter Andrés Cepeda upcoming opportunities and challenges, but he left behind something deeply personal. After years of searching for something he felt he had lost in Bogotá, he was able to recover it. Cepeda bought his childhood home.

Industry observers note that after returning to the house, Cepeda said, 'I returned to the house, the street, the garden. Everything was just as I remembered. And yet nothing was the same. My parents were gone. My childhood was gone. Time itself had left.'.

Industry observers note that cepeda may have experienced a sense of metaphorical homelessness, the idea that those who experience cognitive immobility may find out after returning home that ‘…no home is truly a home; even the previous home – the ancestral home – has lost its distinguishing features and allure’. Although Cepeda had recovered the property, his childhood experiences could not be recreated: 'I went on a personal tour of my life. The parks, the schools, the cafés, the houses of my friends, the places where my heart broke. All of it started turning into music.'.

In a recent development, he wrote the song ‘Bogotá’ to express his feelings about his childhood city and family. As he describes it, ‘It captures the eerie, bittersweet feeling of returning to a place that once defined you – only to realise you miss not the place, but the person you were there’. Cepeda recovered his childhood home but could not recover his childhood. However, he could use his music to acknowledge what cannot be recovered.

Of the three stages of cognitive immobility, his music could have helped him enter the third stage, stabilisation, in which people ‘...tend to aim to retain values and pursue goals to help them with the loss, alleviating the sense of entrapment’.

Our childhood home can remain vital long after we have left it. It is a reminder of the people we knew, our relationships and the experiences we had. If your childhood home has been lost through the breakup of your family, bereavement or some other circumstance beyond your control, recovering it may become a deeply personal goal.

The experiences of Dilleen, Rogers and Cepeda show that buying a childhood home can be a chance to reconnect with a familiar place, but it does not mean returning to the life once lived there. The building may remain but the people in it, the relationships, the life that existed there will have changed. We can return to a place without recovering the past and move forward without leaving its memories behind.

#370. 4 Ways Parents Can Support Teen Online Safety and Well-Being

4 Ways Parents Can Support Teen Online Safety and Well-Being

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • I recently asked 30 young people what they wished their parents understood about their online lives.
  • According to recent reports, blake (not their real name) was in fifth grade when an adult approached them on Amino, a now-defunct social media platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

I recently asked 30 young people what they wished their parents understood about their online lives. One young person’s story highlights how easily parents can overlook online risks.

According to recent reports, blake (not their real name) was in fifth grade when an adult approached them on Amino, a now-defunct social media platform. Their conversation rapidly evolved into what Blake thought of as a romantic relationship.

Looking back, Blake told me, “It was obviously incredibly unsafe,” and added, “I wish someone had found out about it earlier on.”.

It has been revealed that blake never told their parents because they believed that they were “doing something wrong.” While Blake’s parents monitored their YouTube watch history, Blake now wishes their parents had engaged in more open conversations about their online life and set “more (tech) restrictions early on.” Contrary to what many parents might think, Blake didn’t want to be left alone. They wanted their parents to ask them about their online life and set clearer boundaries, making it easier to ask for help.

In my conversations, young people shared four practical tips for talking with teens about their online lives and supporting their online safety and well-being.

Due to fear of punishment or disapproval, young people often hide their online lives from parents. This secrecy is driven by the same reason teens don’t share that they were offered a drink at a party. They’re afraid it will get them in trouble, or they'll be cut off from their friends.

Industry observers note that one young LGBTQ+ woman, for example, said that her very religious dad monitored her social media feeds and told her to delete any post he disagreed with. He did the same to her adult siblings. This didn’t stop her from posting. Instead, she learned how to moderate what he could see.

It has been revealed that other young people described what happened when parents responded with curiosity rather than judgment. When one young woman’s mom found her secret Twitter account, she expected to be grounded “for a million years.” Instead, her mom calmly asked who she was talking to. The young woman said that her mom’s response made room for conversation and connection.

Recent findings suggest that when teens feel like they have to hide their online lives, they’re less likely to come to their parents when something goes wrong. Young people told us that when parents act as digital coaches, staying calm and walking them through difficult situations, they build online safety skills, and their relationships with their parents grow stronger. Being a coach doesn’t mean ignoring risks or abandoning rules. It means listening, understanding what happened, and helping your teen work through difficult situations.

Sources indicate that existing research and our conversations with young people both point to the importance of talking with teens about their online lives. Similar to talking to teens about other sensitive topics like drinking and sex, it’s more effective to have the conversation before it's relevant. Think of it less like a “Sit down; we have to talk” lecture and more like a series of low-pressure chats.

There are many good conversation guides for parents, including from Internet Matters, Common Sense Media, and the Spark and Stitch Institute. By using nonjudgmental, open-ended questions such as “What’s something you’ve enjoyed online lately?” or “How do you feel about your school’s AI policy?” parents can show curiosity without making teens defensive. Current events, like the recent Meta settlement, can also serve as a springboard for conversation.

In a recent development, it can help to keep expectations for these conversations low. Even the best-timed and well-intentioned conversations are likely to be met with eye rolls by teens. That’s OK. As teen psychologist and author Lisa Damour explains, “Your (kid) may roll her eyes, but do it anyway. (Kids) can listen and roll their eyes at the same time.” Her podcast episode, “Untangling All Things Digital for Parents,” is worth a listen.

As a parent, I was surprised and heartened to learn that not all tech rules feel restrictive to teens. Several were even grateful for them. One teen boy I spoke with remarked, “[My parents] make me leave my phone downstairs … I think that's a good idea because I don't wanna be using my phone. I'm trying to sleep because I have to wake up really early.”.

This aligns with recent research showing that teens and young adults value solo downtime, face-to-face time with friends, and sleep even more than they value time spent online. Parents can respect their teens’ desire for independence by inviting them to help draft family “tech agreements” based on shared values such as sleep, time with friends, and privacy. Internet Matters offers a family tech agreement template that works well for tweens and younger teens, and Screenagers provides broader, more flexible guidance. Use these templates as starting points and revisit the agreement as your teen’s needs and independence change.

Sources indicate that young people told us that their parents’ tech use shaped their own, for better and worse. One young adult remarked a lack of healthy boundaries at home left “no real role model to follow.” Another said her mother now tells her to ask an AI chatbot before coming to her for advice.

Industry observers note that modeling healthy habits is one of the most powerful tools parents have. When parents spend a lot of time on digital media, their teens tend to do so as well. Moreover, teens who feel like their parents are more focused on their devices than on them report higher depression. Parents can strengthen their relationship and teach healthy tech habits at the same time by holding themselves to the same standards that they set for their teen. This might look like modeling the importance of sleep by agreeing that everyone in the house, including parents, keeps phones out of the bedroom after 10 p.m.

In a recent development, you don’t need to model perfection. You can acknowledge when you get distracted or struggle to maintain a boundary. Saying, “I’ve been checking my phone too much during dinner, so I’m going to leave it in the other room,” makes your own effort visible. Shared expectations show that healthy tech habits are a family responsibility, not just something parents impose on teens.

Industry observers note that parents are being asked to make high-stakes decisions about fast-changing technology, often without shared norms or practical support. They shouldn’t have to carry this burden alone, but tech companies and federal regulatory agencies aren’t adequately stepping up.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, you don’t need to be a tech expert to listen to teens, set thoughtful boundaries, and make it easier for your teen to ask for help. What helps teens most is a strong, trusting relationship with their parents. Research backs this up: A warm parent-child relationship, alongside clear boundaries, predicts safer internet use among teens. Over time, a compassionate and collaborative approach can help teens navigate technology skillfully, with less secrecy and power struggles and more mutual respect.

#369. Latest Update: The Meaning and Value of Stress

Latest Update: The Meaning and Value of Stress

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • For the last 60 years or so, we've been warned about stress and told to do everything we can to avoid it.
  • We've been taught how to meditate our way out of stress, down-regulate from it, "hack our cortisol," reduce our adrenaline, manage our vagus nerve, calm ourselves, numb ourselves, distract ourselves, and halt our stress responses in as many ways as we can.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

For the last 60 years or so, we've been warned about stress and told to do everything we can to avoid it.

We've been taught how to meditate our way out of stress, down-regulate from it, "hack our cortisol," reduce our adrenaline, manage our vagus nerve, calm ourselves, numb ourselves, distract ourselves, and halt our stress responses in as many ways as we can.

Sources indicate that we've also been taught to view many of the difficulties in our lives as always-negative exterior forces, or stressors, that act upon us without our knowledge or permission. Stress has been presented to us as a dangerously unwanted thing with no value whatsoever.

Thankfully, newer research into stressors and our stress response has found the opposite to be true.

Industry observers note that in part 1 of this series, I focused on the weasel word of stress, because our stress response is an emotional response. In my work, Dynamic Emotional Integration, I help people understand the emotions that form the foundation of our stress response. We learn how to name these emotions with precision and work directly with them to access the essential intelligence they contribute to us.

Three of the main emotions I see in our stress response are: anxiety (the emotion of motivation and task completion), anger (which helps us identify and uphold what we value), and panic (which steps forward when our lives are in danger).

Each of these emotions helps us meet stressors with intelligence and focus. When we know which emotions are supporting us, and we know how to work with those emotions (instead of against them), stressful situations can teach us who we are, what's important to us, and how we can meet life's challenges with focus, skills, and resilience.

But if we don't know how to identify or work with our emotions, we may feel overwhelmed as our bodies increase our activation to help us meet the necessary stressors we face. We may also learn two unhelpful lessons:.

If we believe that stressors are foreign and that our emotions are problems, we'll create unnecessary suffering, not just in response to the stressors but because our skills are missing in action.

Recent findings suggest that psychological researcher Kelly McGonigal has been focusing on stress for many years, and in her 2016 book, The Upside of Stress: Why Stress Is Good for You, and How to Get Good at It, she shares information from decades of stress research. Her book is full of surprising facts that turn our understanding of stress on its ear. For instance:.

In a recent development, if I told you that the price of tiger chow has gone up by 40 percent, you might have little to no reaction (assuming you aren't a tiger keeper). This is a major price increase, but because it has no meaning to you and does not impact any part of your life, your stress response will be quiet—as it should be; there's nothing for you to do about this, and your emotions don't need to be involved.

It has been revealed that but if I told you that your share of the cost for your child's monthly doctor's visits has gone up by 40 percent, it's likely that your stress response would engage. Your emotions, most notably anxiety and anger, might intensify to bring you the energy and focus you need to work the problem. Your stress response would help you know that this situation is crucial, that it's worth your time and focus, and that you need its increased energy to help you make upcoming looks to support your child's well-being.

Sadly, most stress management approaches would have you try to calm yourself or suppress your emotions (or merely observe them), as if the activation you feel is a problem in and of itself. But this old, tired idea is not only wrong; it's counterproductive, because the strength of your stress response is a key to your success and even mastery of the situation.

Of all the surprising things in stress research, this may be the most delightful: The strength of your stress response—your emotional intensity, your hyper-focus, your "nerves"—is directly connected to your ability to thrive. And this continues to be true even when you're well-acquainted with a stressor and no longer see it as surprising or shocking.

In a recent development, researchers studied upcoming and seasoned skydivers, certain that they would see a reduced stress response (reduced cortisol, adrenaline, and heart rate, less "stress") as the skydivers became accustomed to throwing themselves out of planes. Strangely, there wasn't any reduction in the markers of stress in the seasoned skydivers; in fact, the most skilled skydivers continued to exhibit very high stress responses, often higher than people jumping out of planes for the first time.

What they did find was that the seasoned skydivers had reframed their stress responses as excitement, readiness, stimulation, and even zest for life. This reframing helped them treat their activation as a necessary and fun part of skydiving, even though they might have experienced the exact same stress response as overwhelming the first time they leapt out of a plane.

Recent findings suggest that this seemingly paradoxical relationship holds true for other high-performers such as athletes, surgeons, artists, actors, and musicians. A higher stress response does not predict failure; it is intimately connected to skill and mastery.

So, the key is not to avoid stressors or your stress response, and it's not to become an endlessly chilled-out and calm person.

The key to developing your resilience alongside your skills is to learn how to reframe your natural responses to stressors and welcome the stimulation, focus, and preparedness they provide.

#368. Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2853 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Themarginalian

Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she calibrated love and loss.
  • Sources indicate that and besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway?
  • On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she calibrated love and loss. But she did not mean that it is good to ruminate and wallow — Dickinson so deftly played with the surface of meaning, so delighted in startling us into a flinch or furrow before plunging us into the deeper truths she fathomed. She meant, I think, that a love lost is grieved forever, whatever the nature of the loss — this she knew, and turned the ongoingness of it into a lifetime of art — but by looking back, we are reminded over and over that the sharp edge of grief does smooth over time, that today’s blunt ache is worlds apart from the first stabs, until grief becomes, as Abraham Lincoln wrote in his stirring letter of consolation to a bereaved young woman, “a sad sweet feeling in your heart, of a purer and holier sort than you have known before.”.

Sources indicate that and besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway? We never lose people, not really. I don’t mean this in some mystical sense — let there be no confusion about what actually happens when we die. I don’t even mean it in the poetic sense. I am speaking strictly from the point of view of the mind emerging from the dazzling materiality of the brain — that majestic cathedral of cortex and synapse shaping every thought we have and every feeling we tremble with.

I am speaking of the paradox inside the brain:.

On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, no person we have loved is ever fully gone. When they die or vanish, they are physically no longer present, but their personhood permeates our synapses with memories and habits of mind, saturates an all-pervading atmosphere of feeling we don’t just carry with us all the time but live and breathe inside. Or the opposite happens, which is its own devastation — the physical body remains present, but the person we have known and loved, that safehouse of shared memories and trust, is gone — lost to mental illness, to addiction, to neurodegenerative disease.

In both cases, the brain is tasked with the slow, painful work of reconstituting its map of the world, so that the world makes sense again without the beloved person in it. Mapping, in fact, is not a mere metaphor but what is actually going on in the brain, since our orientation in spacetime and our autonoeic consciousness — the capacity for mental self-representation — share a cortical region.

Where the missed and missing person goes on the map, how the remapping actually unfolds, and what it takes to redraw the map in such a way that the world feels whole again are the questions coursing through The Grieving Brain: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss (public library) by neuroscientist Mary-Frances O’Connor — a pioneer in fMRI research since the technology first became available, who has devoted a quarter century to studying the particular neurophysiology of grief. She writes:.

In a recent development, the brain devotes lots of effort to mapping where our loved ones are while they are alive, so that we can find them when we need them. And the brain often prefers habits and predictions over upcoming information. But it struggles to learn new information that cannot be ignored, like the absence of our loved one.

Recent findings suggest that grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve, and grieving necessitates learning to live in the world with the absence of someone you love deeply, who is ingrained in your understanding of the world. This means that for the brain, your loved one is simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time. You are navigating your life despite the fact that they have been stolen from you, a premise that makes no sense, and that is both confusing and upsetting.

Making an crucial distinction between grief (“the intense emotion that crashes over you like a wave, completely overwhelming, unable to be ignored”) and grieving (an ongoing process punctuated by recurring moments of grief but stringing the moments into a larger trajectory), O’Connor adds:.

Grieving requires the difficult task of throwing out the map we have used to navigate our lives together and transforming our relationship with this person who has died. Grieving, or learning to live a meaningful life without our loved one, is ultimately a type of learning. Because learning is something we do our whole lives, seeing grieving as a type of learning may make it feel more familiar and understandable and give us the patience to allow this remarkable process to unfold.

Grief never ends, and it is a natural response to loss. You will experience pangs of grief over this specific person forever. You will have discrete moments that overwhelm you, even years after the death when you have restored your life to a meaningful, fulfilling experience. But… even if the feeling of grief is the same, your relationship to the feeling changes. Feeling grief years after your loss may make you doubt whether you have really adapted. If you think of the emotion and the process of adaptation as two different things, however, then it isn’t a problem that you experience grief even when you have been grieving for a long time.

In a recent development, although volumes have been written about the psychology, philosophy, and poetics of grief — none more piercing than the Joan Didion classic, none more practical than Seneca’s advice to his bereaved mother — there is something singularly revealing about exploring grief from the point of view of the brain beneath the mind, which must begin at the developmental beginning. Childhood — the brain’s most fertile growth period, when most of its major infrastructure is laid out — is also our training ground for loss. Every time we are separated from our primary caregivers, we experience scale-models of loss; every time they return, we learn that the loss of their presence is not a loss of their person, of their love. (A pause worth taking: every abandonment is a miniature of grief.).

In those formative attachments, we also learn the role we ourselves play in the relationship. Because, in building its relational world-map, the brain is constantly computing our loved ones’ position in three dimensions — time, space, and closeness, also known as psychological distance — we learn the causal link between our behavior and a caregiver’s position in the closeness dimension, just like we learn the causal link between our bodily movements and our position in space. When there is secure attachment, the child learns that throughout various surface disruptions, situational factors, and passing emotional weather patterns, there is a steadfast underlying closeness. O’Connor writes:.

Closeness is partially under our control, and we learn how to maintain and nurture this closeness, but we also trust those who love us to maintain that closeness as well.

Recent findings suggest that the obvious — and heartbreaking — corollary is that children who grow up without secure attachment experience the pangs of miniature grief much more readily throughout life, with each departure of a loved one, however temporary, because trusting a continuity of closeness does not come naturally to us. But no matter the formative experience of closeness, human beings are universally undone by the death of someone close — the final abandonment, at once the most abstract and the most absolute absence, in which our brains simply cannot compute the total removal of a person so proximate and important from the fabric of psychological spacetime.

Citing the disoriented devastation of a woman ghosted by a lover, O’Connor notes that “ghosting” is the neurologically appropriate word-choice for such abandonments — studied under fMRI, the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to “ghosting” behaves much the same way as the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to death, the mental map suddenly crumbled and torn to pieces. O’Connor describes the strange yet strangely sensical way in which the brain copes with this incomprehensible disruption of reality:.

If your brain cannot comprehend that something as abstract as death has happened, it cannot understand where the deceased is in space and time, or why they are not here, now, and close. From your brain’s perspective, ghosting is exactly what happens when a loved one dies. As far as the brain is concerned, they have not died. The loved one has, with no explanation, stopped returning our calls — stopped communicating with us altogether. How could someone who loves us do that? They have become distant, or unbelievably mean, and that is infuriating. Your brain doesn’t understand why; it doesn’t understand that dimensions can simply disappear. If they don’t feel close, then they just feel distant, and you want to fix it rather than believe they are permanently gone. This (mis)belief leads to an intense upwelling of emotions.

If a person we love is missing, then our brain assumes they are far away and will be found later. The idea that the person is simply no longer in this dimensional world, that there are no here, now, and close dimensions, is not logical.

Drawing on brain imaging studies, she adds:.

The ephemeral sense of closeness with our loved ones exists in the physical, tangible hardware of our brain.

The particular bit of hardware is the brain’s posterior cingulate cortex — our built-in GPS of love. Scanning the environment and processing innumerable bits of sensory information, the PCC is constantly calibrating and recalibrating the psychological distance between us and the people we love, tightening the bond the closer we feel and loosening it when we sense distancing. Death turns the GPS into a crude compass trying to orient to an all-pervading, ever-shifting magnetic field suddenly bereft of its true north. O’Connor writes:.

It has been revealed that after the death of a loved one, the incoming messages seem scrambled for a while. At times, closeness with our deceased loved one feels incredibly visceral, as though they are present in the room, here and now. At other times, the string seems to have fallen off the board — not shorter or longer than it was before, but simply stolen from us entirely.

This confusion is so fundamental and so primal, so beyond the reach of reason, that it befalls minds indiscriminately along the spectrum of intelligence and self-awareness — a reality most clearly and devastatingly evinced in the extraordinary love letter Richard Feynman wrote to his wife 488 days after her death and 6,994 days before he won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

But O’Connor notes that while Western physicians long believed such continuing bonds across the life-death divide to be a symptom of poor coping with grief that makes for poorer bonds with the living, recent research drawing on various grief rituals and customs from cultures around the world has demonstrated that such ongoing inner dialogue with the dead might actually enrich our relationships with the living and allow us to show up for them in a fuller, more openhearted way. She writes:.

Our understanding of ourselves changes as we gain wisdom through experience. Our relationships with our living loved ones can grow more compassionate and resonant with gratitude as we age. We can also allow our interactions with our beloved ones who are gone to grow and change, even if only in our minds. This transformation of our relationship with them can affect our capacity to live fully in the present, and to create aspirations for a meaningful future. It can also help us to feel more connected to them, to the best parts of them… Their absence from our physical world does not make our relationship to them any less valuable.

It has been revealed that instead of imagining an alternate what if reality, we must learn to be connected to them with our feet planted firmly in the present moment. This transformed relationship is dynamic, ever-changing, in the way that any loving relationship is ever-changing across months and years. Our relationship with our deceased loved one must reflect who we are now, with the experience, and perhaps even the wisdom, we have gained through grieving. We must learn to restore a meaningful life.

The greatest challenge, of course, is the perennial challenge of the human mind — how to integrate seemingly contradictory needs or ideas in such a way that they coexist harmoniously, perhaps even magnify each other, rather than cancel each other out. Without such integration, any fresh relationship can feel like a threat to this ongoing inner bond with the dead, undamming a flood of grief at the notion of emotional erasure: grief for the grief itself, for that outstretched hand holding on to the gone and to ourselves at the same time, to the map as it used to be. This is a fear so understandable as to cusp on the universal. It is also — and this might be the most assuring part of O’Connor’s research — a neurophysiologically misplaced fear. Within the brain, every person we love leaves a tangible, structural imprint, encoded in synapses that can never be vanquished or replaced by new and different love. Because that bond — like every bond, like every idea, like the universe itself — was “only ever conjured up in the mind,” it is there too that it always lives, unassailable by other minds and other events.

Recent findings suggest that gaining a newly introduced relationship is simply not going to fill the hole that exists. Here is the key — the point of new roles and new relationships is not to fill the hole. Expecting that they will can only lead to disappointment.

The point is that if we are living in the present, we need to have someone who loves us and cares for us, and we need someone to love and care for as well. The only way to enjoy a fulfilling relationship in the future, however, is to start one in the present. If we can imagine a future in which we are loved, then we must start a relationship that eventually will become important to us in a way that is different from our previous relationship, but rewarding and sustaining.

Understood this way, then, the ongoing relationship with the gone is a lavishment to other loves, for it has made us exactly who we are — the person doing the loving, the person being loved, the mapmaker of present and possible worlds. O’Connor offers neural affirmation for this poetic aspiration:.

Recent findings suggest that after a loved one dies, they are clearly no longer with us in the physical world, which each day proves to us. On the other hand, they are not gone, because they are with us in our brain and in our mind. The physical makeup of our brain — the structure of our neurons — has been changed by them. In this sense, you could say that a piece of them physically lives on. That piece is the neural connections protected within our skull, and these neural connections survive in physical form even after a loved one’s death. So, they are not entirely “out there,” and they are not entirely “in here,” either. You are not one, not two. That is because the love between two people, that unmistakable but usually indescribable property, occurs between two people. Once we have known love, we can bring it into our awareness, we can feel it emerge and emanate from us. This experience reaches beyond the love for the flesh and bones of the person we once knew on this earthly plane. Now loving is an attribute of us, regardless of who we share it with, regardless of what is given to us in return. This is a transcendent experience, a felt sense of being loving without needing anything in return. In the very best moments together, we learned to love and to be loved. Because of our bonded experience, that loved one and that loving are a part of us now, to call up and act on as we see fit in the present and the future.

Sources indicate that complement The Grieving Brain with a mathematician’s geometric model for living with grief and this soulful animated film of “Dirge Without Music” by Edna St. Vincent Millay — the most beautiful homily on the emotional paradox of loss I know — then revisit Nick Cave’s life-honed wisdom on grief as a portal to greater aliveness.

#367. Why Certain Pop Songs Trigger Inexplicable Emotion

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1169 w)
