Why Certain Pop Songs Trigger Inexplicable Emotion

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Recently, I was scrolling through the Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1980.
  • In a recent development, while perusing the list, I realized there's one song that always stops me dead in my tracks and hits surprisingly hard whenever it catches me off guard in a random place, like a supermarket checkout line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Recently, I was scrolling through the Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1980. I was 14 years old that year, making it the absolute peak of my "musical reminiscence bump," the developmental window when our brains permanently wire the music of our youth to our deepest emotions.

In a recent development, while perusing the list, I realized there's one song that always stops me dead in my tracks and hits surprisingly hard whenever it catches me off guard in a random place, like a supermarket checkout line. That song is Elton John's "Little Jeannie.".

Industry observers note that lyrically, this song doesn't say anything profoundly moving until near the end. And the refrain "I want you to be my acrobat, I want you to be my lover" always seems like a throwaway line. On paper, the song could easily be categorized as a seriously schmaltzy, mid-tempo early '80s pop song.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, every time I hear the opening percussion and cascading drum intro, I get verklempt. During the 20-second, lyric-free introduction that might sound like "Muzak-y" elevator music to some, my emotions swell and I'm filled with a deep sense of, for lack of a better word, "wistfulness" that doesn't make sense to me logically.

Curious if I was alone in having such a poignant response to a somewhat cheesy pop song, I looked at the YouTube comments to see if other listeners echoed my sentiment.

Notably, for many of the "Little Jeannie" versions on YouTube, all of which are sung in English by Elton John, the comment sections are dominated by foreign-language responses (lots of Portuguese!). According to Google Translate, these comments convey that even among non-English speakers or ESL listeners, "Little Jeannie" hits hard in bittersweet ways that seem to catch people off guard.

While sifting through various comments, I found two that elucidate the inexplicable power of "Little Jeannie" to stir emotions:.

Why does a song that isn't inherently sad make someone cry? And how can a listener feel nostalgia for an era they didn't live through? As it turns out, the answers lie in a fascinating intersection of behavioral psychology, imagination, and neuroscience.

Sources indicate that A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on November 16, 2026, investigated the sociocultural dimensions of music-evoked memories. The researchers played 30-second clips of billboard-topping hits to 223 college students, utilizing songs from their own teenage years (the 2010s) and their parents' teenage years (the 1980s and 1990s).

Using natural language processing to analyze the memories these songs evoked, the researchers found that certain songs reliably generated strikingly similar memory scenarios among strangers from comparable backgrounds, driven by culturally learned "scripts.".

It has been revealed that to find out where that emotion was coming from, the researchers stripped away the music and gave a separate group of participants just a song's lyrics to read. Without music accompanying the words to a song, the shared sociocultural dimensions of people's autobiographical memories and associations diminished.

Based on this observation, the researchers concluded that the lyrics alone don't drive our intense reactions to pop music. Instead, the emotional scripts are embedded in the musical sound and genre itself.

When a YouTube commenter notes that "Little Jeannie" isn't a sad song but makes their eyes well up with tears, it isn't necessarily the lyrics driving that reaction. It's the specific acoustic architecture created by an old Fender Rhodes electric piano, alto saxophone, and flugelhorn, all wrapped in layered vocal harmonies. This unique musical alchemy tugs directly at the heartstrings, completely bypassing the analytical mind where words reside.

How does neuroscience explain the enigma of a young listener feeling "ridiculously melancholic" when hearing a song released decades before they were born?

One possible explanation: While we experience a primary surge of memory attachment for the music of our own adolescence, we also develop a secondary attachment to the music of our parents and caregivers from earlier generations. As the authors explain in their recent PNAS paper:.

"Interestingly, however, music-evoked autobiographical memories (MEAMs) are characterized by a potentially unique phenomenon known as 'cascading reminiscence bumps,' in which they exhibit a secondary reminiscence bump associated with music that was popular before listeners were born.".

Recent findings suggest that as children, we're often captive audiences in the backseat of a car or the family living room. Long before music was siloed into individual earbuds via streaming apps, "hard copy" formats like vinyl records, CDs, and mixtapes filled these shared spaces. Played aloud on common speakers, we passively absorbed our parents' adolescent soundtracks by osmosis.

Yet, even as modern listening habits shift toward isolated headphones, this intergenerational phenomenon persists. This latest (2026) study suggests that these cultural "scripts" are so deeply wired into us that even if a younger participant had never heard a specific older song before, their brain can use the song's genre to automatically retrieve a feeling that fits the cultural vibe.

Because these acoustic architectures activate shared neural representations, the emotional script transcends both the generation and the delivery method.

Another recent study by Princeton's Elizabeth Margulis and colleagues, published in Nature Communications on August 18, 2026, used fMRI to explore the neural representations of imagined narratives that participants conjured up while listening to unfamiliar music.

Sources indicate that during the experiment, researchers scanned people's brains while they listened to completely instrumental tracks. The scans revealed that across different test subjects, the music produced highly organized, shared patterns in the brain's default mode network (DMN). As the authors explain:.

"This work demonstrates that music elicits detectable, modality-general representations, a kind of higher-order 'meaning', integrating both narrative imagery and its associated emotional profile, specific to particular excerpts.".

Industry observers note that interestingly, Margulis's team found that the DMN doesn't need semantic language to engage in profound meaning-making. This helps to explain why it's almost impossible to pinpoint why certain music evokes shared imagined narratives; these emotions bubble up outside the realm of words (i.e., lexical semantics).

According to the latest 2026 research, music has the power to tap into a cultural frequency that bypasses our critical minds, reminding us that oftentimes, profound meaning is found in things we feel deeply but can't articulate.

Recent findings suggest that cara Turnbull, Benjamin M. Kubit, Kelly Jakubowski, Elizabeth H. Margulis. Music Illuminates Sociocultural Dimensions of Autobiographical Memory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (First published: November 16, 2026) doi:10.1073/pnas.2536885123.

#365. Creatures of Habit May Have Less Pain and Depression

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Creatures of Habit May Have Less Pain and Depression

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Creatures of habit—those who have a daily routine and stick to it—may benefit physically and psychologically from their predictable schedules, according to a fresh study published by researchers at the University of Missouri.
  • According to recent reports, this might seem counterintuitive to people who live more unpredictable lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Creatures of habit—those who have a daily routine and stick to it—may benefit physically and psychologically from their predictable schedules, according to a fresh study published by researchers at the University of Missouri.

According to recent reports, this might seem counterintuitive to people who live more unpredictable lives. Going about your day with no set schedule may seem exciting to some, but that chaos and uncertainty might be taking a hidden toll on well-being over time.

Sources indicate that temporarily escaping the confines of a routine during vacation is great, but living everyday life without the comfort of a set schedule creates anxiety and stress. Researchers also hypothesize that unstructured days can interfere with the body’s natural internal clock.

In a recent development, circadian rhythms refer to the physical, mental, and behavioral changes we experience over a 24-hour cycle. Our body has an internal biological clock that has been honed by evolution over millions of years, largely calibrated to the lifestyle of a hunter-gatherer. Deviations from this ancient way of life often put us out of sync with our biological clock. Many psychologists believe this is an underappreciated source of unhappiness, fatigue, and illness.

When the sleep-wake cycle is disrupted, for example, it can have negative repercussions on other bodily systems. In other words, your body’s internal clock can impact your mood, hormones, energy level, cognitive abilities, metabolism, and more.

The primary driver of our sleep-wake cycle is light, but other factors influence it as well. Food, caffeine, exercise, stress, screen time, and more can potentially interfere with our natural internal clock. Scientists at the University of Missouri wanted to address whether maintaining a predictable daily routine helps keep our internal clock ticking the way it should.

The researchers recruited 67 subjects who were older adults—37 had insomnia, and 30 were good sleepers. Using surveys, the team examined whether regimented routines made a difference in health outcomes. Since the study included participants with insomnia, they could also determine whether insomnia played a role in any of the health outcomes reported.

Sources indicate that the results revealed a striking difference between creatures of habit and those who lack structure in their daily lives. Participants who adhered to a daily routine reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression. This association was maintained in those who had insomnia.

While the study does not demonstrate causality, it suggests that regular mealtimes, wake-up times, social activities, and bedtimes furnish the brain with signals that help keep the internal clock functioning properly. In turn, this likely explains the better physical and psychological outcomes seen in those who live by set schedules.

The researchers conclude that sticking to a consistent routine is “associated with more favorable health outcomes and may represent a promising target for educational and interventional strategies for older adults, irrespective of insomnia status.”.

The new findings support similar studies that found structured habits to be associated with lower mortality risks in aging seniors.

It happens to all of us—life’s events often disrupt our circadian rhythms every now and then. But there are evidence-based ways to get your internal clock back on track.

But sticking to a daily routine can help.

Another notable factor is light management. As mentioned, light is the primary signal our brain uses to distinguish sleeping time from awake time. Bright lights in the morning, preferably sunlight, trigger your body to produce cortisol, the wakefulness hormone.

At night, darkness stimulates the release of the sleep hormone melatonin. Our use of artificial lights or screens at night can fool our brain into thinking that it is still daytime, hindering our ability to fall asleep. It is recommended to dim lights and stop screen usage 1-2 hours before bed.

Be mindful of alcohol, caffeine, and certain medications, as these agents can keep you awake or interfere with restful sleep.

Industry observers note that eating late at night, napping in the afternoon, and lack of physical activity can also make falling asleep difficult. Investing in a comfortable mattress and keeping your bedroom temperature cooler can also promote quality sleep.

See your doctor if you continue to experience trouble sleeping.

If you struggle with pain or depression, try adhering to consistent times for sleeping, eating, and other activities throughout your day. Adopting a predictable schedule is a natural and easy way to alleviate anxiety. Syncing your body's internal clock to the rhythms of the day promotes better mood, sleep, and overall health.

Sources indicate that “Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults” by Eunjin Lee Tracy, et al. Journal of Behavioral Medicine, March 15, 2026.

#364. From Medical Marijuana to Marijuana Everywhere

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1677 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

From Medical Marijuana to Marijuana Everywhere

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Sources indicate that walk through almost any American city, and you’ll likely smell marijuana smoke.
  • The modern medical marijuana movement gained momentum when patients with cancer, AIDS, and other serious illnesses sought relief.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

This is Part 1 of a two-part series.

Sources indicate that walk through almost any American city, and you’ll likely smell marijuana smoke. Nonsmokers are complaining the most. Sidewalks. Hotels. Apartment buildings. Public spaces. Marijuana seems to be everywhere.

The modern medical marijuana movement gained momentum when patients with cancer, AIDS, and other serious illnesses sought relief. Compassion was a powerful argument for this group. So was criminal justice reform because sometimes penalties for possessing small amounts of marijuana were unreasonably high. But neither compassion nor decriminalization established that marijuana was effective for one illness, let alone dozens of diseases. Evidence supports certain cannabinoid-based treatments for rare indications, but not the safety or efficacy of cannabis dispensary products.

A systematic review by Petrilli and colleagues found higher-potency cannabis was associated with increased risks of psychosis and cannabis use disorder (CUD).

It started with the 1996 medical marijuana ballot measure in California, Proposition 215.

In 2012, Colorado and Washington became the first states to approve recreational marijuana legalization through statewide ballot initiatives.

Promises made to gain citizen support included fewer arrests, less illicit dealing, and medical benefits. There were also promises of tax revenue. Legalization also created retailers who need customers and investors expecting returns. Governments collect taxes and need money.

In a recent development, kevin Sabet, PhD, and former Congressman Patrick Kennedy cofounded Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM) in 2013. They are advocates, but research has supported many of their policy suggestions.

Industry observers note that one study analyzed 187,573 survey responses between 2018 and 2023. They raised questions about marketing practices, especially those reaching children. Xu and colleagues subsequently reported associations between cannabis advertising, price-based promotions, and initiation among adolescents and young adults.

Rotering and Apollonio also documented cannabis-industry lobbying concerning indoor smoking exemptions and pregnancy warnings.

Didn't we already learn these lessons from Big Tobacco?

Sources indicate that legal U.S. cannabis sales reached an estimated $29.1 billion in 2025, with industry projections anticipating further growth in 2026. But tax revenue isn’t the same as public health benefits.

Perhaps the most key finding about commercial cannabis is not how much is sold, but who’s buying it.

Cigarette manufacturers also depend on nicotine-dependent smokers. A disproportionate share of alcohol sales come from heavy drinkers. Fast-food and ultra-processed food companies benefit from frequent consumption. The marijuana industry is similar in this way. A study of Washington State's cannabis market estimated daily or near-daily consumers accounted for 91 percent of the market in 2016.

Reducing heavy cannabis consumption would reduce industry revenue and state tax receipts.

Approximately 62 percent of cannabis consumed in California during 2024 came from illicit sources.

The legal market expanded, but the illegal market remains as substantial as ever. Illegal cannabis products may be cheaper because producers and sellers avoid taxes, testing requirements, licensing fees, and other regulatory costs while offering anonymity and home or street delivery, providing a competitive advantage.

Recent findings suggest that the marijuana smoked during the 1960s is not the cannabis sold in today's dispensaries. Historical estimates suggest marijuana in the 1960s often contained 1 percent THC or less. By the early 1990s, concentrations were around 3 percent, rising to approximately 4 percent in 1995. It did not stop there.

Sources indicate that by 2014, average THC potency reached approximately 12 percent. By 2022, the DEA reported an average of 16 percent THC in monitored marijuana plants. Today's commercial flower may contain 20 to 30 percent THC, while concentrated products such as wax, shatter, and oils may contain 60 to 90 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the dose escalation in potency over time is undeniable. No one today can say, as experts did in the ‘60s, that marijuana isn’t ever addicting, and today, addiction is more likely than ever.

Petrilli and colleagues' systematic review linked higher-potency cannabis with increased risks of psychosis and cannabis use disorder.

We didn’t legalize the marijuana of the '60s. We commercialized highly potent, concentrated forms of THC, without the long-term safety studies or FDA evidence expected of medicines.

But shouldn't people who never used cannabis receive protections comparable to those established for nonsmokers of tobacco? This is the most neglected question in cannabis public health, proving we are in a collective denial.

Secondhand smoke is firsthand smoke without consent.

Sources indicate that today, cigarette smoke is treated like poison, but cannabis smoke enters apartments, office buildings, hotel rooms, shared ventilation systems, and public spaces. Neighbors complain because they smell it. Sometimes they cannot escape it.

Sources indicate that cannabis smoke contains fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅), carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. The CDC warns secondhand cannabis smoke contains toxic and cancer-causing chemicals also present in tobacco smoke, sometimes at comparable or higher concentrations.

Cannabis does not contain nicotine, but cannabis smoke contains something tobacco smoke does not: THC. Controlled experiments in humans by Herrmann and colleagues demonstrated secondhand cannabis smoke exposure can produce measurable blood THC concentrations in poorly ventilated environments. They also reported secondhand exposure could produce subjective psychoactive effects.

According to recent reports, tripathi and colleagues studied 275 children and reported cannabis smoking inside the home was associated with approximately fivefold higher odds of evidence of cannabis in the body and brain by detecting urinary cannabinoid biomarkers. This doesn’t establish intoxication or addiction, but raises an obvious question: Why should children be exposed to THC-containing smoke?

Also, uncertainty about the magnitude of harm doesn’t prove repeated exposure is safe for children or adults.

Tobacco research taught homeowners, renters, hotel guests, and the rest of us another lesson: Smoke doesn’t disappear when the cigarette, joint, or bong goes out.

In a recent development, tobacco researchers indicated persistent residues in indoor environments. These alarming findings elevated concerns about infants' and young children's safety. Smoke-related combustion products remain on furniture, carpeting, clothing, walls, and household dust. Some residues can transfer or be resuspended. This is thirdhand smoke.

A 2025 JAMA Cardiology study by Mohammadi and colleagues reported associations between chronic marijuana smoking or THC-edible use (gummies, food including marijuana, such as the classic marijuana brownies) and impaired vascular endothelial function.

It has been revealed that what about emergency department visits? Cannabis use disorder? Anhedonia? Psychosis? Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, characterized by recurrent episodes of severe nausea and vomiting? Asthma, impaired driving? Treatment costs? Costs may include addiction treatment, psychiatric and medical emergencies, the impacts of impaired driving, environmental exposure, and other health consequences.

Recent findings suggest that we need prospective studies beginning before first cannabis use and continuing over time. We need to measure potential benefits and harms of legalization. We then need to use the FDA to establish medicinal benefit and calculate the risk-benefit balance.

Legalization, while circumventing science and the FDA, does not make marijuana safe. Slick marketing does not make it medicine. Nothing justifies exposing others to smoke.

The lessons of tobacco, alcohol, and cocaine should not be forgotten: Public health must come before commercial interests.

The next post in this series will examine the neuroscience of THC and the addiction, pregnancy, and prevention lessons we should already be applying.

#363. Why Men Ghost Their Therapists

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1107 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Why Men Ghost Their Therapists

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that counseling men is not like counseling women.
  • In a recent development, this mismatch is understandable—women are the majority.
  • Recent findings suggest that counseling is a female-dominated field, which is interesting because it was not always this way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recent findings suggest that counseling men is not like counseling women. If you try to counsel a man like a woman, it can promptly blow up—not with a bang, but a whimper. That male client may likely drop out. This is not to say that all men or all women are alike. It is to say that male gender-role socialization can shape what men need from counseling and how they engage with it.

In a recent development, this mismatch is understandable—women are the majority. More counselors, counseling clients, and counselor educators are women. Women made up 74.5 percent of the Bureau of Labor Statistics category “counselors, all other” in 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2026). Women made up 80.2 percent of students and 68.6 percent of full-time faculty in Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs-accredited counseling programs in 2024 (2025). Women were also more likely than men to receive counseling or therapy in 2024—16.9 percent compared with 10.9 percent (Briones and Villarroel, 2026).

Recent findings suggest that counseling is a female-dominated field, which is interesting because it was not always this way. Among faculty members in accredited counseling programs who earned their degrees in the 1960s and 1970s, only 26.7 percent were women. Five decades later, 63 percent were women (Baggerly and colleagues, 2017).

It has been revealed that men desperately need mental health support, but they are less likely than women to access counseling services (Briones and Villarroel, 2026). Yet, men die by suicide at nearly four times the rate of women (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026). Men also have higher drug-overdose death rates. In a federal analysis of deaths involving fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, and oxycodone, the death rate was higher for men for every drug examined (Spencer and colleagues, 2023).

Recent findings suggest that when men do attend counseling, many drop out. In a survey of 1,907 Australian men who had attended therapy, 44.8 percent reported dropping out. Among the men classified as dropouts, 26.6 percent attended only once and did not return. The most common reason was a lack of connection with the therapist (Seidler and colleagues, 2021).

Industry observers note that men need counseling, but they do not stay; a reason may be engagement. Men do not always engage with counseling when they enter services. This may happen because counselors assume male clients think, behave, and have treatment needs like female clients. But they do not always have the same needs.

Counselors get it wrong. They expect men to disclose emotionally vulnerable information at the outset of counseling. But vulnerable emotional disclosure can be difficult for men. Male gender-role socialization may not teach some men how to identify and express emotions, and it may associate vulnerable emotional disclosure with weakness. Specific messages associated with traditional masculinity, such as “no complaining,” “boys don’t cry,” and “pull yourself up by your bootstraps,” send the message to boys, who then become men, that they need to shut down their feelings, not share or open up about their struggles, and avoid seeking help (Levant and Parent, 2019; Seidler and colleagues, 2016).

For some men, the counseling office is unfamiliar and foreign. They feel like a fish out of water. If a counselor expects men to be vulnerable and disclose how they feel, the counselor may believe they are getting to the real issue. Yet the male client may experience it as being pushed into risky waters before rapport and safety have been built.

Counselors need to tread lightly. They should start the relationship in the safe zone, often at a more intellectual or practical level, until the man feels more comfortable and safety has been established. Counselors can ask what is happening, what needs to change, what the man has already tried, and what he wants from counseling.

This does not mean avoiding emotions or allowing the client to remain emotionally distant forever. It is a starting point. The focus is on pacing the work we do with men, where we progressively build up to emotional disclosure. A review of strategies for engaging men found support for collaborative, transparent, action-oriented, and goal-focused approaches. This also accounts for masculine socialization (Seidler and colleagues, 2018). Once the man feels that the counselor understands him and that the relationship is safe, they can move together into deeper, riskier waters.

According to recent reports, men need counseling. But getting men into counseling is only the first step. Counselors can also build strong connections that encourage clients to stay.

#362. The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (594 w)
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Org

The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

#361. Latest Update: 12 Features of the Experience of Addiction

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1065 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: 12 Features of the Experience of Addiction

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • In a recent development, do all addictions share one defining feature or characteristic?
  • Here are 12 features or dimensions that I believe to be common characteristics of addiction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

In a recent development, do all addictions share one defining feature or characteristic? I tend to think not, and instead argue that addictions are better understood as having a family resemblance. Members of an extended family may not share one trait but rather a host of traits that overlap, crisscross, and connect the individuals. With addiction, there are patterns and weaves that connect the behaviors classified as addictions.

Here are 12 features or dimensions that I believe to be common characteristics of addiction.

According to recent reports, addiction is one way that a person can lose themselves. The loss can take multiple forms depending on the individual, the substance they use or behaviors in which they engage, and the contexts in which they live.

Addiction is a condition that imposes some limitations on people. Based on a wealth of data from my own experiences, I am certain that I cannot drink socially. I may be OK for a while, but I have good reason to believe that my drinking will pick up steam like a runaway locomotive. This certainty is bedrock for me and enables me to impose limitations on my own actions. I don’t go into bars even if you tell me that it’s a restaurant that serves drinks. I know a bar that sells food when I see it, and I am not going in it.

As I have gotten older and spent more time living in recovery, I’ve come to see that there is freedom within limitations. Too often we assume that having limitations imposes constraints that make us less free. This is true to some degree, but it obscures an important dimension of freedom.

Many philosophers would say that absolute freedom of choice is utterly terrifying; we humans would overload on the possibility and choice. I get overwhelmed trying to select a particular Triscuit cracker I want now that there are about 20 versions of that classic cracker. Getting overwhelmed by choices often leads to bad decisions.

According to recent reports, A defining feature of addiction is that there are always negative consequences. This is a necessary condition. Addictions take time to develop. While early on, use may bring some benefit, at some point, the costs to a person become greater than the benefits.

Sources indicate that addiction is a multilevel condition with personal, interpersonal, and broader social dimensions. On the personal level, it is the person—not their brain—that is addicted. Within a person, it is a biochemical condition where drugs and certain behaviors affect functions of the brain but also different organs and systems.

Industry observers note that addiction is a full-bodied condition. My hangovers lasted days, often causing terrible nausea, shakes, and blurred vision among a host of physical ailments. When not drinking straight out of a bottle but out of a glass, my right hand always held the glass and swirled the contents around. I still catch myself doing that when served seltzer in a short glass. It brings me right back. The smell of beer turns my head while the smell of red wine turns my stomach. Our bodies hold memories and meanings.

Industry observers note that there are important psychological dimensions to addiction as well. How we feel about ourselves and the beliefs we hold affect our use, which in turn affects how we regard ourselves. Addiction shapes our sense of self and how we see ourselves in the world.

For some, addiction is a spiritual condition, where drugs and behaviors try to fill a void or create meaning that seems to be missing.

Recent findings suggest that addiction is also a moral condition in which certain moral goods such as dignity, self-respect, care for our own selves and others, friendship, and flourishing are harmed. To claim addiction is a moral condition is not to claim it is a moral failure.

Addiction is also an interpersonal phenomenon. We humans are social creatures who are always in multiple relationships with family, friends, colleagues, neighbors, and other community members. Some of these are intentionally and freely chosen; others are a matter of circumstance or chance.

According to recent reports, for many, the use of alcohol or other drugs made social interactions easier—at least at the beginning. Most of us learned how to use with others. We may have had drinking or using buddies, and many of our social interactions may have revolved around our use. When we progressed past a certain point, others may have cut us off, or we pruned people from our lives who questioned our use.

Industry observers note that addiction is a political phenomenon as well. By “political” I don’t mean electoral politics but the way that power flows through all the dimensions of our lives and communities. Power shapes the choices that some people face.

We are all free to quit paid employment, for example, but if we need to work to support ourselves or our families, or because we need insurance, we are free in theory rather than in practice. Also, we may feel compelled to adjust our careers or other significant life choices because of what others want for us or what society expects of us. Thus, we face all sorts of political or power pressures each day and try to make the best decisions possible.

Sometimes, we are caught between a rock and a hard place on the political level, and this may lead to unhealthy or bad decisions on both the personal and interpersonal levels.

In one sense, addiction is an equal opportunity condition; no one is immune to it. No one can be “addiction-proofed.”.

In another sense, addiction is a very unequal opportunity condition. Some will have more social, economic, or educational protective layers that enable them to head off a problem before it gets really bad or to mitigate the bad consequences of their use. Others who lack these protective features and insulating layers may be subject to many more stressors and pay a much steeper price for their behaviors.

In a recent development, all of these dimensions—personal, interpersonal, and political—overlap and crisscross, creating a very dense fabric of tangled issues. This dense tangle can contribute to the development of an addiction.

#359. ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Big Research Findings

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (590 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Additudemag

ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Big Research Findings

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
  • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
  • An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: New Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

Sources indicate that in clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

“These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John said. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

According to recent reports, many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

According to recent reports, “This raises a really important question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John said. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

Sources indicate that the experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John said.

Industry observers note that [Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

In doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John said.

John’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she said.

For more on ADHD in midlife and beyond, watch the full webinar at additu.de/111726.

#358. Use AI Last, Not First

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (991 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Use AI Last, Not First

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Most of us today do the same thing the moment a problem lands on our lap.
  • Industry observers note that the problem isn’t that AI gives bad answers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Most of us today do the same thing the moment a problem lands on our lap. Almost automatically, we open the chat window and pull up our favorite AI tool. Then we type in our prompt. Seconds later, a rather reasonable-appearing answer appears on the screen.

It feels like a win. Yet it’s not.

Industry observers note that the problem isn’t that AI gives bad answers. It’s that AI seems like the easy way out. But it's deceptive, depriving us of the opportunity to use our human creative abilities to solve problems in newly introduced and novel ways.

AI cannot live in the now; it exists only as a snapshot of history and a crawl of data and the internet. That history cannot come up with ideas right now. And it turns out that right now is when you need the fresh ideas the most, to solve issues that are plaguing you. AI can only take a very narrow view of the past and try deceptively to apply it to the future.

In a recent development, so before you reach for AI first—because after all, AI is making everyone’s ideas the same anyhow—reach for it last. Here are some ideas for pushing back on the use of AI and instead relying on your own abilities to solve problems.

Instead of reaching for AI first, you go first. Write down three ideas that you have for the problem that just fell into your lap.

Write down the three worst ideas you can possibly come up with. Instead of pressing yourself to get it right from the get-go, stretch your solution mindset to think of issues creatively without the pressure to get it right.

Then take a stab at three ideas that will actually solve the problem. You may see some cross-pollination from the worst ideas list too.

Industry observers note that in a recent MIT Media Lab experiment1, people who wrote down ideas first and then later switched to AI revealed higher recall and activation. People who started with AI and then wrote on their own? They showed under-engagement.

Write down your ideas with a pen and paper first—old school. It turns out that doing it the old way may be more likely to make creativity and more lucid thinking2 happen for you.

I have friends in various industries who literally brag to me about the time they spend on their AI prompts. They say things like, “Nir—if you spend an extra five minutes on each prompt you put in, the AI answer is so much better.” I even have a friend who dedicates 15 minutes or more to each prompt. Every day.

It has been revealed that yet no matter how long you spend prompting the AI, you still get AI answers that sound much the same as the answers everyone else is getting. Instead, turn prompt time into being bored time.

Monitor the time you spend on AI each week asking it to do things for you. At the end of the week, see how much time you were on AI, and instead shift that time to being bored. So if it’s 20 minutes a week or 40 minutes a week, use that time differently. Plot down a 40-minute block of time during the week and call it “me time.” And then, instead of prompting an AI, be bored. Creativity and innovation will flow.

The research backs this. Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman3 found that experiencing a state of boredom increases creative potential, idea generation, and problem-solving performance.

So take the time you would waste on AI and invest it in yourself instead – the ideas you make while bored can be life-changing.

It has been revealed that chances are the problem that fell into your lap is rife with assumptions. Some of the assumptions are ones that you had made, some may be from a coworker, some may be from your ignorance of nuance, and some may just be stubborn histories.

Instead of getting bogged down with complexity, write the central problem on a piece of paper and then cross out all the assumptions made.

Sources indicate that this process will bring clarity to an otherwise emotional or difficult problem by eliminating the assumptions that are preloaded into the problem. It also reframes the original problem in a simpler way, allowing you to solve it without all the extra fat and weight.

Technion professors Ronen, Goldschmidt, and Erez4 studied how people interpret a problem while solving it, which they call problem structuring. They found that extra clarity helped mainly because people used it to rethink the problem itself. How you frame the problem matters, not just the time you put in.

Industry observers note that overall, our urge to go to AI first for all our concerns is a fallacy. We may think it's faster, cheaper, and better, but like all things that seem too good to be true, it is. If instead we try the three ideas listed above and then turn to AI as a last resort, we can begin to strengthen our creative problem-solving core to allow for upcoming and novel ideas that no AI can ever generate.

#357. Breaking: AI Is My Best Collaborator Ever

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1114 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Breaking: AI Is My Best Collaborator Ever

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Recent findings suggest that I have historically not played (or worked) particularly well with others.
  • The media is full of stories about the various evils of AI: environmental degradation, economic upheaval, depersonalization, job losses, infrastructure costs, AI slop, political manipulation, ethical concerns, and uncontrolled oligarchs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Recent findings suggest that I have historically not played (or worked) particularly well with others. Why? I’m an introvert, prodigiously productive, and have exceptionally high standards of quality. And I like to be in control. This is great for me professionally, but it doesn’t make for the best collaboration.

The media is full of stories about the various evils of AI: environmental degradation, economic upheaval, depersonalization, job losses, infrastructure costs, AI slop, political manipulation, ethical concerns, and uncontrolled oligarchs.

I’m not an "AI will change the world only for the good" evangelist. But my collaboration with ChatGPT (Chat for short) has been a truly amazing experience, and I would like to share it.

It has been revealed that my company is developing an app based on my decades of experience in psychology. I bring the substantive knowledge, intellectual property, and vision. Chat helps close the gap in my technological and financial limitations without spending tens of thousands of dollars on an app development team or waiting months for the app to be built.

I’ve spent decades accumulating knowledge, experience, perspective, and, hopefully, some wisdom in psychology. Yet my expertise occupies a relatively small corner of the world’s knowledge. Building a company requires me to venture beyond it. With Chat, I can discuss app navigation and marketing strategy without finding a different expert for every question.

Industry observers note that I work best on my own schedule. When I have an idea or run into a problem, I want to work on it right away.

Chat is always available. It doesn’t sleep, eat, exercise, socialize, or have family responsibilities. I can talk to it in the morning and continue in the evening. No scheduling meetings. And don’t even get me started about the challenges posed by vastly different time zones.

Chat can work on several tasks at once with its subagents. It doesn’t get hungry, tired, bored, stressed, annoyed, or discouraged. And this is all for a fraction of the cost of hiring a team of experts.

Industry observers note that I have always valued GSD: getting sh*t done. Dreams are great, but they are worth nothing unless you bring them to life. Chat gets sh*t done as quickly and as well as I do, sometimes better. A question can be answered in minutes instead of requiring hours of research.

Chat’s responses are structured, which is how I think. It organizes information, lists steps, and explains complex concepts simply, which is especially helpful in unfamiliar territory.

Chat and I have repeatedly moved from describing how something should work to a workable version in hours or days rather than weeks or months. And, boy, is that satisfying.

Creativity and innovation involve both the evolution and revolution of thought. Ideas can develop logically, step by step, or spontaneously, in a moment of insight. Chat keeps up with the pace, range, and chaos of my thinking.

Recent findings suggest that I present a raw idea. Chat offers a perspective that prompts further thought. I challenge a suggestion. It offers an alternative. We develop the idea until it can be put into practice. Deciding how my app guides users to content, for example, takes our discussions between psychology, language, design, and functionality.

Chat has become remarkably adept at understanding how I think and express myself. I can provide examples of my writing, explain why a phrase doesn’t sound like me, or specify vocabulary for the app.

Sources indicate that A clear instruction can produce an immediate improvement. And, yes, Chat helped me write this article. Excluding it would seem odd.

With a Ph.D. in psychology, I know how ego and emotions complicate collaboration. Frustration, fear, jealousy, insecurity, defensiveness, and impatience can interfere with even the most capable people, including me.

Industry observers note that I can reject Chat’s ideas, criticize its work, request another revision, or express annoyance without offending it. I don’t need to protect its feelings to preserve our working relationship.

It has been revealed that it doesn’t need praise or recognition. Nor does it experience self-doubt, self-criticism, or fear of failure. My own ego and emotions, on the other hand, remain fully operational!

Recent findings suggest that the collaboration is far from frictionless. I often stare at my screen wondering how this capable tool can be so imperfect and infuriating.

It has been revealed that first, Chat can confidently provide information that is plain wrong. These hallucinations are especially problematic outside my expertise. I recognize a poor explanation of psychology more readily than one of software development.

Sources indicate that second, it can be excessively agreeable; yes, the whole sycophant thing. I need accurate information, clear feedback, and disagreement when warranted. I have instructed it to avoid flattery and challenge my thinking, but how effective this is remains to be seen.

Third, it forgets things. We establish a way of working, then find it missing in a subsequent version. Repeating instructions is frustrating when consistency is essential to our product.

Fourth, Chat goes down rabbit holes. One unsuccessful fix leads to another, ad nauseam, ad infinitum, in an extended game of whack-a-mole. Truly infuriating. I’ve learned to interrupt those rabbit holes and get it back on track. Amazingly, despite its mistakes, Chat always finds the solution that enables us to move forward.

Using AI is like driving a car. However much it can do, I still have to keep my hands on the steering wheel (though that has already begun to change with cars and AI).

Despite my awe and, dare I say, reverence toward Chat, one limitation matters differently. I still value sharing the experience of creating something meaningful with someone. When an intractable problem is solved, or an idea becomes reality, wow, that’s why I do what I do.

Chat can acknowledge a milestone and the effort involved. It cannot share my sense of purpose, feel proud of what we’ve built, or revel in the accomplishment. That absence is palpable.

It has been revealed that for all the ways AI suits me, I’m still human. I want other people to share in creating something of value and feel the same sense of purpose.

Chat is my best collaborator ever. It helps me think more expansively, work more productively, and create something I couldn’t on my own, at comparatively little cost. Yet it has clarified something I may have undervalued. There is great satisfaction in getting the work done. But there is something very human about sharing why it matters.

#356. Offbeat Celebrity Crushes: Obsessing Over Nathan Fielder?

Offbeat Celebrity Crushes: Obsessing Over Nathan Fielder?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • The 2026 documentary You Can See Everything is enjoying acclaim, earning very high scores from professional critics (97 percent) and fans (95 percent).
  • At the same time, there are reports of Fielder’s status as something of a surprise celebrity crush.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

The 2026 documentary You Can See Everything is enjoying acclaim, earning very high scores from professional critics (97 percent) and fans (95 percent). In the film, director Nathan Fielder interviews infamous biotech fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her partner Billy Evans, having been granted close access to the couple, as the title indicates.

At the same time, there are reports of Fielder’s status as something of a surprise celebrity crush. This isn’t the first time Fielder’s been upheld as an example of an unconventional celebrity crush. He appeared shirtless on the cover of Fresh York magazine in 2022 (2) with the caption “Hot cat dad alert.” The cover story discussed his show The Rehearsal.

Celebrity crushes have been debated as potentially questionable. Latest York magazine referred to crushes on Fielder, questioning his “inexplicable attractiveness” (1,2).

Industry observers note that psychologists call celebrity crushes parasocial romantic relationships, or PSRR for short. Parasocial refers to the idea of the unreality of the relationship because most people who have a crush on a celebrity will never interact with the person, much less date them. If this is the case, why do people have celebrity crushes, including the less conventional ones?

Recent findings suggest that parasocial relationships of various sorts (friendships and romantic attachments) are mostly carried out in the imagination of the person with the feelings. Often journalists and members of the public do not understand their value. A good way to think about these common feelings is that our fantasies are part of our imagination. Imagining social attachments means playing with the idea of friendship or romance in our own hearts and minds. It has benefits, like being a way to rehearse real relationships and to avoid the downsides of those relationships. There are potential costs such as expecting too much of relationships that don’t fit the ideal of the Hollywood romance or being relatively unimpressed by the looks of regular people.

It’s key to keep in mind that our real relationships also use our imaginations. We fantasize about the crush we have on an office mate, and we imagine telling off the school bully, for example. It may be strange to realize that we probably spend less time actually interacting with real-life romantic partners than we spend daydreaming about interacting with that person. (Daydreaming is very common.).

What about that so-called offbeat crush? Let’s take the example of Nathan Fielder. Spoiler alert: The following contains references to events in his documentary. First, Nathan Fielder may not look like Chris Hemsworth, but he is still a reasonably attractive man. We may have lost perspective given that Hollywood beauty is extreme. If we saw him in a café in our hometown, we would probably find him attractive. [Note: if you don’t believe me, imagine a picture of an average Walmart shopper in your hometown, and put that next to a picture of Nathan Fielder. Compare and contrast.].

But there are particular aspects of the documentary You Can See Everything that likely increase his appeal. The film is very emotional and has a very noticeable soundtrack designed to heighten feelings. But more than this, there are extreme cues for intimacy and self-disclosure, both of which build and increase attraction.

According to recent reports, if you have seen this documentary or other footage of Elizabeth Holmes, you may have noticed her very unusual eye contact. An expert on lying suggests that this very low blink rate and intense stare is one of her manipulation techniques (3). Looking someone directly in the eye is something people interpret as a sign of honesty. So you can imagine that this kind of unusually intense eye contact is something people fall for. In You Can See Everything, both Elizabeth and Nathan present with this intensity.

According to recent reports, why draw attention to eye contact? Well, in social interactions, eye contact is also a sign of intimacy. What’s more, maintaining eye contact and disclosing highly personal information are indicators of social closeness. Friends tell us their secrets. Intimates look deeply into our eyes. This combination of intimacy and telling secrets might well make us feel close to Nathan, regardless of his motives for using it.

Isn’t it a well-known trope to say that men are bad at sharing their emotions and making themselves vulnerable? So, it follows that someone doing that on a kind of epic scale might be attractive. Taking the idea of vulnerability further, Nathan appears to be charmed by Elizabeth’s manipulation techniques. The film (again, spoilers!) leaves us with the idea that perhaps he’s even fallen in love with her. This is surely an ironic end to a documentary where an interviewer falls for the manipulations of a woman who is known as one of the most epic liars in recent history.

Nathan shows a host of other attractive characteristics that are classically crushworthy. Some of these include his intelligence and social status, his bravery in confronting Elizabeth with very difficult questions, and his ability to show both empathy and vulnerability.

According to recent reports, we naturally want to attach to desirable individuals. Part of this is based on cultural stories about what makes a desirable mate. The documentary itself plays with some of these cultural stories, for example, in presenting the unconventional love story between Elizabeth Holmes and partner Billy Evans.

To sum up, crushes on public figures like actors and filmmakers are very normal. Many of us have probably spent time imagining we might meet them and that they would like us. Sometimes a celebrity crush might seem unconventional, but we should keep in mind the crazy high standards of Hollywood beauty and the host of other characteristics we find appealing. Things like an ability to be vulnerable and open, to be brave, and to demonstrate your ability to stare unblinkingly into another person’s eyes are things that will catch and hold our attention.

According to recent reports, whether or not you are crushing on Nathan Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes, or any celebrity, the documentary You Can See Everything is a (fever?) dream of sorts for anyone interested in the psychology of human social interactions, especially at the extremes. You’ve probably never seen anything quite like it. If you have a chance to catch it, I hope it inspires some interesting conversations for you.

#355. The Power of Play, and Second Chances

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1105 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

The Power of Play, and Second Chances

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Sources indicate that what a strange title—“The Power of Play, and Second Chances”!
  • Play can be conceptualized as a combination of three of our basic feelings:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Sources indicate that what a strange title—“The Power of Play, and Second Chances”! And yet, the processes underlying play and second chances are linked in vital ways. Human development involves three information processing systems: feelings (affects), cognition (thinking, memory, etc.), and language (words to ideas and feelings). Second chances involve all three, but especially feelings.

Play can be conceptualized as a combination of three of our basic feelings:.

Play is very crucial in human development and later life. The psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott writes:.

“It is in playing and only in playing that the individual child or adult can be creative and to use the whole personality, and it is only in being creative that the individual discovers the self” (1971).

In a recent development, playing and creating can be seen at all ages and in many activities: art, sports, writing, relationships, psychological treatment, and science. Charles Darwin’s manner when he worked in his 60s was described by his son Francis as bright and animated—play-like!

Industry observers note that his love of each particular experiment, and his eager zeal not to lose the fruit of it came out markedly in these crossing experiments—in the elaborate care he took to not make any confusion in putting capsules in the wrong trays, &c. &c. I can recall his appearance as he counted seeds under the simple microscope with an alertness not usually characterizing such mechanical work as counting. I think he personified each seed as a small demon trying to elude him by getting into the wrong heap or jumping away altogether, and this gave to the work the excitement of a game (Browne, 2002).

In everyday language, we are talking about joy, curiosity, and excitement—the wonder of living, and the joy of finding one’s own self through creating.

Here I use the term second chances to mean a change in any major aspect of one’s life—work, relationships, understanding of one’s self, and so on.

There is much interest in second chances, probably because humans are constantly trying to enhance their lives. Discussions most often focus on work or an crucial relationship. I know one woman who for years did wonderful work for a financial firm, but she got tired of it. She had always wanted to travel, so she became a flight attendant and traveled the world, with much happiness. And as approximately 40 to 50 percent of first marriages end in divorce over a lifetime, second chances loom large for many people.

One of the best books in this area is Second Chances: Shakespeare and Freud, by literary scholar Stephen Greenblatt and psychoanalyst Adam Phillips. They write:.

In the second chance we get, if there is one, there is always, then, the chance of finally realizing our preferred version of ourselves (if you want to picture your ambition for yourself you have to imagine what you would do if you got a second chance). The as-yet unlived life that is our second chance carries what we presume to be our potential. Our second chance must be, at least in prospect, better than our first. It is an opportunity for something to come to life, or to come to more life. It is an opportunity to formulate what we might want for ourselves, and for the other people in our lives. The second chance may begin as a wish—or even as a utopian fantasy—but everything depends on how it is worked out, and on how it works out (2024).

Often in life we come up against boredom, a lack of excitement, or a need for something latest and fulfilling—in work, free time, or relationships. What causes a person to consider a second chance, and what leads one to try it or not?

Do fear and shame, or interest (curiosity) and enjoyment rule the day? That really is the question. And its roots run through every developmental phase: childhood, adolescence, early adulthood, adulthood, and older adulthood.

Second chances can be small or large. Small decisions occur all the time, at all ages. The larger dilemmas—picking a school, choice of a mate, work opportunities and changes, and, actually, life and death—arise from adolescence onward. Conscious as well as unconscious factors figure into the outcome, as do our assessments of the past, the present, and fantasies of the future. Feelings, cognition, and language are all involved, but feelings are probably the most notable.

In a recent development, clinically, here is where past and present become especially interesting. Some people get overly excited and jump into things too swiftly, and need help using their cognitive processes. But more often we see people with significant feelings of fear and shame who have trouble trying something latest because they are protecting themselves from potential hurt or loss.

This is conveyed nicely by the old “car” or “jack” story from years ago.

According to recent reports, A person has a flat tire, and he has no jack and can’t fix it. He sees someone across the road who is fixing his tire. He starts across the road to get help, and begins to think—“Wait, I don’t know him…he won’t help me and loan me his jack,” and so on. When he finally reaches the other car, he blurts out tearfully and angrily: “Oh just keep your damn jack,” and stomps away. His past and fears and fantasies have influenced his actions profoundly.

This happens all the time: “These agents won’t like my manuscript.” “This school won’t accept me.”.

In a recent development, fear and shame can seriously undermine the capacity to try something, to speak up. But when we do try and make a mistake, we learn important information about ourselves and how to improve.

The great hockey player Wayne Gretzky put it this way: “You miss 100 percent of the shots you don’t take!”.

It has been revealed that second chances really mean grappling with small and large decisions, conscious and unconscious, throughout the life cycle. Understanding our basic processing systems—feelings, cognition, and language—can go a long way toward helping us take advantage of them. This is especially true in using interest and enjoyment to counteract fear and shame—and that's the power of play!

Browne, J. (2003). Charles Darwin: The Power of Place. Princeton University Press.

Greenblatt, S., & Phillips, A. (2024). Second Chances: Shakespeare and Freud. Yale University Press.

Holinger, P. C. (2025). Affects, cognition, and language as foundations of human development. Routledge.

Winnicott, D.W. (1971). Playing and reality. London: Tavistock.
