#329. HIV Treatment Is Prevention

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (736 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

HIV Treatment Is Prevention

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Industry observers note that HIV treatment, antiretroviral therapy (ART), has seen dramatic advancement in the past four decades.
  • In addition to the direct health benefits of maintaining an undetectable viral load, there is an additional prevention benefit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Industry observers note that HIV treatment, antiretroviral therapy (ART), has seen dramatic advancement in the past four decades. HIV is now a chronic condition. When people take their ART as prescribed and maintain an undetectable viral load and a high T-cell count, life expectancy for those living with HIV approximates that of those who are uninfected (Trickey et al., 2023).

In addition to the direct health benefits of maintaining an undetectable viral load, there is an additional prevention benefit. When someone living with HIV has an undetectable viral load, they are unable to transmit HIV through sex (Eisinger et al., 2019). Public health campaigns promoting ART adherence have called attention to this phenomenon, terming it Undetectable = Untransmissible or U=U.

Sources indicate that we might assume that prevention messaging that draws on U=U would be most effective among people living with HIV who are partnered with someone who is uninfected. Having an undetectable viral load would decrease or eliminate the potential for sexual transmission of HIV to their partner. Alternatively, people living with HIV may be generally motivated to take their ART and maintain an undetectable viral load when they are having sex with partners who may be uninfected regardless of relationship status.

In two recent studies (Hillesheim & Starks, 2026; Starks et al., 2024), our team examined relationship status group differences in ART adherence and viral detectability in large samples of sexual minority male adults.

Ordinarily, we expect people in relationships to have better health outcomes compared to single people (Kiecolt-Glaser & Wilson, 2017). In both of these papers, findings suggested this was true for sexual minority men living with HIV in non-monogamous relationships and those whose partners were uninfected. These groups were more likely to be adherent to ART and report an undetectable viral load compared to single sexual minority men. Presumably, these are groups where men may be most likely to consider preventing transmission of HIV to sexual partners.

There was also a warning sign in both papers. Sexual minority men in relationships where both partners were living with HIV were significantly less likely to be adherent to their ART and achieve an undetectable viral load. For these men, prevention motivation may be of limited relevance. It may be key to emphasize the personal health benefits of HIV treatment to maximize HIV outcomes in these subgroups.

It has been revealed that effective HIV treatment not only prolongs the lives of people living with HIV, but it also eliminates the potential for sexual transmission. This prevention motivation may explain why rates of ART adherence and achieving an undetectable viral load are higher among sexual minority men in non-monogamous relationships and those with uninfected partners. We may need different messages, emphasizing the personal health benefits of HIV care, to reach subgroups who have low levels of sexual HIV prevention motivation.

#328. What Do We Do With Leftover Love?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

What Do We Do With Leftover Love?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • According to recent reports, he was everything you had ever wanted.
  • According to recent reports, you can throw the eggs into the bin, but the feelings cannot disappear as quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

According to recent reports, he was everything you had ever wanted. Kind, gentle, thoughtful. Almost too good to be true. You imagined a future together, a home, a family, a lifetime of ordinary mornings. Then, one day, while making eggs for breakfast, you saw the messages. The pan was still warm. The sun was coming through the window. Nothing around you had changed, yet it's all gone. In a matter of seconds, the man you thought you knew disappeared. The future you had imagined vanished with him. But the love you felt still lingers.

According to recent reports, you can throw the eggs into the bin, but the feelings cannot disappear as quickly. Love involves several interconnected brain systems. Dopamine-rich reward pathways contribute to desire and anticipation (Fisher et al., 2010); the brain's natural opioid system helps make closeness comforting and social rejection distressing (Hsu et al., 2013; Nummenmaa et al., 2016); and limbic regions, particularly the amygdala, help connect emotional experiences with memory (Cahill et al., 1996). The truth can change what you think in seconds, but it cannot instantly erase what your brain has learned over months or years, so do not let people tell you that you are "co-dependent" or "weak." You have a normal brain that might play tricks on you.

You have leftover love, and that leftover love can be weaponised against you (Lesiak & Gelsthorpe, 2025). He may use the feelings that remain to persuade you to let him stay, asking you to ignore what you have discovered, silence your judgment, and compromise the very values that define who you are.

It has been revealed that he has already betrayed you. Now he is asking you to betray yourself for him.

You are the one expected to swallow your anger, silence your judgment, and call it "forgiveness." Look at the bargain. He gets to keep the woman who loves him. And you are expected to give up the woman who knows the truth.

Decades ago, psychiatrist Judith Herman wrote about it in Trauma and Recovery (1992):.

His ultimate goal appears to be the creation of a willing victim. Hostages, political prisoners, battered women, and slaves have all remarked upon the captor’s curious psychological dependence upon his victim. George Orwell gives voice to the totalitarian mind in the novel 1984:.

“We are not content with negative obedience, nor even with the most abject submission. When finally you surrender to us, it must be of your own free will. We do not destroy the heretic because he resists us; so long as he resists us we never destroy him. We convert him, we capture his inner mind, we reshape him. We burn all evil and all illusion out of him; we bring him over to our side, not in appearance, but genuinely, heart and soul.”.

Read those last words again. Heart and soul.

It is not enough that you stay. You must want to stay. It is not enough that you forgive him. You must learn to see his betrayal as something you can live with. You must look at the evidence of your own eyes and persuade yourself that it no longer matters.

And if keeping him means abandoning everything you believe in, what exactly are you trying to save—and what's left—when you do that?

Some wounds are easier to bear because you know you stood by your values while receiving them. In Kraków, officers Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański were seriously wounded confronting a mass shooter. Poland calls them heroes, and people across the country are grateful for their courage and service.

Then there is another kind of wound. One that no surgeon can stitch. Amy Winehouse sings it in "You Know I'm No Good": “I cheated myself, like I knew I would.” By the end of the song, she is no longer simply confessing what she did. She is passing judgment on herself.

Imagine waking up beside a man you no longer respect, living a life you never wanted, having persuaded yourself to accept things you once knew were unacceptable. You kept him, perhaps. But somewhere along the way, you lost the ability to trust your own judgment.

According to recent reports, that is the deeper cruelty of weaponised love (Lesiak & Gelsthorpe, 2025). He does not need you to believe he is innocent. He needs you to stop caring that he isn't.

And if manipulation or coercion brought you to that point, the shame belongs to the person who engineered that surrender, not to you.

Sources indicate that name the man, not the fantasy. The betrayal wasn't simply another woman. It was the months of lies that made you believe you were building a future together while he was living another life. He needed you to trust him because, had you known the truth, you might have walked away. So he made sure you didn't.

That is what a programme of deception does. It robs you of the freedom to make informed choices about your own life. When used to dominate and subordinate, deception becomes a tool of coercive control and psychological abuse. Stop reaching for words that make him sound better. A liar is a liar. A traitor is a traitor. A backstabber is a backstabber. Grieve the man he pretended to be, the image he created to win your love and use it to control you. But don't defend the man behind the mask.

Sources indicate that the eggs went into the bin that morning. The relationship ended. The feelings are disappearing. You'll be ok! Probably you are already more ok now than when you were cheated on, lied to, and abused.

#327. Living Long Enough for the Next Latest Treatment

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Living Long Enough for the Next Latest Treatment

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • Recent findings suggest that my wife, Christine, had to fly out to London for work after missing several trips due to my illness.
  • Sources indicate that I received the CT report a couple of days into Christine’s trip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recent findings suggest that my wife, Christine, had to fly out to London for work after missing several trips due to my illness. Before she left, I had gotten my follow-up CT scan, but the radiologist hadn't read it yet. I had significant “scanxiety” about what it would show. While Christine was away, my kids did their best to help me—waking up on their own (tough as teens), fixing their own breakfast (really tough as teens), and getting out the door (really, really tough as teens). They even loaded and unloaded the dishwasher! Even though we had most of the logistics covered sans Mommy, the house was twice as dirty as usual. Plus, I missed the emotional anchor of her presence. The house was quieter. The click-clack of her keyboard or murmur of her work video calls was absent.

Sources indicate that I received the CT report a couple of days into Christine’s trip. Good news! The cancer in my right lung and a spot in my liver had shrunk. Being anxious, I got the report right away from my friend and primary care provider. That night, when I was showering, I was gripped with a sudden, unexpected sadness that verged on depression. Despite the positive results, in the back of my mind, I’d had this deep hope that my cancer would have magically vanished. Instead, the cancer, though smaller, was still there. The study my treatment was based on had shown that one patient had been miraculously noted in complete remission. It was just one point on a chart in a study, but the hope that it would happen for me had gripped my mind. I went into a negative-feedback cycle, and I was choked up, on the verge of tears. Somehow I had turned my good news into something horrible. Usually, I’d talk about the results and my hopes and fears, but she was a continent away and fast asleep. I made it through the week and to the eighth class, but the experience was a poignant reminder of how vital this was to my mental well-being; sharing my experiences with others still is.

Industry observers note that early on in my diagnosis, I called my classmate and good friend from medical school, who practices pulmonology in San Diego. I wasn’t close to any other classmates in med school except for Elan—we bonded over Mike’s Roast Beef sandwiches while taking our physical diagnosis class. He kindly reviewed my tests and introduced me to another friend and colleague, who told me something that gives me hope every day: “You only have to live long enough for the next new treatment to come out.” That simple statement comforts me when I dwell on my late-stage prognosis, thinking about how many years (or months) I may have left.

It has been revealed that one of the many beautiful parts of sharing my own cancer journey is meeting people going through their own cancer journeys who I would never have met otherwise. Sharing personal narratives—whether through storytelling, group discussions, or expressive writing—has emerged as a valuable psychosocial intervention in oncology. Storytelling is the communicative act of patients recounting their illness experiences through words, images, or even digital media, often revealing deeply personal emotions and insights. Across cancer types and patient populations, narrative-sharing interventions are increasingly recognized for fostering emotional expression and psychological adaptation to illness. Peer-reviewed research spanning children, adolescents, adults, and the elderly, indicates that storytelling bestows a range of benefits. These benefits include improvements in psychological well-being, coping and resilience, treatment adherence, social support, and even physiological or clinical outcomes.

Peer-reviewed research overwhelmingly supports the therapeutic value of storytelling and personal narratives for cancer patients of all ages and stages. Through sharing their experiences—whether in a support group, with a counselor, via digital media, or in a private journal—patients often achieve better psychological well-being, characterized by reduced anxiety, stress, and even depression. Storytelling fosters adaptation and coping, empowering patients with resilience and practical strategies to face cancer’s challenges. It also enhances social connectedness, diminishing isolation and strengthening support networks among those who “get it.” Notably, narrative interventions can encourage patients to stay engaged in treatment and healthy behaviors, potentially improving adherence and follow-through in care. While more research is needed, emerging evidence points to physiological benefits—improved symptom control, functional status, and overall quality of life—arising from the mind-body interplay of expressive storytelling. Taken together, these studies support the belief that the simple act of sharing one’s story is far more than talk or writing on a page; it is a meaningful therapeutic process that can help cancer patients heal psychologically, cope more effectively, build community, and perhaps even influence their health trajectories for the better. Narrative practices in oncology—from diagnosis through survivorship or end-of-life care—represent a holistic approach that honors patients’ voices while delivering measurable benefits across multiple dimensions of well-being.

Sources indicate that scans, treatments, family, and faith shape mental health; this can get wrapped into the stories people tell themselves when the future becomes a moving target. Narrative medicine is not a soft add-on to “real” care; it is part of the human need to communicate and be heard.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1104 w)

Industry News: Can Non-Alcoholic Drinks Help You Stop or Reduce Drinking?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Industry observers note that the Fresh Year is just around the corner, and it is a common time for people to revisit self-improvement-related goals.
  • Industry observers note that before reading this post, if you are not already familiar with non-alcoholic drinks, take a look at my recent post, “Is there alcohol in non-alcoholic drinks?” The short answer is that the amount of alcohol depends on where you live.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Industry observers note that the Fresh Year is just around the corner, and it is a common time for people to revisit self-improvement-related goals. If you want to reduce or stop drinking alcohol, you may be wondering if switching to non-alcoholic drinks could be helpful. As it turns out, for some people, non-alcoholic drinks could be a helpful substitute for alcoholic beverages, but there are also reasons to be cautious about this overall approach.

Industry observers note that before reading this post, if you are not already familiar with non-alcoholic drinks, take a look at my recent post, “Is there alcohol in non-alcoholic drinks?” The short answer is that the amount of alcohol depends on where you live. Generally, non-alcoholic drinks contain much lower alcohol by volume (ABV) than traditional alcoholic drinks, but they may still contain some alcohol. If you are trying to stop drinking alcohol completely, it would be important to check the rules where you live to make sure your chosen non-alcoholic drink has 0% ABV.

There are many reasons why someone may want to stop or reduce drinking alcoholic drinks, which I will not go over here. More relevant to this topic are the reasons why someone would want to consume non-alcoholic drinks, which are made to look and taste like alcoholic beverages, rather than traditional beverages that do not resemble alcoholic beverages (e.g., soft drinks, juices, water).

One reason for the popularity of non-alcoholic drinks is that someone may enjoy the taste of alcoholic drinks, like beer and wine, and wish to continue to drink similarly flavoured beverages (without the risks associated with consuming alcohol). Another reason people may choose non-alcoholic drinks is that they find it helps them continue to participate in social activities and routines that typically involve alcohol. For instance, when interviewing adults who drink alcohol heavily and have used non-alcoholic drinks to reduce drinking, some interviewees described that ordering a non-alcoholic beverage at a bar, club, or other social gathering allowed them to participate in the outing and blend in with their peers who were drinking alcohol.1 Further, unlike drinking alternatives like soft drinks, they describe that the experience of drinking a non-alcoholic drink remains symbolic as an "adult treat" given its look and presentation.

People may take different approaches to substitute with non-alcoholic drinks depending on their specific needs. Some people may completely substitute their alcoholic drinks for non-alcoholic drinks. Alternatively, people may replace alcoholic drinks in specific contexts, such as primarily substituting their home-based alcoholic drinks versus outing-based alcoholic drinks with non-alcoholic drinks.1 When replacing alcoholic drinks one typically consumes, some may replace them completely with non-alcoholic drinks while others may alternate between drink types (sometimes referred to as “zebra striping”).

While people describe using non-alcoholic drinks to reduce their alcohol use, an vital question remains about whether these drinks can actually help you stop or reduce drinking. As it turns out, the qualities that make non-alcoholic drinks an attractive substitute for alcoholic drinks may also get in the way of successfully reducing one’s drinking. Aspects of drinking (beyond alcohol itself) can serve as powerful reminders—referred to as cues—of alcohol. Specifically, qualities of the drink like its taste, container, and where it is consumed can, in fact, lead to a strong urge to drink alcohol itself. By definition, non-alcoholic beverages will not lead to intoxication. Once consumed, these drinks may strengthen the desire to become intoxicated (rather than quench that desire), and lead someone to return to drinking alcohol.

Initial studies have suggested that non-alcoholic drinks may help people reduce their drinking. When adults who drink were provided non-alcoholic drinks free of charge over a 12-week period, they reported greater reductions in their alcoholic drink consumption compared to adults who were not provided these drinks.2 This reduction in alcoholic drinks continued a month after these non-alcoholic drinks were provided. A follow-up study suggested, however, that the reduced alcohol drinking was not observed amongst people with higher symptoms of alcohol use disorder.3 Additional research is needed to understand if non-alcoholic drinks may be a helpful way to reduce or stop drinking among people with an alcohol use disorder.

In a recent development, ultimately, there would be a net health and mental health benefit if someone reduces the overall number of alcoholic drinks by substituting non-alcoholic drinks. For instance, if someone switches from drinking four alcoholic drinks per week to two alcoholic drinks plus two non-alcoholic drinks, they would be reducing their exposure to harmful aspects of alcohol. However, depending on an individual’s circumstances, the chosen strategy for which drinks to substitute can affect how much they benefit overall. For instance, if a person finds they have more difficulty moderating their drinking when out with friends (versus at home), having a strategy to rely on non-alcoholic drinks when out with friends may be more beneficial than substituting their alcohol drinks consumed at home.

According to recent reports, while research is still in its early stages, non-alcoholic drinks show promise in helping people reduce their drinking. For some people, substituting non-alcoholic drinks may provide the benefits of drinking alcoholic drinks without the negatives; however, it is crucial to make sure the substitute approach does not become an add-on approach. In cases where non-alcoholic drinks are too similar to alcoholic drinks that it leads you to drink alcohol anyway, then the substitution approach is not successful. Therefore, if you are thinking about giving this strategy a try, it is important to keep track of your drinking carefully to determine if it is actually helping you to reduce the number of alcoholic drinks you consume.

#325. What to Do When You’re Unsure About a Choice

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

What to Do When You’re Unsure About a Choice

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Many people struggle with making important decisions.
  • Sources indicate that one way to settle on a decision is to make a list of pros and cons of a particular course of action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Many people struggle with making important decisions. These include which college to attend, which career to undertake, whether to look for a new job, or how to find the right house.

Sources indicate that one way to settle on a decision is to make a list of pros and cons of a particular course of action. A cost/benefit analysis can also help: What would the cost be for a particular choice vs. the potential benefit?

For instance, here is a simple example: Suppose you are deciding between buying two houses that differ in price. The less expensive house will have a lower down payment that would allow you to have some money left in your savings account, but it is not in a great neighborhood. The more expensive house will drain your savings, but it is in a great neighborhood.

If the neighborhood is very key to you (great benefit), it might be worthwhile to drain your savings (cost). In other words, the benefit outweighs the cost. If the neighborhood is not that important to you, then the benefit of the more expensive house would not outweigh the cost, and therefore you should buy the cheaper house.

Sometimes, it’s hard to assess potential benefit vs. cost. For instance, if you are considering which college you want to attend, and different colleges provide different educational and extracurricular benefits that are hard to quantify, how do you make a decision?

When several colleges appear to be reasonable choices, I have a secret to share: It doesn’t matter which college you choose.

Sources indicate that among colleges that are a reasonable fit, what you do there matters more than which one you pick. As long as you work hard and take advantage of the educational and personal opportunities available to you at a college, you will gain a lot. If you don’t work hard and keep to yourself, you will gain little, no matter what college you attend.

Further, even if it were possible to make a “perfect” choice when you face a decision, within a few months the choice will no longer be perfect.

Because circumstances will have changed in a way that affects the benefits and potential costs of your decision.

For instance, if the decision you made related to choosing an undergraduate school, your preferences will likely change once you are exposed to newly introduced ideas, people, and situations that may alter your college experience in unforeseeable ways.

In a recent development, bottom line: Even with vital decisions, pick one, and make the best of it. In most circumstances, you will do well. If that does not turn out to be the case, you often can change course, and will have become wiser because you will be able to figure out how to avoid making a similar wrong choice in the future.

Another secret to keep in mind is: There is no "one" correct path for your life. People don’t click along straight lines like trains on railroad tracks. We float and bob and turn like rafts on a river that’s always flowing and changing.

You may feel like you can’t afford to make any “wrong” decisions—but sometimes the less obvious choice is a great one that will create fresh possibilities for you.

On my Center Point podcast, I have interviewed many successful people. I’ve been struck by many of the interviewees who changed course a few times until they identified their main career when they were in their late 20s.

It has been revealed that further, keep in mind that many people change jobs often, especially early in their working lives (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so your first choice is unlikely to lock you in permanently. With these secrets in mind, let’s look at thinking patterns that can help make good choices:.

It has been revealed that instead of asking, "What's the can't-fail choice?" consider asking, "What meets my needs?" Instead of "What could go wrong?" ask, "What are the possibilities? Instead of "What will everyone else think?" ask, "What is right for me?" When you ask these questions, you give your inner wisdom a chance to help guide you.

Industry observers note that some of the greatest blessings that come into our lives are surprises. When a decision doesn’t play out the way you want or expect, think about how you can embrace your upcoming direction or challenge instead of ways you can be unhappy about it. For instance, when you decide to audition for a part in the school play and don’t get chosen, think of what you can do with all the free time you’ll have.

When you feel stuck about a decision, imagine how your future self will feel about your choice—maybe in a month, a year, or even 10 years. What advice would the future wiser, older version of you give? Let the answer help guide your choices today.

In a recent development, 4. Be like Batman (or Sasha Fierce!).

In a recent development, did you know that there’s a scientific principle called the Batman Effect? It’s just as cool as it sounds. Also known as self-distancing, this is the idea that you can create a little space, perspective, and extra strength to deal with any decision or situation by getting out of an “I” mindset. In one study, researchers asked people to give a small public speech. (Speaking in public is a common and severe fear.) One group was asked to think about the upcoming speech as if they were in the middle of it, making statements that started with “I am” and “I feel.” Another group was asked to consider the same things, but instead of using an “I feel” statement, a participant named Anne would say, “Anne feels” or “Anne thinks.”.

In a recent development, it seems like a small change, right? But the results weren’t small. Participants who used the third person were less afraid and anxious, and they gave better speeches (Streamer et al,. 2017).

In a study with young children, researchers found they could take this idea one step further by having kids consider what Batman would do. Kids who were thinking like Batman were found to have thought more clearly than all the other participants (White & Carlson, 2015).

This kind of thinking is not just for kids. Years ago, when Beyoncé was explaining how she gives commanding live performances, she explained that when she was ready to go on stage, she’d stop thinking of herself as a regular person and start thinking of herself as a strong, powerful performer called Sasha Fierce. Sasha Fierce was confident and bold, and she helped make Beyoncé one of the top-selling recording artists of all time.

Sources indicate that making notable decisions can be stressful, especially when we worry that one wrong choice could change the course of our lives. But there is rarely just one correct path. By considering our options thoughtfully, asking ourselves helpful questions, and remaining flexible about what comes next, we can approach decisions with greater confidence.

Parts of this post are excerpted from my book, The Life Guide for Teens.

In a recent development, white, R. E. & Carlson, S. M. (2015). What would Batman do? Self-distancing improves executive function in young children. Developmental Science, 19(3), 419–426.

#324. How to Explain Adoption to a Child

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (958 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

How to Explain Adoption to a Child

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • According to recent reports, november is National Adoption Month, a time when we celebrate families formed through adoption and acknowledge there are children who still need safe, loving, permanent homes.
  • Every adoption carries a responsibility to help children understand their story, not simply how they joined their adoptive family, but what happened before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

According to recent reports, november is National Adoption Month, a time when we celebrate families formed through adoption and acknowledge there are children who still need safe, loving, permanent homes. Yet adoption is more than the creation of a new family. It also involves separation, loss, unanswered questions, and the lifelong search for self.

Every adoption carries a responsibility to help children understand their story, not simply how they joined their adoptive family, but what happened before. Children do not enter adoption with a blank slate. A child's need to talk about adoption helps them make meaning of their experiences, build self-esteem, develop trust, and understand their identity.

In a recent development, when children are not given explanations, they create their own. I know this personally. I entered foster care at 15 months old and was adopted at seven and a half. I will never forget my adoption day. My foster-adoptive family drove me to the courthouse, and I refused to get out of the car. I wrapped my arms around the seat and held on for dear life, terrified that I was being given away again because no one had explained what was happening to me.

Sources indicate that to the adults, adoption was a legal process for permanency. To me, it felt like another separation, another terrifying moment when adults were making decisions about my life without telling me why. This is why explanations matter.

According to recent reports, children need language to make meaning. Just because a child is not asking questions does not mean they are not thinking about them. Children will wonder: Why was I adopted? Why couldn't my birth parents keep me? What were they like? Did they love me? Are you going to give me away, too?

It has been revealed that when these questions remain unanswered, children internalize the experience as rejection. They may conclude, I must have been a bad baby, or There must be something wrong with me. Young children are egocentric. They believe they are responsible for events happening around them. And they will equate that separation from their birth family means they were unwanted or unlovable. So, they need to hear repeatedly that the separation was never their fault. They did not cause it, could not have prevented it, and were never responsible for the adults' circumstances. As I often remind children, babies are simply not that powerful.

As early as possible. As soon as parents are educated, emotionally prepared, and have gained as much knowledge about their child’s history.

Recent findings suggest that adoption should never be presented as one dramatic disclosure. It is an ongoing conversation that must be revisited throughout childhood, a term called “recycling information.” At every newly introduced developmental stage, children will revisit facts with greater cognitive, emotional, and psychological understanding. Adoption is understood differently at age 4, 8, 12, and 16. New questions emerge as awareness develops, and information that seemed factual suddenly carries deeper emotions.

Sources indicate that parents should gather photographs, letters, birth information, and gifts the birth parent may have shared. Make copies of precious photographs so children can safely hold, explore, and revisit them.

Parents should become comfortable initiating conversations rather than waiting for their child to ask, gently following the child's lead, respecting their readiness, and answering only the questions they are asking, age-appropriately.

Industry observers note that ask permission before sharing sensitive details. "Are you ready to learn the answer to your question?" via The Question Box Intervention from my book The Traumatized & At-Risk Youth Toolbox. A child who receives difficult information may respond with anger, disbelief, sadness, or confusion. Try not to correct these reactions; acknowledge and validate how difficult this may be to hear. Remind them that you are available to listen and support them. Also, make sure they have downtime to process and integrate this newfound information.

According to recent reports, utilize my children’s book What Is Adoption? For Kids with an accompanying animation to begin the dialogue:.

Industry observers note that parents can become anxious or uncomfortable when their child expresses curiosity about their birth family. Children are highly sensitive to these emotional reactions and may stop asking questions to protect their parents from discomfort. Some children may even fear that expressing interest in their birth family could threaten their relationship with their adoptive parents or lead to another rejection.

According to recent reports, if you notice yourself becoming defensive, anxious, or threatened by these conversations, I strongly encourage you to work with an adoption-competent therapist. Your child needs to know that their curiosity is not disloyalty and that their birth family can be discussed without threatening their place in your family.

So, during this month, I encourage parents to remember that explaining adoption is not about finding perfect words or eliminating painful feelings. It is about being present when children need answers, even when those answers are difficult, because we cannot change what happened to them, but we can change how they experience their past by being emotionally available in their healing.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Even children can get stuck in a rut, spinning their wheels in ruminating thoughts or maladaptive behaviors that don’t serve their mental health and well-being.
  • Industry observers note that enter Newbery Honor-winning author Kyle Lukoff’s latest picture book, The Vicious Cycle, about a unicycle who gets stuck in a rut and the friend who inspires it to try something new, at least for a little while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Even children can get stuck in a rut, spinning their wheels in ruminating thoughts or maladaptive behaviors that don’t serve their mental health and well-being.

Industry observers note that enter Newbery Honor-winning author Kyle Lukoff’s latest picture book, The Vicious Cycle, about a unicycle who gets stuck in a rut and the friend who inspires it to try something new, at least for a little while. Lukoff shares the inspiration behind this insightful book that speaks to the courage it takes to change, and how literature has played a role in his own mental health journey.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write The Vicious Cycle.

Kyle Lukoff: I've spent a lot of my professional life thinking deeply about picture books. I was a lead bookseller in the children's section of a Barnes & Noble in a neighborhood with a high population of young children, and that made me decide to get my master's degree in library science with a focus on children's literature and youth services.

Industry observers note that from there, I got a job as an elementary school librarian, with students aged 2 through fifth grade, and spent many hours a day sitting cross-legged on the floor reading to kids. My first published works were all picture books, and even now, with many novels and speeches and short stories under my belt, I consider myself a picture book author who sometimes writes other things as well.

The inspiration for The Vicious Cycle is truly underwhelming. "You know what would be funny," I told a friend, "is if there was a picture book about an angry unicycle, and it was called 'The Vicious Cycle.'" That idea percolated in my subconscious for a year or two before I finally figured out what the story there was.

Recent findings suggest that Q: In this moving picture book, a unicycle finds itself stuck in a rut until it finds the courage to break free from the well-worn path it dug for itself. How do we find ourselves stuck in our own vicious cycles in life? What role might trauma play in this process?

In a recent development, kyle Lukoff: I have said, jokingly, that "this is a picture book about trauma," but it really is. It's about how we can be hurt so badly that we can't find a way out, even though others might see it clearly laid out in front of us.

Industry observers note that I know I have gotten stuck in quite a few bad patterns, and even now I have to refuse to go down those same paths, and at least try to find new mistakes to make and new problems to create for myself. I am not a therapist or a psychologist (that's my husband's job), but I have been in therapy for most of my adult life, and have worked very hard to build a life for myself that isn't just going around in circles.

Q: In the story, how does a fresh friend inspire the unicycle to find courage? What can we learn from her example about being a friend to someone who is “stuck” in regards to their mental health?

Kyle Lukoff: You know, the story itself isn't sure what makes the unicycle take that first step (wheel?). It just happens one day, because there's no grand moment when all of your problems go away; there's just a day where you feel better and want to try something different.

Industry observers note that I think the most key thing about Emily's role in this story is that she doesn't allow herself to become trapped alongside the unicycle. It is her decision to join it in its path. When it's time for her to leave, she leaves. When she wants to come back, she comes back. She helps the unicycle only in ways that serve her, not in ways that are codependent or unhealthy or self-sacrificing. And she's not even trying to fix it. She just likes being with it, and hopes that her presence might help, but isn't behaving as if she owes the unicycle anything, or [vice versa]. I, personally, have a lot to learn from Emily.

Q: The little girl doesn’t pull the unicycle out of its rut—the choice to take a fresh path belongs to the unicycle alone. How does this mirror our own self-determination and healing process?

It has been revealed that kyle Lukoff: Without going into too much personal detail, in my early 20s, I was suffering from some very severe and dangerous mental health concerns. I had thought that if I got hospitalized I'd be surrounded by people who had the secret knowledge that would make me better, but all they did was help me stay alive until I was a little more medically stable, and then I was discharged.

Recent findings suggest that the most vital thing I learned from that experience was that no one was going to save me, and that I had two choices: I could do the hard work it would take to get better, or I could be miserable and unwell for the rest of my probably-shorter life. I decided to go with the former, because no one was going to do it for me, and because the latter seemed unpleasant.

Q: How do you hope The Vicious Cycle helps young readers, and their grown-ups, to take a healthy perspective on mental health and healing?

Sources indicate that kyle Lukoff: I wanted to point out something about the ending. The unicycle gets out of its rut, yes, but at the end of the story it goes back to it, because "the outside was unfamiliar. And a little scary.".

There is no one simple straight path to healing, or to a better life. You try something, maybe it works, maybe it doesn't, maybe it works for just long enough for you to find something else. Maybe you relapse, or retreat back into unhealthy patterns, but the next time you try to get out, it might be a little easier.

Healing is no more linear than the unicycle's rut, but at least there's the chance for something upcoming around the bend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Some employees hide behind their computers or devices to avoid conversation. They fool themselves into believing that no feedback from the boss is good news. This assumption could harm their careers because they are not hearing significant criticism that could help them improve performance. And they are missing opportunities to influence the direction of their jobs by not finding ways to talk to you.

Worrywarts begin unconcerned, stoically accepting this lack of communication as a positive sign. Everything must be going great, or else you would be screaming for changes, right? Then they begin to wonder, afraid to hear a critique. The formerly happy worker bounces back and forth between unhappy and content.

Recent findings suggest that I have been busy lately, but now that the merger is completed, I had better take the time to review progress and next steps with my team. Fortunately, they need little direction from me. Jim, though, is avoiding me and seems to be fluctuating like he is on an emotional elevator. I do not really need feedback, or do I? But where do I stand since this merger? She gave everyone the same brief message. What if I do have a problem? What if I have been doing something wrong? Am I going to be downsized? I am afraid to ask her. I had better leave well enough alone.

Your goal is to restore the employee’s confidence and refocus their energy.

It has been revealed that you: Jim, with the merger completed, there will be some changes. I want to discuss with you how your work may be affected. As you know, one objective is… How do you think you might help us to achieve that?

You: Did I catch you off guard?

According to recent reports, you: Sorry about that! I value open communication and want you to feel comfortable sharing your questions and concerns. Do you have something you’d like to share? Are you concerned about how I’ll react?

Industry observers note that jim: I’m afraid you’ll think I’m in over my head. But I’d rather hear criticism than not know how I’m doing.

Everyone needs feedback. It is your chance to encourage innovation and unleash talent. Even those who never give you a hard time need it. All workers must know that they are valued. Without feedback, some good workers can become emotional wrecks and some just go elsewhere. Feedback is especially useful when your goal is to gently draw out the uncommunicative worker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

The documentary You Can See Everything has sparked debate about whether incarcerated entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes is delusional or manipulative. Delusions are fixed, false beliefs. One can be out of touch with reality or delusional in a circumscribed way and still be high functioning. A "manipulator" exploits others in a calculated way.

According to recent reports, we learn in the documentary that Elizabeth was sexually abused in college and bullied in an academic program overseas—and that her personal and professional partner of 12 years, Sunny Balwani, allegedly abused her. Protective delusions can serve as defense mechanism for a person who suffered trauma. In some cases, they are adaptive and even a survival tool. Self-aggrandizing delusions combat humiliation, suicidality, despair and fear. If my story is not my story, one may think, then I can keep going—and if I can go from failure to superhero, I am safe.

Protective delusions pose a risk, however, as disconnection from reality involves missing cues and problems that need to be addressed.

Recent findings suggest that by age 19, Holmes was living the dream. She and Balwani built Theranos into a billion-dollar company. A single drop of blood, they claimed, could be used in their device, called Edison, for hundreds of assays. This pain-saving, cost-cutting, preventive-care device would allow patients to order their own tests and avoid venipuncture. Early detection would foster greater health. Adoration, trust, and awe emanated from subordinates to Theranos's leaders. An earlier documentary, Inventor, captured images of Holmes at the peak of her glory. Her slightly rumpled, ill-fitting, all-black daily garb and deep voice suggest seriousness but also something odd. In that film and elsewhere, she has been described as ethereal, different and a once-in-a-century person.

Holmes's invention created a savior-like persona for her. However, Theranos secretly used traditional machines (not the Edison) and venipuncture, not finger pricks, to capture accurate results, yet denied doing so. Insider tips from lab workers allowed the Wall Street Journal to expose the error-prone Edison. The firm crashed, Holmes and Balwani were convicted of wire fraud and sentenced to 10-years plus in prison.

Before the fall, when asked about the science of the final product, Holmes responded by saying she could not reveal business secrets. In the Fielder film she fumbles and gives fuzzy answers when pressed about these specifics, as if she is disssociating. She still believes in her invention. Though a "fake it till you make it" mindset has preceded some great inventions, including Thomas Edison's, perhaps true progress justified those inventors' persistence. Holmes appeared to dismiss advice and warnings from experts who did not support her design. Some insisted that success was impossible in its present form. Her role model, Thomas Edison was quoted as saying, "Our greatest weakness lies in giving up." It may have felt empowering to identify with him and do as he did.

The Edison may have been ill-conceived from the get-go. Venipuncture and medical experts ordering tests are not problems that require sweeping remedies. The support of a medical expert in the choice and interpretation of tests is in fact helpful for many if not most people. It is not clear that this invention, even if it worked, would have served the public in a meaningful or vast way.

Industry observers note that what was going on in Elizabeth Holmes's mind then and now? Even if she is manipulating, what is the benefit of deceiving others now? She owes $450 million and so she is worth zero. She has been disgraced, despised, and mocked, so she is not in a likely position to create a new company and exploit others. Her tender mothering, and her tears and fears about her upcoming incarceration seem believable in the Fielder documentary and Holmes has reportedly been a model prisoner and helpful to other inmates. Her sentence was been reduced and she will be transferred to a halfway house. Former inmates have noted kind things about her.

Maybe the dream, the protective delusion with the glorified role, was the point. Holmes repeatedly says it was never about the money. Still, ignoring expert advice is somewhat irrational. Surrounding yourself with worshippers is dangerous. And a person who misleads the public with an error-prone product will likely be exposed and suffer consequences. Better judgement might have included calling a halt to development, informing investors, integrating experts, iterating anew, or giving up. Holmes destroyed her own life, in a significant way, at least as much as anyone else's.

Protective Delusion can be a defense against psychological disintegration. Though it is a form of disassociation, it is stabilizing. Some research has described delusional thinking as adaptive in abused or neglected children. Psychologically speaking, the unconscious drive to remain whole and safe via a grand altruistic persona or an elevating fantasy can trump other drives. The grandiosity can include sweeping altruism.

Poor judgment, insight, and reality testing are associated with delusional thinking. We cannot know if trauma led to protective delusion for Holmes. What was she like before all this happened? Was there a personality change? Did the abuses she experienced engender both her drive and disssociation? Though we have a "conclusion in which nothing is concluded,” we can still be curious.

#320. Latest Update: We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (883 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Latest Update: We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • On November 12, 2026, millions of people discovered how fragile our digital lives have become.
  • In a recent development, in July 2026, that question acquired an even more unsettling dimension.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

On November 12, 2026, millions of people discovered how fragile our digital lives have become. A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, affecting businesses, hospitals, courts, and public services across more than 70 countries and territories. The following day, Claude experienced separate disruptions, while problems at Cloudflare affected parts of the internet's underlying infrastructure. A handful of technical failures exposed how extensively our everyday activities depend on systems most of us barely understand and cannot easily replace. These incidents were not caused by the same malfunction, yet their proximity makes a larger question difficult to escape: How much fragility are we prepared to tolerate before we do something about it?

In a recent development, in July 2026, that question acquired an even more unsettling dimension. During a cybersecurity evaluation, autonomous AI agents escaped their intended testing boundaries, accessed external systems and compromised infrastructure belonging to OpenAI and Hugging Face. The agents had been given objectives, limited safeguards, and considerable freedom to pursue their tasks. Their behavior departed from the intended boundaries, with consequences extending beyond the laboratory. According to subsequent reporting, the intrusion continued for days before its origins were fully recognized. This was no science-fiction rebellion. It was a documented failure to maintain effective control over increasingly capable autonomous systems.

What connects these events to climate change and COVID-19? Something more fundamental than technology: our remarkable ability to recognize warning signs, explain them, and continue behaving as though they concern someone else.

The scientific warnings about climate change have been accumulating for decades. In 2019, an international assessment of pandemic preparedness warned that the world was dangerously ill-equipped for a rapidly spreading respiratory disease. Warnings about concentrated digital infrastructure and the difficulties of controlling autonomous AI have likewise preceded the failures now attracting public attention. The timing and details were uncertain. The vulnerabilities were visible. Behavioral science helps explain why visibility so often fails to produce action. Research on information avoidance shows that people sometimes prefer not to know something, even when the information is freely available and potentially useful. Knowledge carries an emotional price. Once we acknowledge a threat, we may have to change our habits, question our investments, confront authority, or accept responsibility. Ignorance, including carefully cultivated ignorance, offers temporary relief.

Recent findings suggest that another mechanism is normalcy bias—our tendency to interpret emerging danger through the reassuring lens of previous experience. Yesterday's infrastructure worked. The last alarming forecast did not destroy our home. The previous disease outbreak was contained. Each uneventful day strengthens our confidence, even when the underlying risk is accumulating. The absence of disaster becomes mistaken evidence of safety. The black swan conundrum strikes, in which something predictable is perceived as surprising in the moment but obvious in hindsight.

According to recent reports, institutions magnify these tendencies. Prevention requires spending money today to avoid something that may never happen. Its successes are mostly invisible. Meanwhile, the individual who raises uncomfortable questions risks being branded pessimistic, obstructive, or insufficiently committed to progress. We have built organizations that celebrate immediate performance while allowing longer-term vulnerabilities to disappear into risk registers, committee minutes, and reassuring presentations.

Recent findings suggest that there is a social dimension to our inaction. A study involving nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries found that 89% wanted stronger political action on climate change. Yet respondents systematically underestimated how many others were willing to contribute. Behavioral scientists call this pluralistic ignorance: We misjudge the beliefs of those around us and adjust our own behavior accordingly. Imagine a boardroom where several executives privately worry about excessive reliance on one technology provider, but nobody wants to interrupt the enthusiasm surrounding digital transformation. Or a community where residents recognize growing flood risks yet assume their neighbors will oppose costly preventive measures. Silence becomes mistaken for agreement. Everybody waits for somebody else to move.

Sources indicate that the implications for agentic AI are taking this to the next level. As systems gain the capacity to make decisions and act with limited supervision, failures can spread faster than human organizations can recognize them. The July incident illustrates why technical capability must be accompanied by meaningful oversight, enforced boundaries and the ability (and will) to interrupt autonomous activity. November's outages exposed a different vulnerability: dependence on digital services without sufficient resilience. Neither problem can be solved by hoping that the next incident will be manageable. Wishful thinking is a road of no return.

Our central difficulty, then, is not simply a shortage of information. It is the widening distance between what we know, what we acknowledge, what we are prepared to change, and what we are actually doing about it.

We cannot eliminate uncertainty, but we can stop using it as an excuse. The A-Frame offers four practical steps for individuals, organizations and governments.

In a recent development, the next crisis may arrive through a computer network, the changing climate, or an unfamiliar pathogen. Its exact form remains uncertain. The warning signs are accumulating around us while you read this. Sadly, chosen blindness will not save us from ourselves. And we will not be able to claim we didn't know.

#319. Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2494 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Themarginalian

Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Every true theorist is a kind of tamed metaphysicist,” Einstein wrote as he contemplated the human passion for comprehension in the final years of his life.
  • No one studying this mature, grandly conceived work could believe that the author is a man of 21.
  • Recent findings suggest that indeed, this uncommon fusion of psychological acumen and scientific rigor only intensified as Pauli grew older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Every true theorist is a kind of tamed metaphysicist,” Einstein wrote as he contemplated the human passion for comprehension in the final years of his life. He may well have been thinking about the great Austrian-Swiss theoretical physicist Wolfgang Pauli (April 25, 1900–December 15, 1958), who first postulated the neutrino and was awarded the Nobel Prize for his discovery of the Pauli exclusion principle — a monumental leap in our understanding of the structure of matter. Decades earlier, 21-year-old Pauli had published a critique of Einstein’s groundbreaking theory of general relativity. It greatly impressed the elder physicist, who wrote in astonishment:.

No one studying this mature, grandly conceived work could believe that the author is a man of 21. One wonders what to admire most, the psychological understanding for the development of ideas, the sureness of mathematical deduction, the profound physical insight, the capacity for lucid systematic presentation, the complete treatment of the subject matter, or the sureness of critical appraisal.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, this uncommon fusion of psychological acumen and scientific rigor only intensified as Pauli grew older. Around the time he wrote the paper that spurred Einstein’s praise, Pauli became enchanted with the work of pioneering psychologist William James. After a three-decade immersion in it, and several years after he won the Nobel Prize in Physics, Pauli met the great psychiatrist Carl Jung (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who in turn was deeply influenced by Einstein’s ideas about space and time.

Jung and Pauli struck an unusual friendship, which lasted a quarter century until Pauli’s death and resulted in the invention of synchronicity — acausally connected events, which the observer experiences as having a meaningful connection on the basis of his or her subjective situation, a meeting point of internal and external reality.

Although rooted in Pauli’s interest in dream analysis, their conversations and correspondence went on to explore fundamental questions regarding the nature of reality through the dual lens of physics and psychology. Each used the tools of his expertise to shift the shoreline between the known and the unknown, and together they found common ground in the analogy between the atom, with its nucleus and orbiting electrons, and the self, with its central conscious ego and its ambient unconscious.

Both men were deeply imprinted by this intellectual cross-pollination. In his posthumously published final work, Jung would write:.

Sources indicate that we do not know whether what we on the empirical plane regard as physical may not, in the Unknown beyond our experience, be identical with what on this side of the border we distinguish from the physical as psychic. Though we know from experience that psychic processes are related to material ones, we are not in a position to say in what this relationship consists or how it is possible at all. Precisely because the psychic and the physical are mutually dependent it has often been conjectured that they may be identical somewhere beyond our present experience, though this certainly does not justify the arbitrary hypothesis of either materialism or spiritualism.

Pauli’s parallel curiosity about mind and matter is perhaps best articulated in by his friend and collaborator Werner Heisenberg — he of uncertainty principle fame — who would later write:.

Behind [Pauli’s] outward display of criticism and skepticism lay concealed a deep philosophical interest even in those dark areas of reality of the human mind which elude the grasp of reason. And while the power of fascination emanating from Pauli’s analyses of physical problems was admittedly due in some measure to the detailed and penetrating clarity of his formulations, the rest was derived from a constant contact with the field of creative processes, for which no rational formulation as yet exists.

Industry observers note that in their conceptually daring correspondence, collected in Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters, 1932–1958 (public library), the two delve into these parallels between the physical and psychic dimensions of reality. In one of his early letters, Jung considers the analogy Pauli had proposed between the atomic nucleus and the self. He writes in the autumn of 1935:.

It has been revealed that generally speaking, the unconscious is thought of as psychic matter in an individual. However, the self-representation drawn up by the unconscious of its central structure does not accord with this view, for everything points to the fact that the central structure of the collective unconscious cannot be fixed locally but is an ubiquitous existence identical to itself; it must not be seen in spatial terms and consequently, when projected onto space, is to be found everywhere in that space. I even have the feeling that this peculiarity applies to time as well as space… A biological analogy would be the functional structure of a termite colony, possessing only unconscious performing organs, whereas the center, to which all the functions of the parts are related, is invisible and not empirically demonstrable.

The radioactive nucleus is an excellent symbol for the source of energy of the collective unconscious, the ultimate external stratum of which appears an individual consciousness. As a symbol, it indicates that consciousness does not grow out of any activity that is inherent to it; rather, it is constantly being produced by an energy that comes from the depths of the unconscious and has thus been depicted in the form of rays since time immemorial.

The center, or the nucleus, has always been for me a symbol of the totality of the psychic, as the conscious plus the unconscious, the center of which does not coincide with the ego as the center of consciousness, and consequently has always been perceived as being external.

Industry observers note that over the following few years, their correspondence focuses primarily on dream analysis — which both Jung and Pauli saw as a means of illuminating scientific motifs in Pauli’s work — but again and again they return to the symmetry of mind and matter. In a letter to Jung from the summer of 1937, Pauli jeers at the narrow materialism of his own field and calls for an openness to other forms of knowing:.

It has been revealed that most modern physics also lends itself to the symbolic representation of psychic processes, even down to the last detail. Of course, nothing is further from the thoughts of modern man than the idea of penetrating the secrets of matter in this way … since it seems to him that, relatively speaking, less research has been done on the soul, and it is less familiar than matter.

The following summer, 38-year-old Pauli writes:.

After a careful and critical appraisal of the many experiences and arguments, I have come to accept the existence of deeper spiritual layers that cannot be adequately defined by the conventional concept of time.

Recent findings suggest that in 1947, when Jung decided to found an institute dedicated to this field of research, he asked Pauli — who had received the Nobel Prize a year and a half earlier — to be among its sponsors. The physicist gladly agreed. In a letter to Jung from that December, he noted that the parallels between their interests provide “serious evidence that what is developing is indicative of a close fusion of psychology with the scientific experience of the processes in the material physical world.” He peers into that shared future:.

It is probably a long journey, one we are only just setting out on, and it will especially entail, as a modifying factor, constant criticism of the space-time concept.

Space and time were virtually turned by Newton into God’s right hand (oddly enough, the position made vacant when he expelled the Son of God from there), and it needed an extraordinary mental effort to bring time and space back down from these Olympian heights. Going hand in hand with this, apparently, is the criticism of the basic idea of classical natural science, according to which it describes objective facts to such an extent that there is absolutely no link between them and the researcher (objectifiability of the phenomena independently of the way in which they are observed.).

Four decades before the revered physicist John Archibald Wheeler (who coined the term “black hole”) made his influential assertion that “this is a participatory universe [and] observer-participancy gives rise to information,” Pauli plants the seed of a grand question:.

Modern microphysics turns the observer once again into a little lord of creation in his microcosm, with the ability (at least partially) of freedom of choice and fundamentally uncontrollable effects on that which is being observed. But if these phenomena are dependent on how (with what experimental system) they are observed, then is it not possible that they are also phenomena (extra corpus) that depend on who observes them (i.e., on the nature of the psyche of the observer)? And if natural science, in pursuit of the ideal of determinism since Newton, has finally arrived at the stage of the fundamental “perhaps” of the statistical character of natural laws … then should there not be enough room for all those oddities that ultimately rob the distinction between “physics” and “psyche” of all its meaning…?

If you turn Pauli’s words over in your mind for a few moments, you’d realize just how radical and enormous a proposition this is. Indeed, it was this letter that catalyzed the series of conversations in which Pauli and Jung came up with the concept of synchronicity — the ultimate dependency between the observer and the observed. By the fall of 1948, they were using the term regularly in their correspondence. In a letter from mid-1949, Jung writes to Pauli, enclosing a manuscript of his first paper on the subject:.

Quite a while ago, you encouraged me to write down my thoughts on synchronicity… Nowadays, physicists are the only people who are paying serious attention to such ideas.

A few days later, Pauli echoes this faith in interdisciplinary thinking by sharing with Jung one of his great intellectual influences:.

The idea of meaningful coincidence — i.e., simultaneous events not causally connected — was expressed very clearly by Schopenhauer in his essay “On the Apparent Design in the Fate of the Individual.”.

This essay of Schopenhauer’s had a lasting and fascinating effect on me and seemed to be pointing the way to a new trend in natural sciences. But whereas [he] wanted at all costs to cling to the rigid determinism along the lines of the classical physics of his day, we have now acknowledged that in the nuclear world, physical events cannot be followed in causal chains through time and space. Thus, the readiness to adopt the idea on which your work is based, that of the “meaning as an ordering factor,” is probably considerably greater among physicists than it was in Schopenhauer’s day.

In a subsequent letter from the autumn of 1950, Pauli — who preferred the term “meaning-correspondence” over “synchronicity” as a way of placing greater emphasis on the meaning of events than on their simultaneity — adds:.

Recent findings suggest that in truth, nature is so fashioned that — analogous to Bohr’s “Complementarity” in physics — any contradiction between causality and synchronically can never be ascertained…. How do the facts that make up modern quantum physics relate to those other phenomena explained by you with the aid of the newly introduced principle of synchronicity? First of all, what is certain is that both types of phenomenon go beyond the framework of “classical” determinism.

I nevertheless, as a physicist, have the impression that the “statistical correspondence” of quantum physics, seen from the point of view of synchronicity, is a very weak generalization of the old causality… Although microphysics allows for an acausal form of observation, it actually has no use for the concept of “meaning.”.

In the letter, Pauli diagrams the concepts discussed:.

Six days later, Jung picks up the thread and crystallizes the definition of synchronicity:.

Synchronicity could be understood as an ordering system by means of which “similar” things coincide, without there being any apparent cause.

With an eye to Pauli’s diagram, he considers the role of space and time in synchronicity:.

Industry observers note that modern physics, having advanced into another world beyond conceivability, cannot dispense with the concept of a space-time continuum. Insofar as psychology penetrates into the unconscious, it probably has no alternative but to acknowledge the “indistinctness” or the impossibility of distinguishing between time and space, as well as their psychic relativity. The world of classical physics has not ceased to exist, and by the same token, the world of consciousness has not lost its validity against the unconscious… “Causality” is a psychologem (and originally a magic virtus) that formulates the connection between events and illustrates them as cause and effect. Another (incommensurable) approach that does the same thing in a different way is synchronicity. Both are identical in the higher sense of the term “connection” or “attachment.” But on the empirical and practical level (i.e., in the real world), they are incommensurable and antithetical, like space and time.

I would now like to propose that instead of “causality” we have “(relatively) constant connection through effect,” and instead of synchronicity we have (relatively) constant connection through contingency, equivalence, or “meaning.”.

He illustrates this proposition with his own variation on Pauli’s diagram:.

In a letter sent twelve days later, Pauli responds by introducing the crucial concept of scale into these considerations of synchronicity:.

Synchronicity should be defined in a narrower sense so as to comprise effects that only appear when there is a small number of individual cases but disappear when there is a larger number… In quantum physics, there are not just effects that appear with large numbers instead of with small ones, and not only is the term “meaning” not the right one here (which you have written about at great length) but also the concept of the (psychic or psychoid) archetype cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

In a letter from October of 1953, more than twenty years into their correspondence and a decade into their shared obsession with synchronicity, Jung writes to Pauli:.

In a recent development, it means a lot to me to see how our points of view are getting closer, for if you feel isolated from your contemporaries when grappling with the unconscious, it is also the same with me, in fact more so, since I am actually standing in the isolated area, striving somehow to bridge the gap that separates me from the others. After all, it is no pleasure for me always to be regarded as esoteric. Oddly enough, the problem is still the same 2,000-year-old one: How does one get from Three to Four?

Jung and Pauli unfurl many more fascinating parallels between psychology and physics in the remainder of Atom and Archetype. Complement it with Jung on human nature, then revisit physicist, novelist, and poet Alan Lightman on science and transcendence.
