#318. When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1127 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine you and your partner have just finished having dinner with your parents.
  • Eventually, they sigh right before asking, “Why didn’t you say anything when your mother made that comment?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you and your partner have just finished having dinner with your parents. The drive home seems eerily quiet, even though you feel like the evening went pretty well, and you can’t shake the general impression that your partner is upset.

Eventually, they sigh right before asking, “Why didn’t you say anything when your mother made that comment?”.

It has been revealed that you try to explain that you didn’t want to start an argument. After all, your mother has always been outspoken, and you know from experience that challenging her would have started “a thing” and made everyone uncomfortable. You had assumed your partner understood this and would instinctively know you didn’t agree with what your mother stated.

Your partner sees things differently. They were embarrassed and went on to spend the entire evening feeling unsupported and increasingly resentful. You’re also beginning to realize that while you might have avoided one argument over the dinner table, you set yourself up to face another one at home.

It has been revealed that situations like these are common for couples managing complicated relationships with extended family. Doing your best to keep everyone happy seems like the responsible adult choice, especially when family gatherings can already be tense or stressful. However, avoiding uncomfortable conversations with relatives can easily come at the expense of your partner.

Industry observers note that according to a 2013 longitudinal study, early dynamics with in-laws often correlate with later marital stability. This connection can vary according to factors like race and gender, so complicated family relationships don’t necessarily affect every couple the same way. However, wanting to maintain family harmony is second nature to most people. This can especially be the case for those who grew up in households in which challenging a parent was unacceptable or disagreements almost always escalated into ugly arguments.

It’s easy to go into adulthood with the general idea that keeping quiet is the cleanest way to deal with uncomfortable situations. That doesn’t necessarily stop once you’re in a committed relationship of your own.

Naturally, you love your partner and feel responsible for protecting their feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’re comfortable confronting your parents, siblings, or other relatives.

Industry observers note that picture a situation in which your sibling cracks a joke at your partner’s expense during a family get-together. Everyone laughs, so you join in, even though you also know your partner finds such remarks hurtful.

From your point of view, laughing along was the easiest way to avoid a potential scene, especially if that’s your family’s usual routine when this particular sibling makes off-color comments or gives someone a hard time. Meanwhile, all your partner knows is that you joined in while someone else embarrassed them in front of others.

According to recent reports, disconnects like these can become huge sticking points in a relationship when they happen repeatedly. Your partner may start to associate getting together with your family with having to endure uncomfortable comments and potential embarrassment. If they also feel you expect them to tolerate this, they may eventually wonder whether they can count on you at all when life gets difficult.

A 2019 study published in Social Work Research surveyed 351 women about their relationships with their mothers-in-law. Findings suggested factors like family-triangle dynamics or unclear relationship boundaries directly impacted relationship quality.

Having a partner who stays silent during disagreements can further aggravate relationships that may already be complicated.

When one partner makes a habit of not addressing comments or behaviors that are inappropriate, the other can feel responsible for managing everyone’s discomfort. They’re forced to choose between speaking up and potentially causing a scene or staying silent and dealing with feelings of resentment or abandonment.

Properly supporting your partner doesn’t necessarily mean agreeing with them every time they complain about your family. However, you can (and should) acknowledge your partner’s feelings and talk things out when conflicts come up. There’s a world of difference between saying “You’re right, my family is awful” no matter what and saying “I get why that was hurtful, so let’s talk about it” instead.

Couples can minimize recurring disagreements further by working through expectations before people butt heads and things get tense.

Industry observers note that 1. Discuss potential sticking points beforehand. Some relatives may be notorious for disregarding other people’s boundaries or making intrusive comments. If this is the case in your family, prep for upcoming gatherings by talking to your partner beforehand about how you’ll respond to any possible incidents.

It has been revealed that avoid assuming you already know what your partner will find helpful in the moment. Instead, ask them what would truly help them feel supported and go from there.

2. Address inappropriate behavior calmly. Intervening if things do get tense doesn’t have to mean starting an argument. Try shutting down hurtful comments, intrusive questions, and so forth by simply saying, “We’d rather not discuss that” or “Please don’t make fun of my partner.”.

Statements like these help establish boundaries with relatives and set expectations without necessarily escalating the situation.

According to recent reports, 3. Avoid volunteering your partner to keep others happy. Instead of instantly making commitments or agreeing to family plans that affect both of you, talk to your partner about it first. Being considerate to your family is important, but it shouldn’t mean making decisions and promises on someone else’s behalf.

It has been revealed that 4. Check in privately. If something happens at a family get-together that feels uncomfortable, pull your partner aside and ask how they’re doing. If necessary, talk about it for a moment or offer to leave early. Even a brief check-in is often enough to keep your partner feeling supported and stop resentment from building up through an evening.

It has been revealed that 5. Take responsibility when you get it wrong. You’re only human, so there may be times when you only realize after the fact that staying silent may have hurt your partner. Acknowledge it and explain what happened. Then apologize and express a willingness to respond differently next time.

Conversations like these should go both ways, so be sure to give your partner a chance to explain their own family histories or talk about genuine misunderstandings as well.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, it’s more than possible to keep your family relationships strong while also helping your partner feel properly loved and supported. But doing so might mean learning to manage occasional discomfort instead of simply expecting your partner to absorb the impact and understand.

The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022.

Sources indicate that I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare. Only weeks before, the tree had been so full of persimmons that we collected them in huge plastic garbage cans for our neighbors to take by the grocery bagful. Our Labrador-ish mutt, Buster, was fat from persimmon overconsumption.

Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm. We were real empty-nesters, ready to downsize.

According to recent reports, within weeks, we stripped our house of everything personal. We took down family photos, scraped butterfly stickers from hidden corners, and painted over the teal walls preteen girls had decorated. All traces of our family life vanished. We put our home on the market. It was the end of an era.

According to recent reports, in December, my seemingly super-fit mom was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Our house still hadn’t sold—by the time we put it on the market, mortgage rates had started climbing for the first time in two decades—but I moved into my childhood bedroom at my parents’ home to help my dad care for my mom. She passed away four months later.

Recent findings suggest that A week before my mom’s memorial, I myself was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer. And a few days after my first cancer-related surgery, a close cousin died of an accidental overdose just after his 50th birthday.

In a recent development, also during that time, a dear college friend, a fit, athletic doctor, had a fatal heart attack. And while I was having radiation for my breast cancer, our beloved dog Buster was diagnosed with lymphoma and needed to be put down.

Industry observers note that other losses were expected and even positive. Our house finally sold, and so we said goodbye to the home where we had raised our four kids. I packed up that house through tears—for my mom, for my health, for my beloved dog and cousin and college friend, sobbing as I threw away things that marked my kids’ childhoods: boxes of ribbons from horse shows and swim meets, SAT score reports, so many old shoes and backpacks, homemade Harry Potter wands.

Mark and I put our stuff in storage and moved in with my dad for real while we renovated a newly introduced house in Berkeley. I loved this time with my dad; it made my cancer treatment and everything else bearable. He had always been my person, and now I got to cry and laugh with him every day, with no space between us.

About a year after my mom died, we finally moved into our new house. The first morning I woke up there and looked out the window at the whole Bay Area, I was astonished to see not one, but four rainbows touching down on the water of the San Francisco Bay. I felt welcomed and reassured that I was right where I was meant to be.

But then my brother-in-law Brian was diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor, the kind that doesn’t usually respond to chemo or radiation. They did everything anyway—brain surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, experimental drugs, an electromagnetic cap, expensive immunotherapy from Germany—but less than nine months later, he too passed away. I’ve never known a man with a bigger heart than Brian; when he died, we lost the emotional center on Mark’s side of the family.

Our family was devastated. Again.

Recent findings suggest that with each of these losses and life changes, I picked myself up and told my friends that at least it wasn’t my dad. When my dad dies, I’m going to stay in bed for a year, I said. When my dad dies, expect my complete collapse. I started believing that I could bear anything except for losing my father, my oldest and dearest friend. The loss of my father would leave a hole in my heart I knew I could never fill.

And then, in April of 2025, one month to the day after we lost Brian, my 84-year-old dad passed away.

He was still driving, doing Pilates, and walking his dog Annie around his hilly neighborhood. He was still sharp as a tack, still hilarious, still going out every day to meet his many friends or his brother, Jud. He still volunteered and mentored others.

Industry observers note that one week, he was fully with us, bringing me a burrito for dinner at my nephew’s Little League game, taking us to dinner at the club where he’d been a lifelong member, buying tickets to a Giants game. The next week, he was gone.

In a recent development, my brother and I decided it “made sense” to sell our childhood home, a place that had anchored our extended family for nearly 50 years. But I could not make sense of how I could lose everything that centered me, my whole foundation, so fucking fast.

Industry observers note that still, I didn’t utterly collapse. I learned how to grieve in small moments throughout the day; how to keep putting one foot in front of the other while still feeling loss. I cried before and after work as I walked my dad’s sweet little Annie. I broke down at the grocery store, in restaurants, while hiking with friends, at the post office. I wept while packing up my parents’ house and while pulling apart their photo albums. I was exhausted, hollowed out.

My heart was broken, but I got out of bed every morning.

According to recent reports, I started new, truly energizing work projects and slogged through my parents’ stuff and another year of difficult firsts. The first Father’s Day without my dad, the first family birthday not celebrated at my parents’ house. As the first Thanksgiving without my dad and Brian approached, my therapist remarked that grief was often surprisingly life-enhancing. That was turning out to be true for me.

Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday. I usually host our major family, and I always have a lot to say at dinnertime about what I am grateful for. That year, the intimate connection between loss and gratitude had become painfully obvious to me.

Genuine gratitude—when we really pause to acknowledge how valuable something is—inherently involves recognizing the impermanence of that thing. True gratitude carries the awareness that what we’re grateful for won’t last forever; it’s here now but could be gone tomorrow. That awareness is what makes a moment feel more vivid and precious.

Recent findings suggest that I think one gift of loss is that it can make us more intensely grateful. Not because we’re anxious about losing someone or something, but because we’ve learned viscerally that everything is temporary—and therefore extraordinary.

Sources indicate that this crucible of loss and gratitude burned away my tolerance for anything that didn’t feel essential, helping me return to a deep spirituality. Standing at the edge of my own mortality and watching the structures of my life dissolve one by one fundamentally reordered my sense of what matters. Grief is the price of love, and it teaches us that love is what matters most.

It has been revealed that so much loss has made pretense impossible for me. Grief strips us down and cracks us open, breaking down the defenses and distractions that keep us living on the surface. In the past few years, I’ve been to deep places, emotionally and existentially, that only truth can reach. I can’t un-know that now. Superficiality has started to feel like I’m being asked to forget the hard-won truth about how fragile and precious life actually is.

In a recent development, when we’re grieving, we can’t pretend. We can’t avoid our own vulnerability or the fact that everything ends. And while that’s devastating, it’s also strangely liberating. I feel more at peace, more permeable, more present, more profoundly loving, more alive to the texture of my lived experience. I’m attuned to what’s real and meaningful. I feel closer to and more in love with my friends and family than ever before. I feel things so deeply, and that depth is a kind of richness.

All of this is to say that growth happens in the broken-open places in our hearts. Loss and gratitude both dissolve the boundary between ourselves and the larger human experience. When we love and when we grieve, we join an ancient river of sorrow and love that connects us to everyone who has ever loved and lost.

I would never choose the losses I’ve endured. I’d give anything to have my people back, and not to have had cancer. But this is the grief-gratitude paradox: I also wouldn’t trade what grief has taught me, how deeply I feel, or who I am now because of all I’ve lost.

It has been revealed that so this Thanksgiving, I’ll be at the table again, with fewer people than I’d like but more love than I ever knew I had room for. When it’s my turn to say what I’m grateful for, I won’t need to think about it. Every single moment is a gift. It’s all temporary, and it’s all extraordinary.

Christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with plans, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

Maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

In fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

If you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

With that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

It has been revealed that so what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A big factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

It has been revealed that if you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

Sources indicate that if you’re up for ideas, start here. If you’re feeling low, jump to How to deal with spending Christmas alone when hard feelings come up.

If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

According to recent reports, 8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

Industry observers note that 10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a new trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

There are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

According to recent reports, send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:.

Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

It has been revealed that you can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

Sources indicate that if you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

Industry observers note that give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

Even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

Other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

If the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”.

You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

It’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

It has been revealed that if your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

Industry observers note that if you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

In a recent development, it’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Plan the day around what appeals to you.

According to recent reports, if you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

If you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a upcoming spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

Sources indicate that if you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

It’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday plans is one way to look after yourself.

In a recent development, A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a new ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

Industry News: Before You Proposal Thanksgiving Dinner, Plan Family Dynamics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Industry observers note that by this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving.
  • Sources indicate that will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Industry observers note that by this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving. We’re discussing who’s coming, who’s bringing what, and whether people prefer the canned or fresh cranberry sauce. We may also be planning conversations that haven’t happened.

Sources indicate that will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet? Will our parenting become a topic of discussion? Will we spend another holiday doing the work while everyone else watches football?

I have written about the friction that can accompany family gatherings. As Thanksgiving approaches again, I keep wondering would it would look like to prepare for the family dynamics as thoughtfully as we prepare for the meal.

Industry observers note that think about the moment you’re most concerned about. Perhaps it’s a particular question, a familiar disagreement, or the expectation that you’ll organize everything. Now consider what you’re predicting. Are you anticipating a situation that happens regularly? Or are you imagining several possible arguments and preparing a response to each one? Past experiences give us useful information, but mentally replaying an argument doesn’t necessarily give us a useful plan.

Try making the concern specific: “I’m worried someone will comment on my career decision.” Then identify a response you would feel comfortable using: “I’m comfortable with my decision, and I’m not looking for advice about it today.” You may still feel uncomfortable and dread having the conversation but having a response ready simply gives you somewhere to begin.

We often approach holidays with goals that depend on other people, like everyone will get along, no one will make an insensitive comment, or everyone will appreciate the effort. Those hopes are understandable, but they’re also difficult to guarantee.

Consider a few decisions you can make yourself. How long will you stay? Which preparations can you reasonably take on? What will you do if a conversation becomes uncomfortable? You might decide to visit for dessert rather than spend the entire day. You might ask someone else to bring the side dishes. You might arrange transportation so you can leave when you’re ready.

These decisions deserve space alongside the grocery list.

If a familiar pattern bothers you, consider whether there’s a request you can make before the gathering. For example, if you usually manage the meal and cleanup, “I need more help this year” is a starting point. A more specific request gives others a clearer way to participate: “Can you handle the dishes after dinner, including putting the leftovers away?”.

Industry observers note that the same applies to traditions. If the usual schedule no longer works for your household, raise that glitch while looks are being made. Others may be disappointed. You can acknowledge that disappointment while still explaining what you can offer.

In a recent development, in an uncomfortable moment, finding the right words can be difficult. Choose language that sounds like something you would actually say. For an intrusive question: “I don’t have anything I want to share about that.” For unsolicited advice: “I’ll ask if I need suggestions.” For a conversation you want to leave: “I’m going to step away for a few minutes.”.

Industry observers note that A prepared phrase won’t determine how another person responds. It can help you communicate your own decision more clearly.

Preparation can also include thinking about what you’re looking forward to: Is there someone you’d like to spend time with? A recipe you want to learn? A game, walk, or family story you’d enjoy sharing? Make a little room for that experience rather than assuming it will happen once everything else is finished.

Sources indicate that once you’re home after the gathering, give yourself a fair assessment of the day. One awkward exchange doesn’t have to define the entire gathering. You can appreciate the parts you enjoyed and think honestly about what you’d change next time.

Thanksgiving takes preparation. Along with deciding what belongs on the table, we can decide what we have the time, energy, and willingness to bring to it.

#314. Breaking: J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2704 w)

Breaking: J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,” the great Maurice Sendak once mentioned in an interview.
  • Tolkien (January 3, 1892–September 2, 1973), celebrated as one of the greatest fantasy writers in history, gave a lecture titled “Fairy Stories,” eventually adapted into an essay retitled “On Fairy-Stories” and included in the appendix to Tales from the Perilous Realm (public library).
  • Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,” the great Maurice Sendak once mentioned in an interview. “I don’t write for children,” he told Colbert. “I write — and somebody says, ‘That’s for children!’” This sentiment — the idea that designating certain types of literature as “children’s” is a choice entirely arbitrary and entirely made by adults — has since been eloquently echoed by Neil Gaiman, but isn’t, in fact, a newly introduced idea.

On March 8, 1939, J.R.R. Tolkien (January 3, 1892–September 2, 1973), celebrated as one of the greatest fantasy writers in history, gave a lecture titled “Fairy Stories,” eventually adapted into an essay retitled “On Fairy-Stories” and included in the appendix to Tales from the Perilous Realm (public library). At the crux of his argument, which explores the nature of fantasy and the cultural role of fairy tales, is the same profound conviction that there is no such thing as writing “for children.”.

Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:.

It has been revealed that A “fairy-story” is one which touches on or uses Faerie, whatever its own main purpose may be: satire, adventure, morality, fantasy. Faerie itself may perhaps most nearly be translated by Magic — but it is magic of a peculiar mood and power, at the furthest pole from the vulgar devices of the laborious, scientific, magician. There is one proviso: if there is any satire present in the tale, one thing must not be made fun of, the magic itself. That must in that story be taken seriously, neither laughed at nor explained away.

He then explores the relationship between fairy tales and language, denouncing Max Müller’s view of mythology as a “disease of language”:.

Mythology is not a disease at all, though it may like all human things become diseased. You might as well say that thinking is a disease of the mind. It would be more near the truth to say that languages, especially modern European languages, are a disease of mythology. But Language cannot, all the same, be dismissed. The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale are in our world coeval. The human mind, endowed with the powers of generalization and abstraction, sees not only green-grass, discriminating it from other things (and finding it fair to look upon), but sees that it is green as well as being grass. But how powerful, how stimulating to the very faculty that produced it, was the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent. And that is not surprising: such incantations might indeed be stated to be only another view of adjectives, a part of speech in a mythical grammar. The mind that thought of light, heavy, grey, yellow, still, swift, also conceived of magic that would make heavy things light and able to fly, turn grey lead into yellow gold, and the still rock into a swift water. If it could do the one, it could do the other; it inevitably did both. When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter’s power — upon one plane; and the desire to wield that power in the world external to our minds awakes. It does not follow that we shall use that power well upon any plane. We may put a deadly green upon a man’s face and produce a horror; we may make the rare and terrible blue moon to shine; or we may cause woods to spring with silver leaves and rams to wear fleeces of gold, and put hot fire into the belly of the cold worm. But in such “fantasy,” as it is called, fresh form is made; Faerie begins; Man becomes a sub-creator.

Like Sendak and Gaiman, Tolkien insists that fairy tales aren’t inherently “for” children but that we, as adults, simply decide that they are, based on a series of misconceptions about both the nature of this literature and the nature of children:.

In a recent development, it is usually assumed that children are the natural or the specially appropriate audience for fairy-stories. In describing a fairy-story which they think adults might possibly read for their own entertainment, reviewers frequently indulge in such waggeries as: “this book is for children from the ages of six to sixty.” But I have never yet seen the puff of a new motor-model that began thus: “this toy will amuse infants from seventeen to seventy”; though that to my mind would be much more appropriate. Is there any essential connexion between children and fairy-stories? Is there any call for comment, if an adult reads them for himself? Reads them as tales, that is, not studies them as curios. Adults are allowed to collect and study anything, even old theatre programmes or paper bags.

Among those who still have enough wisdom not to think fairy-stories pernicious, the common opinion seems to be that there is a natural connexion between the minds of children and fairy-stories, of the same order as the connexion between children’s bodies and milk. I think this is an error; at best an error of false sentiment, and one that is therefore most often made by those who, for whatever private reason (such as childlessness), tend to think of children as a special kind of creature, almost a different race, rather than as normal, if immature, members of a particular family, and of the human family at large.

He argues, instead, that the stereotype of fairy tales being associated with children and native to their world is “an accident of our domestic history”:.

In a recent development, fairy-stories have in the modern lettered world been relegated to the “nursery,” as shabby or old-fashioned furniture is relegated to the play-room, primarily because the adults do not want it, and do not mind if it is misused. It is not the choice of the children which decides this. Children as a class—except in a common lack of experience they are not one—neither like fairy-stories more, nor understand them better than adults do; and no more than they like many other things. They are young and growing, and normally have keen appetites, so the fairy-stories as a rule go down well enough. But in fact only some children, and some adults, have any special taste for them; and when they have it, it is not exclusive, nor even necessarily dominant. It is a taste, too, that would not appear, I think, very early in childhood without artificial stimulus; it is certainly one that does not decrease but increases with age, if it is innate.

In a recent development, the nursery and schoolroom are merely given such tastes and glimpses of the adult thing as seem fit for them in adult opinion (often much mistaken). Any one of these things would, if left altogether in the nursery, become gravely impaired. So would a beautiful table, a good picture, or a useful machine (such as a microscope), be defaced or broken, if it were left long unregarded in a schoolroom. Fairy-stories banished in this way, cut off from a full adult art, would in the end be ruined; indeed in so far as they have been so banished, they have been ruined.

Tolkien then moves on to the subject of fantasy, a frequently misunderstood faculty of the imagination.

Recent findings suggest that the mental power of image-making is one thing, or aspect; and it should appropriately be called Imagination. The perception of the image, the grasp of its implications, and the control, which are necessary to a successful expression, may vary in vividness and strength: but this is a difference of degree in Imagination, not a difference in kind. The achievement of the expression, which gives (or seems to give) “the inner consistency of reality,” is indeed another thing, or aspect, needing another name: Art, the operative link between Imagination and the final result, Sub-creation. For my present purpose I require a word which shall embrace both the Sub- creative Art in itself and a quality of strangeness and wonder in the Expression, derived from the Image: a quality essential to fairy-story. I propose, therefore, to arrogate to myself the powers of Humpty-Dumpty, and to use Fantasy for this purpose: in a sense, that is, which combines with its older and higher use as an equivalent of Imagination the derived notions of “unreality” (that is, of unlikeness to the Primary World), of freedom from the domination of observed “fact,” in short of the fantastic. I am thus not only aware but glad of the etymological and semantic connexions of fantasy with fantastic: with images of things that are not only “not actually present,” but which are indeed not to be found in our primary world at all, or are generally believed not to be found there. But while admitting that, I do not assent to the depreciative tone. That the images are of things not in the primary world (if that indeed is possible) is a virtue, not a vice. Fantasy (in this sense) is, I think, not a lower but a higher form of Art, indeed the most nearly pure form, and so (when achieved) the most potent.

He goes on to argue that, despite the many misconceptions that envelop it, fantasy is far more challenging an art than nonfiction, for it necessitates the creation of an elaborate, immersive world from scratch, without the crutch of reality:.

Industry observers note that fantasy … is difficult to achieve. Fantasy may be, as I think, not less but more sub-creative; but at any rate it is found in practice that “the inner consistency of reality” is more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images and the rearrangements of primary material to the actual arrangements of the Primary World. It is easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material. Fantasy thus, too often, remains undeveloped; it is and has been used frivolously, or only half-seriously, or merely for decoration: it remains merely “fanciful.” Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun. Many can then imagine or picture it. But that is not enough — though it may already be a more potent thing than many a “thumbnail sketch” or “transcript of life” that receives literary praise.

Recent findings suggest that to make a Secondary World inside which the green sun will be credible, commanding Secondary Belief, will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill, a kind of elvish craft. Few attempt such difficult tasks. But when they are attempted and in any degree accomplished then we have a rare achievement of Art: indeed narrative art, story-making in its primary and most potent mode.

Tolkien makes a curious argument about the oil-and-water relationship between fantasy and drama, managing to slip in a subtle dig at none other than The Bard:.

In human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature. … It is a misfortune that Drama, an art fundamentally distinct from Literature, should so commonly be considered together with it, or as a branch of it. Among these misfortunes we may reckon the depreciation of Fantasy. For in part at least this depreciation is due to the natural desire of critics to cry up the forms of literature or “imagination” that they themselves, innately or by training, prefer. And criticism in a country that has produced so great a Drama, and possesses the works of William Shakespeare, tends to be far too dramatic. But Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy. Fantasy, even of the simplest kind, hardly ever succeeds in Drama, when that is presented as it should be, visibly and audibly acted. Fantastic forms are not to be counterfeited. Men dressed up as talking animals may achieve buffoonery or mimicry, but they do not achieve Fantasy. . . .

In Macbeth, when it is read, I find the witches tolerable: they have a narrative function and some hint of dark significance; though they are vulgarized, poor things of their kind. They are almost intolerable in the play. They would be quite intolerable, if I were not fortified by some memory of them as they are in the story as read. I am told that I should feel differently if I had the mind of the period, with its witch-hunts and witch-trials. But that is to say: if I regarded the witches as possible, indeed likely, in the Primary World; in other words, if they ceased to be “Fantasy.” That argument concedes the point. To be dissolved, or to be degraded, is the likely fate of Fantasy when a dramatist tries to use it, even such a dramatist as Shakespeare. Macbeth is indeed a work by a playwright who ought, at least on this occasion, to have written a story, if he had the skill or patience for that art.

Another misconception Tolkien debunks — speaking to Susan Sontag’s conviction that polarities only rob life of dimension — is the notion that the fantastical is somehow diametrically opposed to the rational:.

Fantasy is a natural human activity. It certainly does not destroy or even insult Reason; and it does not either blunt the appetite for, nor obscure the perception of, scientific verity. On the contrary. The keener and the clearer is the reason, the better fantasy will it make. If men were ever in a state in which they did not want to know or could not perceive truth (facts or evidence), then Fantasy would languish until they were cured. If they ever get into that state (it would not seem at all impossible), Fantasy will perish, and become Morbid Delusion.

In a recent development, for creative Fantasy is founded upon the hard recognition that things are so in the world as it appears under the sun; on a recognition of fact, but not a slavery to it. So upon logic was founded the nonsense that displays itself in the tales and rhymes of Lewis Carroll. If men really could not distinguish between frogs and men, fairy-stories about frog-kings would not have arisen.

Returning to his notion of the Secondary World driven by Secondary Belief, Tolkien contributes to history’s greatest definitions of art:.

Art is the human process that produces by the way (it is not its only or ultimate object) Secondary Belief.

He then adds to the psychological functions of art by exploring the psychological functions of fairy tales, chief among which is their capacity for rebooting our chronically blunted attention:.

Industry observers note that recovery (which includes return and renewal of health) is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view. I do not say “seeing things as they are” and involve myself with the philosophers, though I might venture to say “seeing things as we are (or were) meant to see them”—as things apart from ourselves. We need, in any case, to clean our windows; so that the things seen clearly may be freed from the drab blur of triteness or familiarity—from possessiveness. Of all faces those of our familiares are the ones both most difficult to play fantastic tricks with, and most difficult really to see with fresh attention, perceiving their likeness and unlikeness: that they are faces, and yet unique faces. This triteness is really the penalty of “appropriation”: the things that are trite, or (in a bad sense) familiar, are the things that we have appropriated, legally or mentally. We say we know them. They have become like the things which once attracted us by their glitter, or their colour, or their shape, and we laid hands on them, and then locked them in our hoard, acquired them, and acquiring ceased to look at them.

Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.

The full fifteen-page essay, as well as the rest of Tales from the Perilous Realm, is well worth a read. Complement it with Tolkien’s little-known illustrations for the first edition of The Hobbit.

#313. How to Become Change-Curious

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

How to Become Change-Curious

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Sources indicate that we are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station).
  • What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Sources indicate that we are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station). Messages about change are inescapable and part of the background noise of everyday life. Often we ignore the onslaught of “be better, do better” messaging, and other times we eagerly try to change ourselves because we so passionately want our lives to be different.

What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?

Like any troubling relationship, it can be useful to explore some of the dynamics that are not working for us. If we are fortunate to find ourselves changing with ease and little friction, that is a cause to celebrate. For most of us, at least some of the time, we have some difficult experiences engaging in change. We might tell ourselves that change is good; that we should want it. Such a message is difficult to accept when we are not certain change is what we want or need. We might also believe that if we don’t want change, there must be something wrong with us; we are resistant or self-sabotaging or anxious or overwhelmed. Some of these things might be true, but labeling ourselves brings up shame, and shame can be crippling, as it can bring to mind past failures or negative messaging.

Change can also be hard because it takes work. Even if we are completely inspired and motivated to change, developing habits and learning newly introduced ways to do things takes time; a recent study found it takes an average of 66 days for a habit to form. For any individual, it can take more or less time for a behavior change to become automatic.

Change is work; it takes time and disrupts our lives. We have cognitive, emotional, and behavioral friction that makes it more difficult to start and complete. Yet, despite the difficulty, we seek change. We want our lives to improve, so we purchase lots of self-help, coaching, therapy, gym memberships, food looks, and surgeries to get started. Across cultures throughout the lifespan, some aspects of change and growth are constantly occurring as we seek to change ourselves and our circumstances.

In a recent development, given that change is both hard and something we desire, what if we considered approaching the change process with a learner’s mind? Instead of forcing ourselves to endure change or shaming ourselves into it, we can befriend change through cultivating curiosity about all it has to offer. Wondering about change and being open to all the ways we show up in the change process has the potential to make change less daunting.

We have many options to be curious about change.

Noticing change in our environment, and then noticing change in ourselves. We can start by spending some time noticing change in the weather or change in plants. Maybe we notice how construction or demolition is changing a neighborhood, or how our neighbor's families are changing and growing. We can then consider changes in our own experience over the years—in our living situations, job, or social life. We can notice the ones that have been the most meaningful. How did these changes happen? Some changes occur because of luck or circumstances, and it is likely that we were able to take advantage of our good fortune. Some changes occur because we worked hard at making change. How did we do it? What characteristics helped us become a “changer,” and how could we tap into those characteristics if we wanted to change again?

Envisioning what change might look like. This is a common approach to increasing motivation for change. What if we decided we could envision something for ourselves in the same way we read a book or watch a movie? We could envision being in a few different situations and view our story with wonder instead of expectation.

It has been revealed that looking at the process more than the outcome. We tend to be outcome-oriented. We see products that promise to help us build muscle, learn a language, or see younger, more beautiful skin in a few weeks or a couple of months. The promise of relatively quick fixes is so compelling that even when we logically understand there is no way a product can live up to our expectations, we might find ourselves literally buying it. Purchasing a service or product to help us change is not necessarily a problem, and it can be a good thing. Expecting the product to have specific outcomes is where we can become discouraged. So many things impact the actual outcome of our attempts to change: time, environment, our body limits and composition, other demands taking our time.

Shifting our attention to the process requires that we step away from holding the outcome as our top priority. Instead, it’s about going along for the ride and adopting a perspective that we are learning and improving our lives by noticing how we feel after engaging in exercise, making the effort to practice a new instrument, or consuming nutritious foods.

In a recent development, sampling change. We can check it out and see what it does for us. Events such as Sober October or Dry January were created to help drinkers wanting to explore, but not commit to, changing their drinking behaviors—to test out life without (or with less) alcohol. Virtually any change can be tested out and explored. Sampling a newly introduced behavior is not the same as engaging in a dedicated lifestyle change, but it allows for some action. It also provides an opportunity to approach a new way of being in a manner that reduces overwhelm; a chance to wonder about what might be possible.

Curiosity is a powerful frame of mind. It has the potential to tame the intensity of change and open up possibilities for transformation that come from the power of exploration and wonder.

Shigeoka, S. (2024, June 6). How deep curiosity can change the world [Interview by T. Burnett]. John Templeton Foundation. https://www.templeton.org/news/how-deep-curiosity-can-change-the-world.

#312. The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship

The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a upcoming attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone newly introduced.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, demonstrated a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also revealed a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

#311. Self-Affirmation, Self-Integrity, and You

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1584 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

Self-Affirmation, Self-Integrity, and You

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Recent findings suggest that brief self-affirmation activities have been reliably shown to help people change and grow by reducing a perceived threat.
  • The vulnerability to stereotype threat we discussed in Part 1 of this series is grounded in a basic human need to see ourselves as “adaptively and morally adequate”: good, capable, reasonable and sensible people who are able to achieve the outcomes that matter to us.1 Named the self-integrity motive by Claude Steele, the psychologist who identified it,2 it differs from the better-known construct of self-esteem in that it is our motivation to view ourselves as “good enough,” rather than to maximize our positive thoughts and feelings about ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

This post is Part 2 of a series.

Recent findings suggest that brief self-affirmation activities have been reliably shown to help people change and grow by reducing a perceived threat. But what kind of threat do they reduce? And how does self-affirmation reduce it?

The vulnerability to stereotype threat we discussed in Part 1 of this series is grounded in a basic human need to see ourselves as “adaptively and morally adequate”: good, capable, reasonable and sensible people who are able to achieve the outcomes that matter to us.1 Named the self-integrity motive by Claude Steele, the psychologist who identified it,2 it differs from the better-known construct of self-esteem in that it is our motivation to view ourselves as “good enough,” rather than to maximize our positive thoughts and feelings about ourselves.

Our sense of self-integrity can be based on any valued qualities we believe we possess.3,4,5 Unfortunately, our self-integrity can also be threatened by anything we see as reflecting negatively on who we are: failure, bad things that happen to us, criticism or rejection, information that challenges what we believe, recognition that we’ve acted in ways that conflict with our values—any experience we take as evidence that we are bad, wrong, incompetent, irrational, foolish, or unable to deal effectively with life.

We feel bad about ourselves (ashamed, humiliated, unworthy) when our self-integrity is threatened, which triggers defensive efforts to protect or restore it: We may dismiss or minimize the threat; attack its source; marshal evidence against it; rationalize or justify our behavior, or deny being responsible for it; try to puff ourselves up through self-aggrandizing statements or comparing ourselves with people who we believe are worse.6,7,8 Any of these strategies may reestablish our self-integrity, but only temporarily—and they leave us vulnerable to more of the same kinds of threats.

This is where self-affirmation can change the story. Focusing on notable or valued aspects of the self that are not affected by the self-integrity threat bolsters our global sense of being “good enough”— protectively, if we self-affirm before we feel threatened, or restoratively, if we self-affirm afterward. It also makes all our defensive responses unnecessary, and in doing so promotes honest self-awareness and constructive responses to the challenges we face. Put simply, self-affirmation creates a protective buffer by putting the threat in perspective and helping us take a broader view of ourselves: Yes, I may have been wrong, made a bad decision, acted in a way I regret—but I’m a good and capable person, and my flaws and mistakes don’t define me.2,4,9.

The research on self-affirmation indicates how it benefits us in concrete ways. Self-affirmation increases our acceptance of information about risks to our health that would otherwise feel threatening.10,11,12 It increases our openness to evidence that challenges dearly held beliefs, and decreases our tendency to evaluate arguments for and against those beliefs in favor of what we already believe.13,14 It reduces the mental energy spent ruminating on failures and flaws and frees our mental resources for more productive activities, improving performance under stress on tasks that require focused attention, problem-solving, creativity, and insight.9,15,16,17 It increases our self-compassion and fosters helping behavior toward others.18.

Recent findings suggest that most broadly, self-affirmation activities have consistently been shown to enhance the well-being of those who engage in them:9 It improves the general sense of feeling good, of having community and belonging; it offers relief from symptoms like depression and anxiety that create barriers to well-being; and it improves one's sense that they are a person of competence and value. And just as in the case of the studies of women dissatisfied with their weight that we began with in Part 1, these effects on well-being are long-lasting and get larger with the passage of time.

Can self-affirmation make a difference for you? Here’s an activity that will allow you to experience it for yourself. (For the most meaningful experience, please have paper and pen ready. And please do each of these steps in turn, waiting until you’ve finished the one you’re doing to go on to the next, rather than reading ahead to the end.).

Recent findings suggest that 1. Think of an area of your life that you have been struggling with. It could be a behavior you’ve been trying to change, but have not changed; something you’ve been wanting to do, but have not done; a decision you’ve been trying to make, but have not made. Once you identify it, please spend the next minute just thinking about the struggle and what it has been like for you.

Recent findings suggest that 2. From the following list, please choose one value that a) is very important to you, and has been important in your life, b) is not related to the area of your life you have been struggling with.

It has been revealed that 3. Think of a time when the value you chose was notable to you. For the next few minutes, please write about that time and why that value was important to you.

Self-affirmation is most powerful when we’re facing a challenge of high personal importance, which is when our self-integrity is most likely to be threatened.19 Because self-affirmation works by focusing us on an aspect of ourselves that we feel good about and that does not feel threatened, it’s crucial to choose a value that’s unrelated to the challenge at hand; trying to affirm a threatened aspect of the self often makes us more defensive rather than less.19 And self-integrity is strengthened the most when we affirm “self-transcendent” values (values that express concern for others), rather than values that primarily benefit ourselves.4.

The positive effects of self-affirmation on how we feel and how we act reinforce a key tenet of motivational interviewing: we’re most likely to change and grow not when we feel sufficiently bad about ourselves, but when we feel accepted and valued.20 When you embark on a path toward change, don’t neglect to focus on what makes you worthy of value and respect just as you are.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday

What Else Is True?: Lessons About Suffering and Healing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • According to recent reports, twenty years ago, I helped establish a nonprofit organization called the Trauma Resource Institute.
  • Yet, amid the suffering and the heartache, I have encountered something else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

According to recent reports, twenty years ago, I helped establish a nonprofit organization called the Trauma Resource Institute. I could not have imagined where that decision would take me, the people I would meet, or how profoundly the journey would change my understanding of human suffering and resilience. My work has brought me into communities experiencing extraordinary adversity. I have witnessed the aftermath of natural disasters, the heartbreak of war and conflict, and the suffering of people whose lives have been disrupted by trauma, violence, and loss.

Yet, amid the suffering and the heartache, I have encountered something else. I have witnessed extraordinary courage, generosity, humor, creativity, kindness, and compassion. I have seen people reach toward one another as their own lives unraveled. I learned that suffering can profoundly alter the course of our lives, but suffering is never the only truth about who we are or what remains possible.

Recent findings suggest that throughout my work, I have returned again and again to a simple question:“What else is true?” When something terrible happens, what else is true? When we feel overwhelmed by loneliness, grief, or fear, what else is true? When the world seems divided or hopeless, what else is true? This question is not an invitation to deny suffering nor does it ask us to turn away from injustice, grief, trauma, or pain. Rather, it invites us to widen the lens through which we experience ourselves and the world.

According to recent reports, alongside fear, there may also be courage. Alongside grief, there may be love. Alongside helplessness, there may be one small place where choice still exists. And sometimes, amid tremendous suffering, hope begins to emerge. We can grieve and still experience gratitude. We can feel frightened and still recognize moments when we feel safer. The presence of suffering does not erase our capacity for well-being.

One of the most profound discoveries is that trauma is not only a cognitive or emotional experience. It is also physiological. Our nervous systems continually respond to what is happening around and within us. When we perceive danger, our bodies mobilize to protect us. Our hearts may race, our muscles tighten, or we may become numb or disconnected. These responses are not signs of weakness but reflect our biology working to help us survive. The body carries a wisdom that words alone cannot always express. Our nervous systems communicate distress and danger, but they can also register safety, connection, comfort, strength, and possibility.

The Trauma Resiliency Model (TRM) and Community Resiliency Model (CRM), approaches I developed, make knowledge about trauma and the nervous system accessible. Central to these models is body literacy: learning to recognize and understand the sensations through which our bodies communicate. People can begin to tell the difference between sensations of distress and well-being without judgment. Distress does not necessarily disappear, but it need not be the only experience available to us.

Recent findings suggest that as my understanding of trauma deepened, I began asking another question: What if knowledge about our nervous systems did not remain only within therapy rooms? This question flooded my waking moments: What if teachers, nurses, parents, children, first responders, and entire communities could learn simple skills to restore well-being?

These questions changed the direction of my life. I have watched people adapt CRM and TRM wellness skills for schools, hospitals, shelters, recovery programs, disaster response, and communities affected by war and other disasters. I have learned that resilience grows between us. Our nervous systems respond to the presence of others. A caring voice, a compassionate expression, or the steady presence of someone we trust may help us feel safer and more connected.

Industry observers note that I invite you to consider your own life's journey: Who or what has lifted you when you stumbled? Who or what reminded you of your worth when you doubted yourself? When loneliness or despair entered your life, who or what helped you reconnect with hope?

Recent findings suggest that as I reflect on this journey, I find myself increasingly drawn to the idea of human flourishing. Healing from trauma can open possibilities beyond the reduction of distress. As people experience greater safety and physiological regulation, there may be more room for curiosity, creativity, meaningful relationships, purpose, and joy.

Flourishing does not mean living without pain, nor is it an inevitable outcome of adversity. It is the possibility of living with greater meaning, connection, and agency while acknowledging life's complexities. Communities flourish when compassion becomes action, human dignity is protected, and people recognize their shared humanity.

Sources indicate that I no longer think of hope simply as optimism about the future. I understand it as an openness to possibility, even when we cannot predict what comes next. Hope may begin with an unexpected kindness, a moment of physiological steadiness, or discovering that we still have a choice. After twenty years, I continue returning to the question that has accompanied my journey: “What else is true?”.

Sometimes the answer is someone I love. Sometimes it is the generosity of a stranger, the beauty of nature, or the quiet recognition that my body can still experience peace in the midst of chaos. And sometimes the answer is simply that I do not yet know what else is possible.

Resilience reminds us that suffering never gets to tell the whole story. Within the human spirit, the wisdom of the body, and the connections we share, another truth may be waiting to be discovered—a possibility for connection, healing, and hope.

Sources indicate that I began this journey wanting to help people recover from trauma. Twenty years later, the people I have met have taught me something equally key: Even in a world filled with suffering, our capacity for compassion, connection, and hope remains one of the most remarkable expressions of our shared humanity, and it provides a pathway to healing. And fundamentally, the body has a wisdom that words cannot speak.

How Lead Exposure Erodes Long-Term Memory

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation.
  • Environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains.
  • Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation. The study reveals that lead disrupts oxidation-reduction balance inside neuronal mitochondria, shutting down the de novo protein synthesis needed to consolidate lasting memories, while showing that targeted antioxidants can restore memory function in fruit fly models.

Source: China Medical University.

Environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains. Yet despite decades of clinical observation, the precise molecular chain reaction through which lead disrupts memory storage inside individual neurons has remained elusive.

Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.

Published online on November 4, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study demonstrates that lead exposure hijacks mitochondrial redox homeostasis inside memory-consolidation neurons, starving the cell of the newly synthesized proteins required to lock short-term experiences into long-term memory.

To dissect how lead alters neural circuits without the confounding variables of mammalian systemic toxicity, the team turned to the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), a premier model organism whose memory-encoding circuits are mapped down to single identified neurons.

Behavioral assays revealed a striking dissociation:.

To observe what occurs inside the brain during memory consolidation, the researchers deployed genetically encoded redox biosensors paired with live fluorescence microscopy.

The imaging pinpointed a pair of dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, cells previously established by Chiang’s group as critical hubs for translating newly synthesized proteins during long-term memory formation. Within these DAL neurons, lead exposure severely disrupted redox homeostasis, tipping mitochondrial oxidation-reduction reactions into acute oxidative stress.

This mitochondrial redox imbalance directly suppressed de novo protein synthesis within the DAL neurons. Without fresh structural and synaptic proteins to remodel neural connections, newly formed memories failed to consolidate.

To verify whether mitochondrial oxidative stress was the primary driver of memory loss, and whether the deficit could be reversed, the investigators administered several antioxidant compounds to lead-exposed flies, including N-acetylcysteine (NAC), astaxanthin, resveratrol, and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a major catechin found in green tea.

Under controlled experimental conditions, these antioxidants significantly improved long-term memory performance. Deeper cellular imaging confirmed that EGCG reduced mitochondrial oxidative imbalance and restored normal protein synthesis inside the DAL neurons. Furthermore, administering either EGCG or the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO after a period of lead exposure restored the flies’ ability to form new long-term memories.

In a recent development, the authors emphasize that while these results demonstrate functional reversibility in fruit flies, they do not show the recovery of previously lost memories, nor do they establish that green tea or over-the-counter supplements can treat human lead poisoning. Further mammalian and clinical studies are necessary to determine whether targeting mitochondrial redox pathways can protect human cognition against heavy metal neurotoxicity.

How does lead exposure specifically affect memory?

In fruit fly experiments, researchers found that lead does not impair immediate learning or short-term memory. Instead, it selectively blocks the consolidation of long-term memories by preventing neurons from manufacturing the upcoming proteins needed to stabilize those memories.

What role do mitochondria play in lead-induced memory loss?

Mitochondria regulate cellular energy and oxidation-reduction (redox) balance. Lead causes oxidative stress inside the mitochondria of memory-consolidation neurons (specifically DAL neurons), which shuts down local protein synthesis and prevents long-term memory storage.

Can antioxidants reverse memory damage caused by lead?

In the fruit fly study, antioxidants such as EGCG (found in green tea), NAC, resveratrol, and mitochondria-targeted MitoTEMPO reduced mitochondrial stress, restored neuronal protein synthesis, and allowed lead-exposed flies to form upcoming long-term memories. However, researchers caution that more studies are needed before applying these findings to humans.

Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila.

Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood.

Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms.

Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation.

In a recent development, antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation.

Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.
